## The Matrix Factorization $A = C R$ and the Nullspace

This is our chance to complete Chapter 1. That chapter introduced the factorization $A = C R$ by small examples: We learned the meaning of independent columns, but we had no systematic way to find them. Now we have a way : Apply elimination to reduce A to $R _ { 0 }$ Then I in $\scriptstyle { \mathbf { } } _ { R _ { 0 } }$ locates the matrix C of independent columns in A. And removing any zero rows from $R _ { 0 }$ produces the row matrix R in $A = C R$

We find two special solutions ${ \pmb { \mathscr { s } } } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \pmb { \mathscr { s } } } _ { 2 }$ —one solution for every column of $\pmb { F }$ in R.

Example 2 again

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { R s _ { 1 } = 0 } & { { } \left[ \begin{array} { c c c c } { 1 } & { 7 } & { 0 } & { 8 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 9 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { c } { - 7 } \\ { 1 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}
$$

Put 1 and 0 in positions 2 and 4

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { R s _ { 2 } = 0 \ } &  { } \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 7 } & { 0 } & { 8 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 9 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { - 8 } \\ { \phantom { - } 0 } \\ { - 9 } \\ { 1 } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] \quad \begin{array} { l l l l } { \qquad \mathrm { P u t \ } 0 \ \mathrm { a n d \ } 1 } \\ { \mathrm { i n \ p o s i t i o n s \ 2 a n d \ } 4 } \end{array} \end{array}
$$

I think ${ \pmb s } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \pmb { \mathscr { s } } } _ { 2 }$ are easiest to see using the matrices -F and I and $P ^ { \mathrm { T } }$

The two special solutions to $\left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { I } & { F } \end{array} } \right] \pmb { x } = \mathbf { 0 }$ are the columns of $\left[ { - F } \right]$ in Example 1   
The special solutions to $\left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { I } & { F } \end{array} } \right] P x = 0$ are the columns of $P ^ { \mathrm { T } } \left[ { - F } _ { I } \right]$ in Example 2

The first one is easy because the permutation is $P = I$ The second one is correct because $P P ^ { \mathrm { { T } } }$ is the identity matrix for any permutation matrix $P$

$$
\begin{array} { r } { R x = 0 \qquad \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { I } & { F } \end{array} \right] P \mathrm { ~ t i m e s ~ } P ^ { \operatorname { T } } \left[ \begin{array} { c } { - F } \\ { I } \end{array} \right] \mathrm { ~ r e d u c e s ~ t o ~ } \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { I } & { F } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { c } { - F } \\ { I } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { 0 } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}
$$

Review Suppose the m by n matrix A has rank r. To find the $\pmb { n } - \pmb { r }$ special solutions to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ , compute the reduced row echelon form $R _ { 0 }$ of A. Remove the $m - r$ zero rows of $R _ { 0 }$ to produce $R = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { I } & { F } \end{array} \right] P$ and $A = C R$ . Then the special solutions to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ are the $\textit { \textbf { n } } - \textit { \textbf { r } }$ columns of $\bar { P ^ { \tilde { \operatorname { r } } } } \left[ \begin{array} { c } { - F } \\ { I } \end{array} \right]$ . Please see the last page of Chapter 3.

Example 3 Elimination on A gives $\scriptstyle { \mathbf { } } _ { \mathbf { } } { \mathbf { } } _ { \mathbf { } }$ and R. Then R reveals the nullspace of A.

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 1 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 } & { 5 } \\ { 3 } & { 6 } & { 9 } \end{array} \right] } \to { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 3 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 6 } \end{array} \right] } \to { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } = R _ { 0 } { \mathrm { ~ w i t h ~ r a n k ~ } } 2
$$

Then $\pmb { R } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { \mathbf { 1 } } & { \mathbf { 2 } } & { \mathbf { 0 } } \\ { \mathbf { 0 } } & { \mathbf { 0 } } & { \mathbf { 1 } } \end{array} \right]$ and the independent columns of A and $R _ { 0 }$ and R are 1 and 3.

To solve Ax = 0 and $R { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 } ,$ set ${ \pmb x } _ { 2 } = 1$ . Solve for $x _ { 1 } = - 2$ and $x _ { 3 } = 0$ Special solution $\pmb { \mathscr { s } } = \left( - 2 , 1 , 0 \right)$ . All solutions $\pmb { x } = \left( - 2 c , c , 0 \right)$ . And here is $A = C R$

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 1 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 } & { 5 } \\ { 3 } & { 6 } & { 9 } \end{array} \right] } = C R = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 1 } \\ { 2 } & { 5 } \\ { 3 } & { 9 } \end{array} \right] } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] } = { \pmod { \mathrm { u m n ~ b a s i s } } } { \mathrm { ( r o w ~ b a s i s ) } }
$$

Can you write each row of A as a combination of the rows of R? Yes. Just use $A = C R$ The three rows of A are the three rows of C times the two rows of R.

For many matrices, the only solution to ${ \pmb A } { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ is $\textbf { \em x } = \textbf { 0 }$ .The columns of A are independent. The nullspace $\mathbf { N } ( A )$ contains only the zero vector: no special solutions. The only combination of the columns that produces $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ is the zero combination $\pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$

This case of a zero nullspace Z is of the greatest importance. It says that the columns of A are independent. No combination of columns gives the zero vector (except x = 0). But this can't happen if $\pmb { n } > \pmb { m }$ We can't have n independent columns in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { m }$

Important Suppose A has more columns than rows. With n > m there is at least one free variable. The system $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ has at least one nonzero solution.

Suppose Ax = 0 has more unknowns than equations $( n > m )$ . There must be at least n − m free columns. Ax = 0 must have nonzero solutions in N(A).

The nullspace is a subspace. Its "dimension" is the number of free variables. This central idea—the dimension of a subspace—is explained in Section 3.5 of this chapter.

Example 4 Find the nullspaces of A, B, M and the two special solutions to $M \pmb { x } = \mathbf { 0 }$

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 3 } & { 8 } \end{array} \right] } B = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { A } \\ { 2 A } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 3 } & { 8 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 } \\ { 6 } & { 1 6 } \end{array} \right] } M = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { A } & { 2 A } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 2 } & { 4 } \\ { 3 } & { 8 } & { 6 } & { 1 6 } \end{array} \right] } .
$$

Solution The equation Ax = 0 has only the zero solution ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ . The nullspace is Z. It contains only the single point x = 0 in $\bar { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } }$ This fact comes from elimination :

$$
A x = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 3 } & { 8 } \end{array} \right] } \to { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] } \to { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] } = R = I
$$

No free variables, no F

A is invertible. There are no special solutions. Both columns of this matrix have pivots.

The rectangular matrix B has the same nullspace Z. The first two equations in $\pmb { B x = 0 }$ again require x = 0. The last two equations would also force ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ When we add extra equations (giving extra rows), the nullspace certainly cannot become larger. Extra rows impose more conditions on the vectors x in the nullspace.

The rectangular matrix M is different. It has extra columns instead of extra rows. The solution vector x has four components. Elimination will produce pivots in the first two columns of M. The last two columns of M are "free". They don't have pivots.

$$
M = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 2 } & { 4 } \\ { 3 } & { 8 } & { 6 } & { 1 6 } \end{array} \right] } \qquad R = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { 0 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { I } & { F } \end{array} \right] }
$$

For the free variables $\pmb { x _ { 3 } }$ and $\pmb { x _ { 4 } }$ , we make special choices of ones and zeros. First ${ \pmb x } _ { 3 } = 1$ $\pmb { x _ { 4 } } = \pmb { 0 }$ and second ${ x _ { 3 } = 0 , x _ { 4 } = 1 }$ . The pivot variables $\pmb { x _ { 1 } }$ and $\pmb { x _ { 2 } }$ are determined by the equation $R { \pmb x } = { \bf 0 }$ . We get two special solutions in the nullspace of $M$ . This is also the nullspace of R: elimination doesn't change solutions.

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \mathrm { S p e c i a l ~ s o l u t i o n s ~ t o ~ } } M x = 0 } \\ & { \qquad R = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { 0 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] } } \\ & { \qquad R s _ { 1 } = \mathbf { 0 } \ R s _ { 2 } = \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array} } \quad \quad s _ { 1 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { - 2 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 1 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] } { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } s _ { 2 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 0 } \\ { - 2 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 1 } \end{array} \right] } \ \gets \quad { \mathrm { v a r i a b l e s ~ } }
$$

## Block Elimination in Three Steps : Final Thoughts

The special value of matrix notation is to show the big picture. So far we have described elimination as it is usually executed, a column at a time. But if we work with blocks of the original A, then block elimination can be described in three quick steps. A has rank r.

Step 1 Exchange columns of A by $P _ { C }$ and exchange rows of A by $P _ { R }$ to put the r independent columns first and r independent rows first in $P _ { R } A P _ { C }$

$$
P _ { R } A P _ { C } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { W } & { H } \\ { J } & { K } \end{array} \right] \qquad C = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { W } \\ { J } \end{array} \right] \mathrm { a n d } B = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { W } & { H } \end{array} \right] \mathrm { h a v e ~ f u l l ~ r a n k ~ } r
$$

Step 2 Multiply the r top rows by $W ^ { - 1 }$ to produce $\operatorname { W } ^ { \ l - 1 } B = \left[ I \quad \operatorname { W } ^ { \ l - 1 } H \right] = \left[ I \quad F \right]$

Step 3 Subtract $\ J \left[ I \quad W ^ { - 1 } H \right]$ from the $m - r$ lower rows $\textstyle \left[ J \ K \right]$ to produce $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right]$

The result of Steps 1, 2, 3 is the reduced row echelon form $\scriptstyle { R _ { 0 } }$

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \boxed { P _ { R } A P _ { C } = [ \begin{array} { c c } { W } & { H } \\ { J } & { K } \end{array} ]  [ \begin{array} { c c } { I } & { W ^ { - 1 } H } \\ { J } & { K } \end{array} ]  [ \begin{array} { c c } { I } & { W ^ { - 1 } H } \\ { \mathbf { 0 } } & { \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array} ] = R _ { 0 } } } \end{array}\tag{1}
$$

There are two facts that need explanation. They led to Step 2 and Step 3 :

1. The r by r matrix W is invertible

2. The blocks satisfy $J W ^ { - 1 } H = K$

1. For the invertibility of W, we look back to the factorization $A = C R$ . Focusing on the r independent rows of A that go into B, this is $B = W R$ . Since B and R have rank r and W is r by r, W must have rank r and must be invertible.

2. We know that the first r rows $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { I } & { W ^ { - 1 } H } \end{array} \right]$ are linearly independent. Since A has rank r, the lower rows $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { J } & { K } \end{array} \right]$ must be combinations of those upper rows. The combinations must be given by J to get the first r columns correct: $J I \ = \ J$ Then J times $W ^ { - 1 } H$ must equal K to make the last columns correct.

The conclusion is that

$$
P _ { R } A P _ { C } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { { W } } \\ { { J } } \end{array} \right] \ W ^ { - 1 } \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { { W } } & { { H } } \end{array} \right] \ = C W ^ { - 1 } B
$$

We need that middle factor $W ^ { - 1 }$ because the columns C and the rows B both contain W.

## 3.3 The Complete Solution to $A { \pmb x } = { \pmb b }$

1 Complete solution to Ax = b: x = (one particular solution ${ \pmb x } _ { p } ) + ( \mathrm { { a n y } } \ { \pmb x } _ { n }$ in the nullspace).   
2 Elimination on Ax = b leads to R0x = d: Solvable when zero rows of $R _ { 0 }$ have zeros in d.   
3 When $R _ { 0 } \pmb { x } = \pmb { d }$ is solvable, one very particular solution $\pmb { x _ { p } }$ has all free variables equal to zero.   
4 A has full column rank r = n when its nullspace N(A) = zero vector: no free variables.   
5 A has full row rank r = m when its column space C(A) is Rⁿ : Ax = b is always solvable.

The last section totally solved Ax = 0. Elimination converted the problem to $R _ { 0 } { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 } .$ The free variables were given special values (one and zero). Then the pivot variables were found by back substitution. We paid no attention to the right side b because it stayed at zero. Then zero rows in $R _ { 0 }$ were no problem.

Now b is not zero. Row operations on the left side must act also on the right side. Ax = b is reduced to a simpler system $R _ { 0 } { \pmb x } = { \pmb d }$ with the same solutions (if any). One way to organize that is to add b as an extra column of the matrix. I will "augment" A with the right side $( b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } , b _ { 3 } ) = ( 1 , 6 , 7 )$ to produce the augmented matrix [ A b] :

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 0 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } \\ { 1 } & { 3 } & { 1 } & { 6 } \end{array} \right] } { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } } \\ { x _ { 3 } } \\ { x _ { 4 } } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 1 } \\ { 6 } \\ { 7 } \end{array} \right] } \quad \quad { \mathrm { h a s ~ t h e } } } \end{array} }
$$

$$
{ \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l l l } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } & { 6 } \\ { 1 } & { 3 } & { 1 } & { 6 } & { 7 } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { A } & { b } \end{array} \right] } .
$$

When we apply the usual elimination steps to A, reaching $R _ { 0 }$ , b turns into $\pmb { d } .$

In this example we subtract row 1 and row 2 from row 3. Elimination produces a row of zeros in $R _ { 0 }$ , and it changes $\pmb { b } = ( 1 , 6 , 7 )$ to a new right side $\pmb { d } = ( \mathbf { 1 } , \mathbf { 6 } , \mathbf { 0 } )$

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 0 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } } \\ { x _ { 3 } } \\ { x _ { 4 } } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 1 } \\ { 6 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] } { \mathrm { ~ u a t h e } } } \end{array} }
$$

$$
{ \begin{array} { r } { \left[ { \begin{array} { l l l l l l } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } & { 6 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} } \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { R _ { 0 } } & { d } \end{array} \right] } . } \end{array} 
$$

That very last row is crucial. The third equation has become 0 = 0. So the equations can be solved. In the original matrix A, the first row plus the second row equals the third row. To solve Ax = b, we need $b _ { 1 } + b _ { 2 } = b _ { 3 }$ on the right side too. The all-important property of b was 1 + 6 = 7. That led to ${ \boldsymbol { \mathsf { 0 } } } = { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { 0 } } }$ in the third equation. This was essential.

Here are the same augmented matrices for a general $\pmb { \ b } = ( b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } , b _ { 3 } )$

$$
{ \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { A } & { b } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l l } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { b _ { 1 } } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } & { b _ { 2 } } \\ { 1 } & { 3 } & { 1 } & { 6 } & { b _ { 3 } } \end{array} \right] } \longrightarrow { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l l } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { b _ { 1 } } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } & { b _ { 2 } } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { b _ { 3 } - b _ { 1 } - b _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { R _ { 0 } } & { d } \end{array} \right] }
$$

Now we get 0 = 0 in the third equation only if $b _ { 3 } - b _ { 1 } - b _ { 2 } = 0$ . This is $b _ { 1 } + b _ { 2 } = b _ { 3 }$

## One Particular Solution $\boldsymbol { A } \boldsymbol { x } _ { p } = \boldsymbol { b }$

For an easy solution $\pmb { x _ { p } } .$ , choose the free variables to be zero: $x _ { 2 } = x _ { 4 } = 0$ . Then the two nonzero equations give the two pivot variables $x _ { 1 } ~ = ~ 1$ and $\pmb { x _ { 3 } } \ = \ \pmb { 6 }$ Our particular solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ (and also $R _ { 0 } x = \mathbf { \delta } d )$ is ${ \pmb x } _ { p } = ( { \bf 1 } , { \bf 0 } , { \bf 6 } , { \bf 0 } )$ . This particular solution is my favorite: free variables = zero, pivot variables from d.

For a solution to exist, zero rows in $\scriptstyle { \mathbf { } } _ { \mathbf { } } { \mathbf { } } _ { 0 }$ must also be zero in d. Since I is in the pivot rows and pivot columns of $\mathbf { { \mathit { R } } _ { 0 } } ,$ the pivot variables in xparticular come from d :

$$
R _ { 0 } \pmb { x } _ { p } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { \mathbf { 1 } } & { 3 } & { \mathbf { 0 } } & { 2 } \\ { \mathbf { 0 } } & { 0 } & { \mathbf { 1 } } & { 4 } \\ { \mathbf { 0 } } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \mathbf { 1 } } \\ { \mathbf { 0 } } \\ { \mathbf { 6 } } \\ { \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \mathbf { 1 } } \\ { \mathbf { 6 } } \\ { \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array} \right] = d \qquad \begin{array} { l l l l } & { \mathrm { P i v o t ~ v a r i a b l e s ~ 1 , 6 } } \\ { \mathrm { F r e e ~ v a r i a b l e s ~ 0 , 0 } } \\ & { \mathbf { x _ { p a r t i c u l a r } = ( 1 , \mathbf { 0 } , \mathbf { 6 } , \mathbf { 0 } ) . } } \end{array}
$$

Notice how we choose the free variables (as zero) and then solve for the pivot variables. After the row reduction to $R _ { 0 }$ , those steps are quick. When the free variables are zero, the pivot variables for $\pmb { x _ { p } }$ are already seen in the right side vector d.

That particular solution is (1, 0, 6, 0). The $4 - 2$ special (nullspace) solutions came in Section 3.3 from the two free columns of $R _ { 0 }$ , by reversing signs of 3.2. and 4. Please notice how the complete solution ${ \pmb x } _ { p } + { \pmb x } _ { n }$ to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ includes all ${ \pmb x _ { n } }$

$$
\begin{array} { r l r l } & { \mathrm { C o m p l e t e ~ s o l u t i o n } } \\ & { \mathrm { o n e ~ } x _ { p } + \operatorname* { m a n y } x _ { n } } \\ & { \mathrm { p a r t i c u l a r } x _ { p } } \\ & { \mathrm { n u l l s p a c e ~ v e c t o r s } x _ { n } } \end{array} \quad  & &  x = x _ { p } + x _ { n } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 1 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 6 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] + x _ { 2 } \left[ \begin{array} { l } { - 3 } \\ { 1 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] + x _ { 4 } \left[ \begin{array} { l } { - 2 } \\ { 0 } \\ { - 4 } \\ { 1 } \end{array} \right] .
$$

Question Suppose A is a square invertible matrix, $m = n = r$ . What are $\pmb { x _ { p } }$ and ${ \pmb x } _ { n } \overset { \cdot } { . }$ Answer The particular solution is the one and only solution $\pmb { x _ { p } } = \pmb { A } ^ { - 1 } \pmb { b } .$ There are no special solutions or free variables. $R _ { 0 } ~ = ~ I$ has no zero rows. The only vector in the nullspace is $\pmb { x _ { n } = 0 }$ . The complete solution is $\pmb { x } = \pmb { x _ { p } } + \pmb { x _ { n } } = \pmb { A } ^ { - 1 } \pmb { b } + \pmb { 0 }$

We didn't mention the nullspace in Chapter 2, because A was invertible. A was reduced all the way to $I . \ [ A \ b \ b ]$ went to $\left[ I \ \right] \ A ^ { - 1 } \ b { \ b } \big ]$ . Then $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ became ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb A } ^ { - 1 } { \pmb b }$ which is d. This is a special case here, but square invertible matrices are the best. So they got their own chapter before this one.

For small examples we can reduce $[ A \ \pmb { b } ]$ to $[ R _ { 0 } \textbf { } d ]$ For a large matrix, MATLAB does it better. One particular solution (not necessarily ours) is $\textbf { \em x } = \textbf { \em A } \backslash \boldsymbol { b }$ from backslash. Here is an example with full column rank. Both columns have pivots.

Example 1 Find the condition on $\left( b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } , b _ { 3 } \right)$ for $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ to be solvable, if

$$
A = \left[ { \begin{array} { r r r } { 1 } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { - 2 } & { - 3 } \end{array} } \right] { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } b = \left[ { \begin{array} { r r r } { b _ { 1 } } \\ { b _ { 2 } } \\ { b _ { 3 } } \end{array} } \right] .
$$

Solution Elimination uses the augmented matrix $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \pmb { A } } & { \pmb { b } } \end{array} \right]$ with its extra column b. Subtract row 1 of $\left[ A \ b \right]$ from row 2. Then add 2 times row 1 to row 3 to reach $[ R _ { 0 } \textbf { } d ]$

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 1 } & { b _ { 1 } } \\ { 1 } & { 2 } & { b _ { 2 } } \\ { - 2 } & { - 3 } & { b _ { 3 } } \end{array} \right] \to \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 1 } & { b _ { 1 } } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { b _ { 2 } - b _ { 1 } } \\ { 0 } & { - 1 } & { b _ { 3 } + 2 b _ { 1 } } \end{array} \right] \to \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 0 } & { 2 b _ { 1 } - b _ { 2 } } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { b _ { 2 } - b _ { 1 } } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { b _ { 3 } + b _ { 1 } + b _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { R _ { 0 } } & { d } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}
$$

Equation 3 is ${ \bf 0 } = { \bf 0 }$ provided $b _ { 3 } + b _ { 1 } + b _ { 2 } = 0$ This is the condition to put b in the column space. Then $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ will be solvable. The rows of A add to the zero row. So for consistency (these are equations!) the entries of b must also add to zero.

This example has no free variables since $n - r = 2 - 2$ .Therefore no special solutions The nullspace solution is $\pmb { x _ { n } } = \pmb { 0 }$ The particular solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ and $R _ { 0 } { \pmb x } = { \pmb d }$ is at the top of the final column d:

r = n One solution to

$$
A x = b \qquad x = x _ { p } + x _ { n } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 2 b _ { 1 } - b _ { 2 } } \\ { b _ { 2 } - b _ { 1 } } \end{array} \right] } + { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] } .
$$

If $b _ { 3 } + b _ { 1 } + b _ { 2 }$ is not zero, there is no solution to $A x = b ( x _ { p }$ and x don't exist).

This example is typical of an extremely important case: A has full column rank. Every column has a pivot. The rank is $r = n$ . The matrix is tall and thin $( m \geq n )$ Row reduction puts $\boldsymbol { R } = \boldsymbol { I }$ at the top, when A is reduced to $R _ { 0 }$ with rank $\pmb { n }$

Full column rank

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } { r = n } & { { } R _ { 0 } = { \binom { I } { 0 } } = { \binom { n { \mathrm { ~ b y ~ } } n { \mathrm { ~ i d e n t i t y ~ m a t r i x } } } { m - n { \mathrm { ~ r o w s ~ o f ~ z e r o s ~ } } } } } \end{array} }\tag{1}
$$

This matrix A has independent columns. The nullspace of A is $\mathbf { Z } = \left\{ \mathsf { z e r o } \mathsf { v e c t o r } \right\}$

We will collect together the different ways of recognizing this type of matrix.

Every matrix A with full column rank $( { \pmb r } = { \pmb n } )$ has all these properties :

1. All columns of A are pivot columns (independent). No free variables.

2. The nullspace N(A) contains only the zero vector ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$

3. If Ax = b has a solution (it might not) then it has only one solution.

$\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ only happens when ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ .Later we will add one more fact to the list above: The square matrix $\overset { \cdot } { A ^ { \mathrm { T } } A }$ is invertible when the rank of A is n. A may have many rows.

In this case the nullspace of A has shrunk to the zero vector. The solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ is unique (if there is a solution). There will be ${ \pmb m } - { \pmb n }$ zero rows in $R _ { 0 }$ . So there are m – n conditions on b in order to have ${ \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { \mathbf { 0 } } } } } = { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { \mathbf { 0 } } } } }$ in those rows, and b in the column space. With full column rank, $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ will have one solution or no solution.

## Full Row Rank and the Complete Solution

The other extreme case is full row rank. Now Ax = b has one or infinitely many solutions In this case A must be short and wide $( m \leq n )$ . A matrix has full row rank if $\pmb { r } = \pmb { m }$ "The rows are independent." Every row has a pivot, and here is an example.

Example 2 This system Ax = b has $\pmb { n = 3 }$ unknowns but only ${ \pmb m } = 2$ equations:

Full row rank

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { x + y + z = 3 \quad } & { { } { \mathrm { ( r a n k ~ } } r = m = 2 { \mathrm { ) } } } \\ { x + 2 y - z = 4 \quad } & { { } { \mathrm { ( r a n k ~ } } r = m = 2 { \mathrm { ) } } } \end{array}
$$

These are two planes in $\pmb { x y z }$ space. The planes are not parallel so they intersect in a line. This line of solutions is exactly what elimination will find. The particular solution will be one point on the line. Adding the nullspace vectors ${ \pmb x _ { n } }$ will move us along the line in Figure 3.1. Then ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb x } _ { p } + \mathrm { { a l l } } { \pmb x } _ { n }$ gives the whole line of solutions.

We find x and $\pmb { x _ { p } }$ $\pmb { x _ { n } }$ by elimination downwards and then upwards on $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \boldsymbol { A } } & { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { \pmb { b } } } } \end{array} \right]$

\begin{array} { r } { [ \begin{array} { c c c c } { 1 } & { 1 } & { 1 } & { 3 } \\ { 1 } & { 2 } & { - 1 } & { 4 } \end{array} ]  [ \begin{array} { c c c c } { 1 } & { 1 } & { 1 } & { 3 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { - 2 } & { 1 } \end{array} ]  [ \begin{array} { c c c c } { 1 } & { 0 } & { 3 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { - 2 } & { 1 } \end{array} ] = [ \begin{array} { c c } { R } & { d } \end{array} ] . } \end{array}
$$

The particular solution $( 2 , 1 , 0 )$ has free variable ${ \pmb x } _ { 3 } = 0$ . It comes directly from d. The special solution s has ${ \pmb x } _ { 3 } = 1$ . Then $- { \pmb x } _ { 1 }$ and $- \pmb { x _ { 2 } }$ come from the free column of R.

It is wise to check that $\clubsuit$ and s satisfy the original equations $\mathbf { \nabla } A \mathbf { x } _ { p } = \mathbf { \nabla } \mathfrak { b }$ and $\pmb { A } \pmb { s } = \pmb { 0 }$

$$
\begin{array} { l c l } { { 2 + 1 } } & { { = } } & { { 3 } } \\ { { 2 + 2 } } & { { = } } & { { 4 } } \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array} { l c l } { { - 3 + 2 + 1 } } & { { = } } & { { 0 } } \\ { { - 3 + 4 - 1 } } & { { = } } & { { 0 } } \end{array}
$$

The nullspace solution $\pmb { x _ { n } }$ is any multiple of s. It moves along the line of solutions, starting at xparticular. Please notice again how to write the answer :

Complete solution

Particular + nullspace

$$
\pmb { x } = \pmb { x _ { p } } + \pmb { x _ { n } } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 2 } \\ { 1 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] + \pmb { x _ { 3 } } \left[ \begin{array} { l } { - 3 } \\ { 2 } \\ { 1 } \end{array} \right] .
$$

This line of solutions is drawn in Figure 3.1. Any point on the line could have been chosen as the particular solution. We chose $\pmb { x _ { p } }$ as the point with ${ \pmb x } _ { 3 } = { \bf 0 }$

The particular solution is not multiplied by an arbitrary constant !

Every matrix A with full row rank (r=m) has all these properties :   
1. All rows have pivots, and $\pmb { R _ { 0 } }$ has no zero rows : $\begin{array} { r } { R _ { 0 } = R . } \end{array}$   
2. Ax = b has a solution for every right side b.   
3. The column space of A is the whole space $\mathbf { R } ^ { m } .$   
4. If m < n the equation Ax = b is underdetermined (many solutions).

In this case with m pivots, the m rows are linearly independent. So the columns of $A ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } }$ are linearly independent. The nullspace of $A ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } }$ contains only the zero vector

The four possibilities for linear equations depend on the rank r

$$
{ \begin{array} { l l l l l l } { { \boldsymbol { r } } = m } & { { \mathrm { a n d } } } & { { \boldsymbol { r } } = n } & { S q u a r e a n d i n v e r i b l e } & { A x = b } & { { \mathrm { h a s ~ 1 ~ s o l u t i o n } } } \\ { { \boldsymbol { r } } = m } & { { \mathrm { a n d } } } & { { \boldsymbol { r } } < n } & { S h o r t a n d w i d e } & { A x = b } & { { \mathrm { h a s ~ \infty ~ s o l u t i o n s } } } \\ { { \boldsymbol { r } } < m } & { { \mathrm { a n d } } } & { { \boldsymbol { r } } = n } & { T a l l { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } t h i n } & { A x = b } & { { \mathrm { h a s ~ 0 ~ o r ~ 1 ~ s o l u t i o n } } } \\ { { \boldsymbol { r } } < m } & { { \mathrm { a n d } } } & { { \boldsymbol { r } } < n } & { N o t f u l l { \boldsymbol { r } } a n k } & { A x = b } & { { \mathrm { h a s ~ 0 ~ o r ~ \infty ~ s o l u t i o n s } } } \end{array} }
$$

The reduced $R _ { 0 }$ will fall in the same category as the matrix A. In case the pivot columns happen to come first, we can display these four possibilities. For $R _ { 0 } { \pmb x } = { \pmb d }$ and $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ to be solvable, d must end in $m - r$ zeros. F is the free part of $R _ { 0 }$

$$
{ \begin{array} { l c c c c c } { { \mathrm { F o u r ~ t y p e s ~ f o r ~ } } R _ { 0 } } & { } & { \left[ I \right] } & { } & { \left[ I \quad F \right] } & { } & { \left[ I ^ { I } \quad F \right] } \\ { { \mathrm { T h e i r ~ r a n k s } } } & { } & { r = m = n } & { r = m < n } & { r = n < m } & { r < m , r < n } \end{array} }
$$

Cases 1 and 2 have full row rank r = m. Cases 1 and 3 have full column rank $\pmb { r } = \pmb { n }$

To end this important section of the book, here is a note about computational linear algebra. Linear equations $A x = b$ are obviously fundamental. In practice, the steps of elimination are reordered for the sake of speed and numerical stability. We can solve systems of order 1000 on a laptop (allowing roundoff errors in single precision or double precision). Supercomputers can solve much larger systems. But there is a limit on the matrix size. What to do beyond that limit ?

The surprising answer is randomized linear algebra. We sample the columns of A. We accept the errors involved. In practice matrices are not completely random, and the final results are remarkably good. Often the approximation to A is expressed in the 3-factor form $\pmb { A } \approx \pmb { C } \pmb { M } \pmb { R } . \pmb { C }$ comes from sampling the columns of A and R comes from the rows of A.

The smaller mixing matrix M (sometimes called U) is constructed as we go. With high probability, the approximate solution is surprisingly accurate.

Linear algebra is alive. The demands of computation (speed and accuracy) lead to new ideas. The same will be true for eigenvalues and singular values—later in this book.

\begin{array} { r } { [ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 \ 2 \ 3 } & { 5 } & { \mathbf { b _ { 1 } } } \\ { 2 \ 4 \ 8 \ 1 2 \ \mathbf { b _ { 2 } } } \\ { 3 \ 6 \ 7 \ 1 3 \ \mathbf { b _ { 3 } } } \end{array} ]  [ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 3 } & { 5 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { - 2 } & { - 2 } \end{array} ] \mathbf { b _ { 2 } } - 2 \mathbf { b _ { 1 } } ]  [ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 3 } & { 5 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} ] \mathbf { b _ { 2 } } - 2 \mathbf { b _ { 1 } } } \end{array}

3. First description : The column space is the plane containing all combinations of the pivot columns (1, 2, 3) and (3, 8, 7). The pivots are in columns 1 and 3. All columns of A pass this test $b _ { 3 } + b _ { 2 } - 5 b _ { 1 } = 0$ . This is the equation for the plane in the first description !

3.3 B Suppose you have this information about the solutions to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ for a specific b.   
What does that tell you about m and n and r (and A itself)? And possibly about b.

1. There is exactly one solution

2. All solutions to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ have the form $\pmb { x } = \left[ \pmb { \imath } \mathbf { \imath } \right] + c \left[ \pmb { \imath } \right]$

3. There are no solutions.

4. All solutions to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ have the form $\pmb { x } = \left[ \pmb { 1 } \atop \pmb { 1 } \right] + c \left[ \pmb { 0 } \atop \pmb { 1 } \right]$

Solution In case 1, with exactly one solution, A must have full column rank $r = n$ The nullspace of A contains only the zero vector. And b is in the column space.

In case 2, A must have ${ \pmb n } = 2$ columns (and m is arbitrary). With [1] in the nullspace of A, column 2 is the negative of column 1. Also $A \neq 0 ;$ the rank is 1. With $\pmb { x } = \left[ \pmb { 2 } \right]$ as a solution, $\pmb { b } = 2 ( \mathsf { c o l u m } \ 1 ) + ( \mathsf { c o l u m n } \ 2 )$ . My choice for $\pmb { x _ { p } }$ would be $( 1 , 0 )$

In case 3 we only know that b is not in the column space of A. The rank of A must be less than m. I guess we know $\pmb { \theta } \neq \pmb { 0 }$ , otherwise ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ would be a solution.

In case 4, A must have $\pmb { n = 3 }$ columns. With (1, 0, 1) in the nullspace of A, column 3 of A is -(column 1). The rank is $3 - 1 = 2$ and b is column 1 + column 2.

3.3 C Find the complete solution ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb x } { \pmb p } + { \pmb x } { \pmb n }$ by forward elimination on $[ A \ b ]$

Solution Elimination leads us to $\pmb { R _ { 0 } x } = \pmb { d }$

$$
\left[ \begin{array} { r r r r r } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 1 } & { 0 } & { 4 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 } & { 4 } & { 8 } & { 2 } \\ { 4 } & { 8 } & { 6 } & { 8 } & { 1 0 } \end{array} \right] \longrightarrow \left[ \begin{array} { r r r r } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 1 } & { 0 } & { 4 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 2 } & { 8 } & { - 6 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] \longrightarrow \left[ \begin{array} { r r r r } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 0 } & { - 4 } & { 7 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } & { - 3 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] .
$$

For the nullspace part ${ \pmb x } _ { \pmb n }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { b } = \pmb { 0 } . } \end{array}$ , set the free variables $\pmb { x } _ { 2 } , \pmb { x } _ { 4 }$ to 1, 0 and also 0, 1 :

Special solutions $\pmb { \mathscr { s } } _ { 1 } = \left( - 2 , 1 , 0 , 0 \right)$ and $\pmb { \mathscr { s } } _ { 2 } = ( 4 , 0 , - 4 , 1 )$ Particular $\pmb { x _ { p } } = ( 7 , 0 , - 3 , 0 )$

Then the complete solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ is ${ \pmb x } _ { \mathrm { c o m p l e t e } } = { \pmb x } _ { { \pmb p } } + c _ { 1 } { \pmb s } _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } { \pmb s } _ { 2 }$

$$
2 ( \mathsf { r o w \ 1 } ) + ( \mathsf { r o w \ 2 } ) - ( \mathsf { r o w \ 3 } ) = ( 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 )
$$

The same combination for $\pmb { b } = ( 4 , 2 , 1 0 )$ gives $2 ( 4 ) + ( 2 ) - ( 1 0 ) = 0 .$

If a combination of the rows of A (on the left side) gives the zero row, then the same combination must give zero on the right side. Of course! Otherwise no solution.

We could say this again in different words: If every column of A is perpendicular to ${ \pmb y } = ( 2 , 1 , - 1 )$ , then any combination b of those columns must also be perpendicular to y. Otherwise b is not in the column space and $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ is not solvable.

And again: If y is in the nullspace of $\pmb { A } ^ { \pmb { \mathrm { T } } }$ then y must be perpendicular to every b in the column space of A.

## 3.4 Independence, Basis, and Dimension

```latex
1 Independent vectors: The only zero combination $c _ { 1 } v _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + c _ { k } v _ { k } = 0$ has all ${ \dot { \mathbf { c } } } { \mathbf { \acute { s } } } = \mathbf { 0 } .$
2 The vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { k }$ span the space S if S = all combinations of the $\pmb { v } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathrm { s } } .$
3 The vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { k }$ are a basis for S if (1) they are independent and (2) they span S.
4 The dimension of a vector space S is the number k of vectors in every basis for S.
```

This important section is about the true size of a subspace. There are n columns in an m by n matrix. But the true “dimension" of the column space is not necessarily n. The dimension of C(A) is measured by counting independent columns. We will see again that the true dimension of the column space is the rank r. This is partly review.

The idea of independence applies to any vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { n }$ in any vector space. Most of this section concentrates on the subspaces that we know and use—especially the column space and the nullspace of A. In the last part we also study “vectors" that are not column vectors. They can be matrices and functions; they can be linearly independent or dependent. First come the key examples using column vectors.

The goal is to understand a basis : independent vectors that “span the space"

Every vector in the space is a unique combination of the basis vectors.

We are at the heart of our subject, and we cannot go on without a basis. The four essential ideas in this section (with first hints at their meaning) are :

<table><tr><td>1. Independent vectors (no extra vectors)</td><td></td></tr><tr><td>2. Spanning a space</td><td>(enough vectors to produce the rest)</td></tr><tr><td>3. Basis for a space</td><td>(not too many and not too few)</td></tr><tr><td></td><td>4. Dimension of a space (the number of vectors in every basis)</td></tr></table>

## Linear Independence

Our first definition of independence is not so conventional, but you are ready for it.

DEFINITION The columns of A are linearly independent when the only solution to Ax = 0 is x = 0. No other combination Ax of the columns gives the zero vector.

The columns are independent when the nullspace N(A) contains only the zero vector. Let me illustrate linear independence (and dependence) with three vectors in ${ \mathbb { R } } ^ { 3 }$

1. If three vectors in ${ \mathbb R } ^ { 3 }$ are not in the same plane, those vectors are independent No combination of ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } , { \pmb v } _ { 2 } , { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ in Figure 3.2 gives zero except $0 { \pmb v } _ { 1 } + 0 { \pmb v } _ { 2 } + 0 { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$

2. If three vectors ${ \pmb w } _ { 1 } , { \pmb w } _ { 2 } , { \pmb w } _ { 3 }$ are in the same plane in ${ \mathbb R } ^ { 3 }$ , they are dependent.

![](images/d95124fc7bf3b87c61a810512b8fea046eac5085fa3a1d297d5a2784f95ca9c4.jpg)  
Figure 3.2: Independent : Only $0 { \pmb v } _ { 1 } + 0 { \pmb v } _ { 2 } + 0 { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ gives 0. Dependent : $\pmb { w } _ { 1 } - \pmb { w } _ { 2 } + \pmb { w } _ { 3 } = \pmb { 0 }$

This idea of independence applies to 7 vectors in 12-dimensional space. If they are the columns of $A ,$ and independent, the nullspace of the 12 by 7 matrix only contains ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 } .$ None of the column vectors is a combination of the other six vectors.

Now we choose different words to express the same idea in any vector space.

DEFINITION The sequence of vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { n }$ is linearly independent if the only combination that gives the zero vector is $0 { \pmb v } _ { 1 } + 0 { \pmb v } _ { 2 } + \dots + 0 { \pmb v } _ { n }$

Linear independence   
x1v1 + x2v2 + · . · + xnvn = 0 only happens when all $\pmb { x } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathsf { s } }$ are zero.

(1)

If a combination gives 0, when the $\pmb { x } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ are not all zero, the vectors are dependent.

```yaml
Correct language: "The sequence of vectors is linearly independent." Acceptable
shortcut: "The vectors are independent." Unacceptable: "The matrix is independent."
```

A sequence of vectors is either dependent or independent. They can be combined to give the zero vector (with nonzero ${ \pmb x } ^ { * } )$ or they can't. So the key question is: Which combinations of the vectors give zero? We begin with some small examples in ${ \mathbb { R } } ^ { 2 }$

(a) The vectors (1,0) and (1, 0.00001) are independent.

(b) The vectors (1, 1) and (−1, −1) are dependent.

(c) The vectors (1, 1) and (0, 0) are dependent because of the zero vector.

(d) In $\scriptstyle \mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ , any three vectors (a, b) and $( c , d )$ and $( e , f )$ are dependent.

Dependent columns x ≠ 0 in the nullspace

$$
\left[ { \begin{array} { r l } { 1 } & { - 1 } \\ { 1 } & { - 1 } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } } \end{array} } \right] = \left[ { \begin{array} { l } { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} } \right] \quad { \mathrm { f o r ~ } } x _ { 1 } = 1 { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } x _ { 2 } = 1 .
$$

Three vectors in $\scriptstyle \mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ cannot be independent! One way to see this : the matrix A with those three columns must have a free variable and then a special solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 } .$

Now move to three vectors in $\Re ^ { \mathfrak { s } }$ . If one of them is a multiple of another one, these vectors are dependent. But the complete test involves all three vectors at once. We put them in a matrix and try to solve $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$

Full column rank The columns of A are independent exactly when the rank is $\pmb { r } = \pmb { n } .$ There are n pivots and no free variables and $A = C$ Only ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ is in the nullspace.

One case is of special importance because it is clear from the start. Suppose seven columns have five components each $( m = 5$ is less than ${ \pmb n } = { \pmb 7 } )$ . Then the columns must be dependent. Any seven vectors from $\mathbf { R } ^ { 5 }$ are dependent. The rank of A cannot be larger than 5. There cannot be more than five pivots in five rows. $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ has at least ${ \boldsymbol { 7 } } - { \boldsymbol { 5 } } = 2$ free variables, so it has nonzero solutions—which means that the columns are dependent.

Any set of n vectors in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { m }$ must be linearly dependent if $n > m$

This type of matrix has more columns than rows—it is short and wide. The columns are certainly dependent if $\pmb { n } > m$ , because $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ has a nonzero solution.

The columns might be dependent or might be independent if $n \leq m$ . Elimination will reveal the r pivot columns. It is those r pivot columns that are independent in C.

Note Another way to describe linear dependence is this: “One vector is a combination of the other vectors." That sounds clear. Why don't we say this from the start? Our definition was longer: "Some combination gives the zero vector, other than the trivial combination with every $\pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 } . ^ { \prime \prime }$ We must rule out the easy way to get the zero vector.

The point is, our definition doesn't pick out one particular vector as guilty. All columns of A are treated the same. We look at $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ , and it has a nonzero solution or it hasn't.

## Vectors that Span a Subspace

The first subspace in this book was the column space. Starting with columns $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { \pmb { n } }$ $\mathbf { C } ( A )$ includes all combinations $x _ { 1 } { \pmb v } _ { 1 } + \dots + x _ { n } { \pmb v } _ { n }$ . The column space consists of all combinations Ax of the columns. The single word “span" describes $\mathbf { C } ( A )$

The columns of a matrix span its column space. They might be dependent.

Example 2 Describe the column space and the row space of A.

$$
{ \begin{array} { l l l } { m = 3 } & { } & { A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 4 } \\ { 2 } & { 7 } \\ { 3 } & { 5 } \end{array} \right] } { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } A ^ { \operatorname { T } } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 3 } \\ { 4 } & { 7 } & { 5 } \end{array} \right] } . } \end{array} }
$$

The column space of $\pmb { A }$ is the plane in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ spanned by the two columns of A. The row space of A is spanned by the three rows of A (which are columns of $A ^ { \mathrm { T } } )$ . This row space is all of ${ \mathbb R } ^ { 2 }$ . Remember: The rows are in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { \pmb { n } }$ spanning the row space. The columns are in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { m }$ spanning the column space. Same numbers, different vectors, different spaces.

A Basis for a Vector Space

Two vectors can't span all of $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ , even if they are independent. Four vectors can't be independent, even if they span $\Re ^ { 3 }$ .We want enough independent vectors to span the space (and not more). A “basis" is just right

DEFINITION A basis for a vector space is a sequence of vectors with two properties :

The basis vectors are linearly independent and they span the space.

This combination of properties is fundamental to linear algebra. Every vector v in the space is a combination of the basis vectors, because they span the space. More than that, the combination that produces v is unique, because the basis vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { n }$ are independent:

There is one and only one way to write v as a combination of the basis vectors.

Reason: Suppose ${ \pmb v } = { \pmb a } _ { 1 } { \pmb v } _ { 1 } + \cdots + { \pmb a } _ { n } { \pmb v } _ { n }$ and also $\pmb { v } = b _ { 1 } \pmb { v } _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + b _ { n } \pmb { v } _ { n }$ . By subtraction $( a _ { 1 } - b _ { 1 } ) { \pmb v } _ { 1 } + \dots + ( a _ { n } - b _ { n } ) { \pmb v } _ { n }$ is the zero vector. From the independence of the $\pmb { v } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \ S } ,$ each $a _ { i } - b _ { i } = 0$ . Hence $a _ { i } = b _ { i }$ , and there are not two ways to produce v.

Example 3 The columns of $I = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] }$ produce the “standard basis"for $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$

The basis vectors $\ i = { \binom { 1 } { 0 } }$ and $\pmb { j = \left[ 0 \atop 1 \right] }$ are independent. They span ${ \mathbb { R } } ^ { 2 }$

Everybody thinks of this basis first. The vector i goes across and $\pmb { j }$ goes straight up. The columns of the n by n identity matrix give the “standard basis" for $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { \pmb { n } }$

Now we find many other bases (infinitely many). The basis is not unique!

Example 4 (Important) The columns of every invertible n by n matrix give a basis for $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$

Invertible matrix Independent columns Column space = R³

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { 1 } & { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 1 } & { 1 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] }
$$

Singular matrix Dependent columns Column space $\neq \mathbf { R } ^ { 3 }$

$$
B = \left[ { \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 1 } & { 1 } & { 2 } \end{array} } \right]
$$

The only solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ is $\pmb { x } = \pmb { A } ^ { - 1 } \pmb { 0 } = \pmb { 0 }$ . The columns are independent. They span the whole space $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ —because every vector b is a combination of the columns. $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ can always be solved by ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb A } ^ { - 1 } { \pmb b } .$ Do you see how everything comes together for invertible matrices? Here it is in one sentence :

The vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { n }$ are a basis for $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ exactly when they are the columns of an n by n invertible matrix. $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ has infinitely many different bases.

When the columns are dependent, we keep only the pivot columns—the first two columns of B above. Those two columns are independent and they span the column space.

Every set of independent vectors can be extended to a basis.   
Every spanning set of vectors can be reduced to a basis.

Example 5 This matrix is not invertible. Its columns are not a basis for anything!

One pivot column One pivot row $( r = 1 )$

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 2 } & { 4 } \\ { 3 } & { 6 } \end{array} \right] }
$$

$$
R _ { 0 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] }
$$

Example 6 Find bases for the column and row spaces of this rank two matrix :

$$
R _ { 0 } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 1 } & { 2 } & { 0 } & { 3 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 4 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] .
$$

Columns 1 and 3 are the pivot columns. They are a basis for the column space of $R _ { 0 }$ The column space is the $\ " { } x y$ plane" inside xyz space ${ \pmb R } ^ { 3 }$ . That plane is not ${  { \mathbb { R } } } ^ { 2 }$ , it is a subspace of ${ \bar { \mathbf { R } } } ^ { \mathbf { \bar { 3 } } }$ . Columns 2 and 3 are also a basis for the same column space. Which pair of columns of $R _ { 0 }$ is not a basis for its column space ?

The row space is a subspace of $\mathbb { R } ^ { 4 }$ . The simplest basis for that row space is the two nonzero rows of $R _ { 0 }$ . The zero vector is never in a basis.

Question Given five vectors in ${ \pmb R } ^ { 7 }$ , how do you find a basis for the space they span?

First answer Make them the rows of A, and eliminate to find the nonzero rows in R. Second answer Put the five vectors into the columns of A. Eliminate to find the pivot columns. Those pivot columns in $c$ are a basis for the column space.

Could another basis have more vectors, or fewer? This is a crucial question with a good answer : No. All bases for a vector space contain the same number of vectors.

The number of vectors in any and every basis is the "dimension" of the space.

## Dimension of a Vector Space

We have to prove what was just stated. There are many choices for the basis vectors, but the number of basis vectors doesn't change.

$\mathbb { \mathbf { I f } } \pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \dots , \pmb { v } _ { m }$ and $\pmb { w } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { w } _ { n }$ are both bases for the same vector space, then ${ \pmb m } = { \pmb n } .$

Proof Suppose that there are more $\pmb { w } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ than $\pmb { v } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathbb { s } } .$ From $\textbf { \em n } > \textbf { \em m }$ we want to reach a contradiction. The $\pmb { v } \mathbf { \hat { s } }$ are a basis, so each w must be a combination of the ${ \pmb v } ^ { \prime } { \pmb s }$ . If ${ \pmb w } _ { 1 }$ equals $\pmb { a } _ { 1 1 } \pmb { v } _ { 1 } + \cdots + \pmb { a } _ { m 1 } \pmb { v } _ { m }$ , this is the first column of a matrix multiplication $V A = W$

Each w is a combination of the ${ \pmb v } ^ { \prime } { \pmb s }$

$$
W = \left[ \pmb { w } _ { 1 } \pmb { w } _ { 2 } \dots \pmb { w } _ { n } \right] = \left[ \pmb { v } _ { 1 } \dots \pmb { v } _ { m } \right] \left[ \begin{array} { c c c } { a _ { 1 1 } } & & { a _ { 1 n } } \\ { \vdots } & & { \vdots } \\ { a _ { m 1 } } & & { a _ { m n } } \end{array} \right] = V \pmb { A } .
$$

We don't know each ${ \pmb a } _ { \mathbf { i } \mathbf { j } }$ , but we know the shape of A (it is m by n). The second vector ${ \pmb w } _ { 2 }$ is also a combination of the $\clubsuit 3 .$ The coefficients in that combination fill the second column of A. The key is that A has a row for every v and a column for every w. A is a short wide matrix, since we assumed $\pmb { n } > \pmb { m } ,$ So $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ has a nonzero solution.

$\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ gives $V A x = \mathbf { 0 }$ which is ${ \pmb W } { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 } .$ A combination of the $\pmb { w } ^ { \prime } \pmb { s }$ gives zero! Then the $\pmb { w } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ could not be a basis—our assumption $\pmb { n } > m$ is not possible for two bases.

If $\textbf { \em m } > \pmb { n }$ we exchange the $\pmb { v } \mathbf { \hat { s } }$ and $\pmb { w } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ and repeat the same steps. The only way to avoid a contradiction is to have ${ \pmb m } = { \pmb n }$ . This completes the proof that $m = n$

The number of basis vectors is the dimension. So the dimension of $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { n }$ is $\pmb { n } .$ We now define the important word dimension.

DEFINITION The dimension of a space is the number of vectors in every basis.

The dimension matches our intuition. The line through $\pmb { v } = ( 1 , 5 , 2 )$ has dimension one. It is a subspace with this one vector v in its basis. Perpendicular to that line is the plane $x + 5 y + 2 z = 0$ . This plane has dimension 2. To prove it, we find a basis $( - 5 , 1 , 0 )$ and $( - 2 , 0 , 1 )$ . The dimension is 2 because the basis contains two vectors.

The plane is the nullspace of the matrix $\pmb { A } = \left[ \pmb { 1 } \ \textbf { 5 } \ \pmb { 2 } \right]$ , which has two free variables. Our basis vectors $( - 5 , 1 , 0 )$ and $( - 2 , 0 , 1 )$ are the “special solutions" to $\begin{array} { l } { \pmb { A } \pmb { x } } \ = \ \pmb { 0 } .  \end{array}$ The $\pmb { n } - \pmb { r }$ special solutions always give a basis for the nullspace: dimension $\pmb { n } - \pmb { r }$

## Bases for Matrix Spaces and Function Spaces

The words “independence" and “basis" and “dimension" are not limited to column vectors. We can ask whether three matrices $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , A _ { 3 }$ are independent. When they are 3 by 4 matrices, some combination might give the zero matrix. We can also ask the dimension of the full 3 by 4 matrix space. (That dimension is 12. Twelve matrices in every basis.)

In differential equations, $d ^ { 2 } y / d x ^ { 2 } = y$ has a space of solutions. One basis is $\pmb { y } = \pmb { e } ^ { \pmb { x } }$ and $y = e ^ { - { \pmb x } }$ . Counting the basis functions gives the dimension 2 for this solution space. (The dimension is 2 because the linear equation starts with the second derivative.)

Matrix spaces The vector space M contains all 2 by 2 matrices. Its dimension is 4.

One basis is

$$
A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , A _ { 3 } , A _ { 4 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \mathbf { 1 } } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } , { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { \mathbf { 1 } } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } , { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { \mathbf { 1 } } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } , { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { \mathbf { 1 } } \end{array} \right] } .
$$

Those matrices are linearly independent. We are not looking at their columns, but at the whole matrix. Combinations of those four matrices can produce any matrix in M.

Every A combines

the basis matrices

$$
c _ { 1 } A _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } A _ { 2 } + c _ { 3 } A _ { 3 } + c _ { 4 } A _ { 4 } = { \binom { c _ { 1 } } { c _ { 3 } } } \ c _ { 2 } { \Bigg ] } = A .
$$

A is zero only if the $\pmb { c } \mathbf { \ ' } _ { \pmb { s } }$ are all zero—this proves independence of $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , A _ { 3 } , A _ { 4 }$

The three matrices $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , A _ { 4 }$ are a basis for a subspace—the upper triangular matrices. Its dimension is 3. $A _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 4 }$ are a basis for the diagonal matrices. What is a basis for the symmetric matrices? Keep $A _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 4 }$ , and throw in $A _ { 2 } + A _ { 3 }$

The dimension of the whole n by n matrix space is $n ^ { 2 }$

The dimension of the subspace of upper triangular matrices is ${ \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } n ^ { 2 } + { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } n$

The dimension of the subspace of diagonal matrices is n.

The dimension of the subspace of symmetric matrices is ${ \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } n ^ { 2 } + { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } n ( { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { w } } } { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { h } } } y ? )$

Function spaces The equations $d ^ { 2 } y / d x ^ { 2 } = 0$ and $d ^ { 2 } y / d x ^ { 2 } = - y$ and $d ^ { 2 } y / d x ^ { 2 } = y$ involve the second derivative. In calculus we solve to find the functions ${ \pmb y } ( { \pmb x } )$

y″ = 0 is solved by any linear function $y = c x + d$

y" = -y is solved by any combination $y = c \sin x + d$ cos x

y″ = y is solved by any combination $\pmb { y } = c e ^ { \pmb { x } } + d e ^ { - \pmb { x } }$

That solution space for ${ \boldsymbol { y } } ^ { \prime \prime } = - { \boldsymbol { y } }$ has two basis functions: sin x and cos x. The space for ${ \pmb y } ^ { \prime \prime } = { \bf 0 }$ has x and 1. It is the “nullspace" of the second derivative! The dimension is 2 in each case (these are second-order equations).

The solutions of $y ^ { \prime \prime } = 2$ don't form a subspace—the right side ${ \pmb { b } } = { \pmb { 2 } }$ is not zero. A particular solution is $\begin{array} { r } { y ( x ) = x ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . The complete solution is $y ( x ) = x ^ { 2 } + c x + d .$ All those functions satisfy $\pmb { y } ^ { \prime \prime } = \pmb { 2 }$ . Notice the particular solution plus any function $c x + d$ in the nullspace. A linear differential equation is like a linear matrix equation $\mathbf { { \pmb A } } \mathbf { { \pmb x } } = \mathbf { { \pmb b } } .$

We end here with the space Z that contains only the zero vector. The dimension of this space is zero. The empty set (containing no vectors) is a basis for Z. We can never allow the zero vector into a basis, because then linear independence is lost.

The key words in this section were independence, span, basis, dimension.

1. The columns of A are independent if ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ is the only solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$

2. The vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { r }$ span a space if their combinations fill that space.

3. A basis consists of linearly independent vectors that span the space. Every vector in the space is a unique combination of the basis vectors.

4. All bases for a space have the same number of vectors. This number of vectors in a basis is the dimension of the space.

5. The pivot columns are one basis for the column space. The dimension of $\mathbf { C } ( A )$ is r.

## WORKED EXAMPLES

3.4 A (Important example) Suppose $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { n }$ is a basis for $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ and the n by n matrix A is invertible. Show that $A v _ { 1 } , \ldots , A v _ { n }$ is also a basis for $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$

Solution In matrix language: Put the basis vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { n }$ in the columns of an invertible (!) matrix V. Then $A v _ { 1 } , \ldots , A v _ { n }$ are the columns of AV. Since A is invertible, so is AV. Its columns give a basis.

In vector language: Suppose $c _ { 1 } A v _ { 1 } + \cdots + c _ { n } A v _ { n } = 0$ This is ${ \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla \ m } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla \nabla } { \bf \nabla \ m }  { \bf \nabla \nabla \ m } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \nabla \ m } { \bf \nabla } { \bf \bf \nabla } { \bf \ m }  { \bf \bf \nabla \nabla \nabla } { \bf \ m } { \bf \ m \ m } { \ m } { \bf \ m \ m }  \ m { \bf \ m \ m } { \ m \ m } { \ m \ m \ m } { \ m \ m }  { \bf \ m \ m \ m } { \ m \ m \ m } { \ m \ m }  { \bf \ m \ m \ m \ m } { \ m \ m \ m }  \ m { \ m \ m \ m } { \ m \ m \ m }  \ m \ m { \ m \ m } { \ m \ m \ m } { { \ m \ m \ m \ m \ m } { \ m \ m \ m } { \ m \ m \ m } { { \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n } { \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n } \ c o n { \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n } \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n { \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n } \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n \ c o n m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m } }  { } { { \ c o n } { \ c o n \ c o n m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m m } \ c o n }  m m m m m m m m$ with $\pmb { v } = c _ { 1 } \pmb { v } _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + c _ { n } \pmb { v } _ { n }$ . Multiply by $A ^ { - 1 }$ to reach ${ \pmb v } = { \bf 0 }$ . By linear independence of the ${ \pmb v } ^ { \prime } { \pmb s } ,$ all $\pmb { c } _ { i } = \pmb { 0 } .$ This shows that the $\pmb { A } \pmb { v } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathsf { s } }$ are independent.

To show that the $\pmb { A } \pmb { v } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathsf { s } }$ span $\pmb { R } ^ { n }$ , solve $c _ { 1 } A v _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + c _ { n } A v _ { n } = b$ which is the same as $c _ { 1 } \pmb { v } _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + c _ { n } \pmb { v } _ { n } = A ^ { - 1 } \pmb { b } .$ Since the v's are a basis, this must be solvable.

3.4 B Start with the vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } = ( 1 , 2 , 0 )$ and $\pmb { v } _ { 2 } = ( 2 , 3 , 0 )$ (a) Are they linearly independent ? (b) Are they a basis for any space V ? (c) What is the dimension of V? (d) Which matrices A have V as their column space ? (e) Which matrices have V as their nullspace? (f) Describe all vectors ${ \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ that complete a basis ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } , { \pmb v } _ { 2 } , { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ for $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$

Solution

(a) ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \pmb v } _ { 2 }$ are independent—the only combination to give 0 is $\mathbf { 0 } v _ { 1 } + \mathbf { 0 } v _ { 2 }$

(b) Yes, they are a basis for the space V that they span : All vectors $( { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } , { \pmb 0 } )$

(c) The dimension of V is 2 since the basis contains two vectors.

(d) This V is the column space of any 3 by n matrix A of rank 2, if every column is a combination of ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \pmb v } _ { 2 }$ . In particular A could just have columns ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \pmb v } _ { 2 }$

(e) This V is the nullspace of any m by 3 matrix B of rank 1, if every row is a multiple of $( \mathbf { 0 } , \mathbf { 0 } , 1 )$ . In particular take $B = \left[ 0 \ 0 \ 1 \right]$ . Then $B { \pmb v } _ { 1 } = { \pmb 0 }$ and $B { \pmb v } _ { 2 } = { \pmb 0 }$

(f) Any third vector $v _ { 3 } = \left( a , b , c \right)$ will complete a basis for $\Re ^ { 3 }$ provided $c \neq 0$

3.4 C Start with three independent vectors ${ \pmb w } _ { 1 } , { \pmb w } _ { 2 } , { \pmb w } _ { 3 }$ . Take combinations of those vectors to produce ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } , { \pmb v } _ { 2 } , { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ . Write the combinations in matrix form as $V = W B$

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l r l } & { } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 1 } = \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 1 } + \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 2 } } \\ & { } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 2 } = \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 1 } + 2 \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 2 } + \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 3 } \quad { \mathrm { ~ w h i c h ~ i s ~ } } } \\ & { } & { { \boldsymbol { v } } _ { 3 } = \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 2 } + c \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 3 } } \end{array} } { \mathrm { ~ w h i c h ~ i s ~ } } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 1 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 2 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 3 } } \\ { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 1 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 2 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { v } } } _ { 3 } } \\ { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 1 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 2 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 3 } } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 1 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 2 } } & { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 3 } } \\ { \mathbf { { \boldsymbol { w } } } _ { 2 } } & { 1 } & { c } \end{array} \right] }
$$

What is the test on B to see if $V \ : = \ : W B$ has independent columns? If $c \neq 1$ show that ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } , { \pmb v } _ { 2 } , { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ are linearly independent. If $\pmb { c } = 1$ show that the ${ \pmb v } ^ { \prime } { \pmb s }$ are linearly dependent.

Solution For independent columns, the nullspace of V must contain only the zero vector. $V { \pmb x } = 0$ requires ${ \pmb x } = ( \mathbf 0 , \mathbf 0 , \mathbf 0 )$

If $\pmb { c } = \pmb { 1 }$ in our problem, we can see dependence in two ways. First, ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } + { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ will be the same as ${ \pmb v } _ { 2 }$ . Then ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } - { \pmb v } _ { 2 } + { \pmb v } _ { 3 } = { \pmb 0 }$ —which says that the $\pmb { v } \mathbf { \hat { s } }$ are dependent.

The other way is to look at the nullspace of B. If $c = 1$ , the vector ${ \pmb x } = ( 1 , - 1 , 1 )$ is in that nullspace, and $\pmb { B x = 0 }$ .Then certainly $W B { \pmb x } = { \bf 0 }$ which is the same as $V { \pmb x } = 0$ So the ${ \pmb v } ^ { \prime } { \pmb s }$ are dependent : ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } - { \pmb v } _ { 2 } + { \pmb v } _ { 3 } = { \pmb 0 }$

Now suppose c ≠ 1. Then the matrix B is invertible. So if x is any nonzero vector we know that Bx is nonzero. Since the $\pmb { w } ^ { \prime } \pmb { s }$ are given as independent, we further know that W Bx is nonzero. Since $V = W B$ , this says that x is not in the nullspace of $V$ In other words ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 } , { \pmb v } _ { 2 } , { \pmb v } _ { 3 }$ are independent.

The general rule is “independent ${ \pmb v } ^ { \prime } { \pmb s }$ from independent $\pmb { w } ^ { \prime } \pmb { s }$ when B is invertible". And if these vectors are in ${ \pmb R } ^ { 3 }$ , they are not only independent—they are a basis for $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { 3 }$ "Basis of v's from basis of w's when the change of basis matrix B is invertible."

## 3.5 Dimensions of the Four Subspaces

1 The column space $\mathbf { C } ( A )$ and the row space $\mathbf { C } ( A ^ { \mathrm { T } } )$ both have dimension r (the rank of A).   
2 The nullspace $\mathbf { N } ( A )$ has dimension $\mathbf { \nabla } \pmb { n } - \pmb { r } .$ The left nullspace $ { \mathbf { N } } ( A ^ {  { \mathbf { T } } } )$ has dimension $m - r .$   
3 Elimination from A to $R _ { 0 }$ changes $\mathbf { C } ( A )$ and $ { \mathbf { N } } ( A ^ {  { \mathbf { T } } } )$ (but their dimensions don't change).

The main theorem in this chapter connects rank and dimension. The rank of a matrix counts independent columns. The dimension of a subspace is the number of vectors in a basis. We can count pivots or basis vectors. The rank of A reveals the dimensions of all four fundamental subspaces. Here are the subspaces, including the new one.

Two subspaces come directly from A, and the other two come from $A ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } }$

Four Fundamental Subspaces Dimensions   
1. The row space is $\mathbf { C } ( A ^ { \mathrm { T } } )$ , a subspace of $\mathbf { R } ^ { n } .$ r   
2. The column space is $\mathbf { C } ( A )$ , a subspace of $\mathbf { R } ^ { m }$ r   
3. The nullspace is $\mathbf { N } ( A )$ , a subspace of $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ n−r   
4. The left nullspace is $ { \mathbf { N } } ( A ^ { \mathrm { T } } )$ , a subspace of $\mathbf { R } ^ { m }$ m − r

We know $\mathbf { C } ( A )$ and $\mathbf { N } ( A )$ pretty well. Now $\mathbf { C } ( A ^ { \mathrm { T } } )$ and $ { \mathbf { N } } ( A ^ {  { \mathbf { T } } } )$ come forward. The row space contains all combinations of the rows. This row space is the column space of $A ^ { \mathrm { T } }$

For the left nullspace we solve $\pmb { A } ^ { \dagger } \pmb { y } = \pmb { 0 }$ —that system is n by m. In Example 2 this produces one of the great equations of applied mathematics—Kirchhoff's Current Law. The currents flow around a network, and they can't pile up at the nodes. The matrix A is the incidence matrix of a graph. Its four subspaces come from nodes and edges and loops and trees. Those subspaces are connected in an absolutely beautiful way.

Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem finds the dimensions of the four subspaces. One fact stands out: The row space and column space have the same dimension r. This number r is the rank of A (Chapter 1). The other important fact involves the two nullspaces :

N(A) and $ { \mathbf { N } } ( A ^ {  { \mathbf { T } } } )$ have dimensions n — r and $m - r ,$ to make up the full n and m.

Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem will describe how the four subspaces fit together : Nullspace perpendicular to row space, and $\mathbf { N } ( A ^ { \mathrm { T } } )$ perpendicular to $\mathbf { C } ( A )$ . That completes the “right way" to understand $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ . Stay with it—you are doing real mathematics.

The Four Subspaces for $\mathbf { R _ { 0 } }$

Suppose A is reduced to its row echelon form $R _ { 0 }$ . For that special form, the four subspaces are easy to identify. We will find a basis for each subspace and check its dimension. Then we watch how the subspaces change (two of them don't change!) as we look back at A. The main point is that the four dimensions are the same for A and $\mathbf { { \mathit { R } } _ { 0 } }$

For A and R, one of the four subspaces can have different dimensions—because zero rows are removed in R, which changes m

As a specific 3 by 5 example, look at the four subspaces for this echelon matrix $R _ { 0 }$ ••

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } { m = 3 } & { { } } & { { } } \\ { n = 5 } & { { } } & { { } { \cal R } _ { 0 } = \left[ 0 \begin{array} { c c c c c } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 5 } & { 0 } & { 7 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}
$$

pivot rows 1 and 2

pivot columns 1 and 4

The rank of this matrix is r = 2 (two pivots). Take the four subspaces in order.

1. The row space has dimension 2, matching the rank.

Reason : The first two rows are a basis. The row space contains combinations of all three rows, but the third row (the zero row) adds nothing to the row space.

The pivot rows 1 and 2 are independent. That is obvious for this example, and it is always true. If we look only at the pivot columns, we see the r by r identity matrix. There is no way to combine its rows to give the zero row (except by the combination with all coefficients zero). So the r pivot rows (the rows of R) are a basis for the row space.

The dimension of the row space is the rank r. The nonzero rows of $\mathbf { { \mathit { R } } _ { 0 } }$ form a basis.

2. The column space of $R _ { 0 }$ also has dimension $\pmb { r } = 2 .$

Reason: The pivot columns 1 and 4 form a basis. They are independent because they contain the r by r identity matrix. No combination of those pivot columns can give the zero column (except the combination with all coefficients zero). And they also span the column space. Every other (free) column is a combination of the pivot columns. Actually the combinations we need are the three special solutions!

Column 2 is 3 (column 1). The special solution is $( - 3 , 1 , 0 , 0 , 0 )$

Column 3 is 5 (column 1). The special solution is $( - 5 , 0 , 1 , 0 , 0 , )$

Column 5 is 7 (column 1) + 2 (column 4). That solution is $( - 7 , 0 , 0 , - 2 , 1 )$

The pivot columns are independent, and they span $\mathbf { C } ( R _ { 0 } )$ , so they are a basis for $\mathbf { C } ( R _ { 0 } )$

The dimension of the column space is the rank r. The pivot columns form a basis.

3. The nullspace of $R _ { 0 }$ has dimension $\pmb { n } - \pmb { r } = \pmb { 5 } - \pmb { 2 }$ The 3 free variables give 3 special solutions to $R _ { 0 } { \pmb x } = \mathbf { 0 }$ . Set the free variables to 1 and 0 and 0.

$$
\begin{array} { r } { s _ { 2 } = \left[ \begin{array} { r } { - 3 } \\ { 1 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] \quad s _ { 3 } = \left[ \begin{array} { r } { - 5 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 1 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] \quad s _ { 5 } = \left[ \begin{array} { r } { - 7 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \\ { - 2 } \\ { 1 } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \cal R } _ { 0 } { \pmb x } = 0 \mathrm { ~ h a s ~ t h e } \qquad } \\ { \mathrm { c o m p l e t e ~ s o l u t i o n } \qquad } \\ { { \pmb x } = x _ { 2 } { \pmb s } _ { 2 } + x _ { 3 } { \pmb s } _ { 3 } + x _ { 5 } { \pmb s } _ { 5 } \qquad } \\ { \mathrm { T h e ~ n u l l s p a c e ~ h a s ~ d i m e n s i o n } 3 . } \end{array}
$$

Reason : There is a special solution for each free variable. With n variables and r pivots, that leaves $\boldsymbol { n } - \boldsymbol { r }$ free variables and special solutions. The special solutions are independent, because you can see the identity matrix in rows 2, 3, 5.

The nullspace $\mathbf { N } ( A )$ has dimension $\mathbf { \nabla } \pmb { n } - \pmb { r } .$ The special solutions form a basis.

4. The nullspace of ${ R } _ { \mathbf { 0 } } ^ { \mathbf { T } }$ (left nullspace of $\pmb { R _ { 0 } } )$ has dimension $\pmb { m } - \pmb { r } = \pmb { 3 } - \pmb { 2 } .$

Reason : $R _ { 0 }$ has r independent rows and m — r zero rows. Then $R _ { \mathbf { 0 } } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ has r independent columns and $\mathbf { \nabla } m - \mathbf { \nabla } r$ zero columns. So y in the nullspace of $R _ { 0 } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ can have nonzeros in its last $m - r$ entries. The example has $m - r = 1$ zero column in $R _ { 0 } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ and 1 nonzero in y.

$$
\begin{array} { r } { R _ { 0 } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { y } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { \mathbf { 1 } } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { \mathbf { 3 } } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { \mathbf { 5 } } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { \mathbf { 1 } } & { 0 } \\ { \mathbf { 7 } } & { \mathbf { 2 } } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \\ { y _ { 3 } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 0 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}
$$

is solved by

$$
\pmb { y } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { { 0 } } \\ { { 0 } } \\ { { y _ { 3 } } } \end{array} \right] .\tag{1}
$$

Because of zero rows in $R _ { 0 }$ and zero columns in $R _ { 0 } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ , it is easy to see the dimension (and even a basis) for this fourth fundamental subspace :

If $\scriptstyle { \mathbf { } } _ { R _ { 0 } }$ has m — r zero rows, its left nullspace has dimension ${ \pmb m } - { \pmb r } .$

Why is this a “left nullspace"? Because we can transpose $R _ { 0 } ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } } \pmb { y } = \pmb { 0 }$ to ${ \pmb y } ^ { \mathsf T } R _ { 0 } = { \pmb 0 } ^ { \mathsf T }$ Now ${ \pmb y } ^ { \dagger }$ is a row vector to the left of R. This subspace came fourth, and some linear algebra books omit it—but that misses the beauty of the whole subject.

In $\mathbf { R } ^ { \pmb { n } }$ the row space and nullspace have dimensions r and n — r (adding to n).   
$\pmb { I n } \pmb { R } ^ { \pmb { m } }$ the column space and left nullspace have dimensions r and m — r (total m).

We have a job still to do. The four subspace dimensions for A are the same as for $\pmb { R _ { 0 } } .$ The job is to explain why. A is now any matrix that reduces to $R _ { 0 } = { \mathsf { r r e f } } ( A )$

This A reduces to $\mathbf { \delta R _ { 0 } }$

$$
A { = } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l l } { 1 } & { 3 } & { 5 } & { 0 } & { 7 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 1 } & { 3 } & { 5 } & { 1 } & { 9 } \end{array} \right] }
$$

Same row space as $\mathbf { \delta } \mathbf { R _ { 0 } }$ Different column space But same dimension!
