## Thoughts on the Victory of Orthogonality

If I look back at the linear algebra in this book, orthogonal vectors and matrices have won. You could say that they deserved to win. Their success goes all the way back to Chapter 1 on lengths and dot products. Let me recall some of their victories and add new ones.

1 The length of $\pmb { Q x }$ equals the length of x : $( Q x ) ^ { \mathrm { { T } } } ( Q x ) = x ^ { \mathrm { { T } } } Q ^ { \mathrm { { T } } } Q x = x ^ { \mathrm { { T } } } x = | | x | | ^ { 2 } .$

2 The dot product $( Q x ) ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } } ( Q y )$ equals the dot product $\pmb { x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { y } : ~ \pmb { x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { Q } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { Q } \pmb { y } = \pmb { x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { y } .$

3 The projection matrix onto the column space of Q (m by n) is $P = Q Q ^ { \mathrm { \bf T } } = ( Q Q ^ { \mathrm { \bf T } } ) ^ { 2 }$

4 The least squares solution to $Q x = b ( m > n )$ is ${ \widehat { \pmb { x } } } = Q ^ { \mathrm { T } } { \pmb { b } } = Q ^ { + } { \pmb { b } }$ (pseudoinverse).

If we add that $Q$ is square, then $Q ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } } = Q ^ { - 1 }$ . More is coming in Chapters 5, 6, 7.

5 All powers $Q ^ { N }$ and products $Q _ { 1 } Q _ { 2 } \dots Q _ { N }$ are orthogonal : | determinant $| = 1$

6 The eigenvectors q of a symmetric matrix $s$ can be chosen orthonormal.

7 The singular vectors of every matrix are orthonormal.

That list shows something important. The success of orthogonal matrices is tied to the sum of squares definition of length : $| | \pmb { x } | | ^ { 2 } = \pmb { x } ^ { \mathsf { T } } \pmb { x }$ .In least squares, the derivative of $| | A \pmb { x } - \pmb { b } | | ^ { 2 }$ leads to a symmetric matrix ${ \pmb S } = { \pmb A } ^ { \dagger } { \pmb A }$ . Then $s$ is diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix $Q$ (the eigenvectors will come in Chapter 6).

Every A is diagonalized by two orthogonal matrices $Q _ { 1 }$ and $Q _ { 2 }$ (the singular vectors in Chapter 7). And here is more about orthogonal matrices : $\pmb { A } = \pmb { Q } \pmb { S }$ and $A = Q R$

8 Every invertible matrix equals an orthogonal $\pmb { Q }$ times a symmetric S.

Example

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 3 } & { 0 } \\ { 4 } & { 5 } \end{array} \right] } = { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 5 } } } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] } { \sqrt { 5 } } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 2 } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] } = Q S
$$

9 Every invertible matrix equals an orthogonal $\pmb { Q }$ times an upper triangular R.

Example $Q$ and R come from the Gram-Schmidt algorithm in Section ${ 4 . 4 }$

$$
\pmb { A } = \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { { 3 } } & { { 0 } } \\ { { 4 } } & { { 5 } } \end{array} \right] = \frac { 1 } { 5 } \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { { 3 } } & { { - 4 } } \\ { { 4 } } & { { 3 } } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { { 5 } } & { { 4 } } \\ { { 0 } } & { { 3 } } \end{array} \right] = \pmb { Q R }
$$

## 5 Determinants

## 5.1 3 by 3 Determinants and Cofactors

## 5.2 Computing and Using Determinants

## 5.3 Areas and Volumes by Determinants

The determinant of a square matrix is an astonishing number. If det $A = 0$ , this signals that the column vectors are dependent and A is not invertible. If det A is not zero, the formula for $A ^ { - 1 }$ will have a division by the determinant. Section 5.1 will find 3 by 3 determinants and then the “cofactor formulas" for det A and the inverse matrix.

There are three useful formulas for det A. After elimination we can multiply the pivots from the triangular matrix U in $P A = L U$ . Always det $P = 1 \ \mathrm { o r } - 1$ and det $L = 1$ So the product of pivots in $\pmb { U }$ gives det A or - det A. This is usually the fastest way.

A second formula uses determinants of size $\pmb { n } - 1$ : the “cofactors" of A. They give the best formula for $A ^ { - 1 }$ . The $i , j$ entry of $A ^ { - 1 }$ is the j, i cofactor divided by det A.

The big formula for det A adds up n ! terms—one for every path down the matrix. Each path chooses one entry from every row and column, and we multiply the n entries on the path. Reverse the sign if the path has an odd permutation of column numbers. A 3 by 3 matrix has six paths and the big formula has six terms—one for every 3 by 3 permutation.

Section 5.2 begins with key properties like det AB = (det A) (det B). To prove that great fact, we begin with three simple properties that lead to every determinant. From those three, everything else follows—including the famous Cramer's Rule to solve linear equations $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$

Section 5.3 moves to geometry: The volume of a tilted box in n dimensions. The column vectors in the edge matrix E give n edges going out from the corner at $( 0 , \ldots , 0 )$ Then the volume of the box is | det E|. This connects geometry to linear algebra.

This chapter could easily become full of formulas! When an n by n matrix multiplies all points in an n-dimensional shape, it produces another shape. A cube goes to a tilted box. A circle goes to an ellipse, and a sphere goes to an ellipsoid. The ratio of the output volume to the input volume is always | det $\pmb { A } |$

Determinants could tell us everything, if only they were not so hard to compute.

## 5.1 3 by 3 Determinants and Cofactors

1 The determinant of $A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] }$ is $\mathbf { a d } - b \mathbf { c } .$ The singular matrix $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { 2 a } \\ { c } & { 2 c } \end{array} \right]$ has $\mathbf { d e t } = \mathbf { 0 } .$

Row exchange 2 reverses signs

$$
P A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { c } & { d } \\ { a } & { b } \end{array} \right] }
$$

$$
P A = b c - a d = - \operatorname* { d e t }
$$

$\begin{array} { r l }  \left[ { x a + y A } & { { x b + y B } } \\ { c } & { \qquad d \right] \mathrm { i s } x ( a d - b c ) + y ( A d - B c ) . } \end{array}$ Det is linear in 3 The determinant of row 1 by itself.

4 3 by 3 determinants have ${ \mathfrak { Z } } ! = 6$ terms in equation (1). They are separated into 3 terms using cofactors in equation (4). Those cofactors divided by det A produce $A ^ { - 1 }$ in equation (7).

Determinants lead to beautiful formulas. But often they are not practical for computing. This section will focus on 3 by 3 matrices, to see how determinants produce the matrix $A ^ { - 1 }$ (This formula for $A ^ { - 1 }$ was not seen in Chapters 1 to 4.) First come 2 by 2 matrices :

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] } = \mathbf { 1 } \quad \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } = - \mathbf { 1 } \quad \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] } = a d - b c \quad \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { c } & { d } \\ { a } & { b } \end{array} \right] } = b c - a d - b c \quad \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] } = b c + b c
$$

Those examples show an important rule. Determinants reverse sign when two rows are exchanged (or two columns are exchanged). This rule becomes a key to determinants of all sizes. The matrix has no inverse when its determinant is zero.

For 2 by 2 matrices, det $A = 0$ means $a / c = b / d$ The columns are parallel. For n by n matrices, det $\pmb { A } = \pmb { 0 }$ means that the columns of A are not independent. Then a combination of columns gives the zero vector : $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ with $\pmb { x } \neq \pmb { 0 }$ . A is not invertible.

These properties and more will follow after we define the determinant.

## 3 by 3 Determinants

2 by 2 matrices are easy : ad – bc. 4 by 4 matrices are hard. Better to use elimination (or a laptop). For 3 by 3 matrices, the determinant has $3 ! = 6$ terms, and often you can compute it by hand. We will show how. Every permutation has determinant 1 or -1.

Start with the identity matrix (det $I = 1 )$ and exchange two rows (then det = -1). Exchanging again brings back det = +1. You quickly have all six permutation matrices. Each row exchange will reverse the sign of the determinant (+1 to -1 or else -1 to +1) :

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & & \\ & { 1 } & \\ & & { 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & & \\ { 1 } & & \\ & & { 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } & { 1 } & \\ { 1 } & & { 1 } \\ & & { + 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & & \\ & { - 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & & { 1 } \\ & { 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & & \\ & { 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & \\ & { 1 } \end{array} \right] } \\ & { ~ \mathbf { d e t } = + \mathbf { 1 } } \end{array}
$$

If I exchange two rows of A—say rows 1 and 2—then its determinant changes sign.   
This will carry over to all determinants : Row exchange multiplies det A by -1.

When you multiply a row by a number, this multiplies the determinant by that number. Suppose the three rows are a b c and $\pmb { p q r }$ and $\pmb { x y z }$ .Those nine numbers multiply ±1.

$$
{ \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & \\ & { q } \\ & { z } \end{array} \right] } \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { b } & \\ { p } & \\ & { z } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { ~ b } & \\ & { ~ r } \\ { x } & \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } & { c } \\ & { q } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } & { c } \\ { p } & \\ & { y } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { a } & \\ & { ~ r } \\ & { ~ y } \end{array} } \right]
$$

Finally we use the most powerful property we have. The determinant of A is linear in each row separately. As equation (4) will show, we can add those six determinants. To remember the plus and minus signs, I follow the arrows in this picture of the matrix.

![](images/2dd39ad940c9d6fcf60d29e1305ff7a5d251b6d79e405d3f6bd1f246084fcfbe.jpg)

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \mathrm { C o m b i n e ~ t h o s e ~ 6 ~ s i m p l e ~ d e t e r m i n a n t s ~ i n t o ~ d e t } } A = } \\ & { \quad { \frac { + ~ a q z + b r x + c p y - a r y - b p z - c q x } { } } \quad \ ( } \\ & { } \end{array} }\tag{1}
$$

Notice! Those six terms all have one entry from each row of the matrix. They also have one entry from each column. There are $6 = 3 !$ terms in det A because there are six $\mathbf { 3 \times 3 }$ permutation matrices. A 4 × 4 determinant will have $4 ! = 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 2 4$ terms.

Let me jump in with examples of sizes 1, 2, 3, 4. This is pretty sudden but you can see their determinants. My favorite matrices have $\mathbf { \vec { \nabla } } ^ { 2 } \mathbf { \vec { s } }$ on the main diagonal and -1's on the diagonals above and below. Here are sizes $\pmb { n = 1 , 2 , 3 }$

$$
\pmb { A _ { 1 } } = \left[ \pmb { 2 } \right]
$$

$$
A _ { 2 } = \left[ { \begin{array} { r r } { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 } \end{array} } \right]
$$

$$
A _ { 3 } = \left[ { \begin{array} { r r r } { 2 } & { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { 0 } & { - 1 } & { 2 } \end{array} } \right]
$$

$$
\mathbf { d e t } \pmb { A _ { 1 } } = \pmb { 2 }
$$

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } A _ { 2 } = 4 - 1 = 3
$$

det A3 = 8 - 2 - 2 = 4

What are the six terms for det $A _ { 3 } = 4 ?$ The diagonal gives (2) (2) (2) = 8. Five more:

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { \mathsf { D t h e r } } & { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ & { - 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \phantom { - } - 1 } & { } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \phantom { - } - 1 } & { - 1 } \\ { 0 } & { - 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { - 1 } & { - 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \phantom { - } 2 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] } & { \mathsf { d e t e r m i n a n t s } } \\ & { } & { - 2 , - 2 , \mathsf { 0 } , \mathsf { 0 } , \mathsf { 0 } , 0 } \end{array}
$$

So the six terms add to $8 - 2 - 2 = 4$ and this will be det $\pmb { A _ { 3 } }$ . Please watch the pattern: Each of the $n ! = 3 ! = 6$ terms involves one number from every row and every column. When any of these numbers is zero, that whole term is zero. Computing det A is much easier when the matrix has many zeros.

Now we move to the $4 \times 4$ matrix $\pmb { A _ { 4 } }$ with 24 terms. Here is the key simplification and it will teach us a lot. The $4 \times 4$ determinant comes from two $\Im \times \Im$ determinants!

$$
A _ { 4 } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c c } { { { \bf 2 \sigma \left| - 1 \right]} } } & { { { \bf - 1 } } } & { { { \bf \sigma } } } \\ { { { \bf - 1 } } } & { { { \bf 2 \sigma - 1 } } } & { { } } \\ { { { \bf - 1 } } } & { { { \bf 2 \sigma - 1 } } } \\ { { { \bf - 1 } } } & { { { \bf 2 } } } & { { } } \end{array}  \quad \operatorname* { d e t } A _ { 4 } = 2 \operatorname* { d e t } \left[ \begin{array} { c c c } { { 2 { \bf \sigma - 1 } } } & { { } } \\ { { - { \bf 1 } } } & { { { \bf 2 \sigma - 1 } } } \\ { { - 1 } } & { { { \bf 2 } } } \end{array} \right] - ( - 1 ) \operatorname* { d e t } \left[ \begin{array} { c c c } { { - 1 { \bf \sigma - 1 } } } & { { { \bf 0 } } } \\ { { { \bf 0 } } } & { { { \bf 2 \sigma - 1 } } } \\ { { { \bf 0 } } } & { { - 1 } } & { { { \bf 2 } } } \end{array} \right] \quad { \bf - 1 } \quad { \bf 2 } \right] .
$$

Those $\mathbf { 3 \times 3 ^ { \circ } s }$ from rows 2, 3, 4 are the cofactors of 2 and -1 in row 1.

(2)

Notice : 2 in the top row of A is multiplying a 3 by 3 from the other rows. One number from each row and each column! The 2 came from row 1, column 1. So 2 multiplies the $\Im \times \Im$ determinant in rows and columns 2, 3, 4. That $\mathbf { 3 \times 3 }$ matrix is $\pmb { A _ { 3 } }$ with $\mathbf { d e t } = 4$

The final 3 by 3 matrix in equation (2) also uses rows 2, 3, 4 of A. The bold –1 comes from row 1, column 2. So the 3 by 3 matrix must use columns 1, 3, 4. The determinant of that 3 by 3 is —3 (please check this). Finally the overall determinant of $\pmb { A _ { 4 } }$ is $\mathbf { 8 } - \mathbf { 3 } = \mathbf { 5 }$

One more thing to learn about that last 3 by 3 from columns 1, 3, 4. In equation (2) it is multiplied by the -1 from row 1, column 2 of $\pmb { A _ { 4 } }$ . But equation (2) has another mysterious —1!Where does that minus come from ? It is there because row 1, column 2 is a “minus position”. $\mathbf { 1 } + \mathbf { 2 }$ is an odd number! The sign pattern was already set for $2 \times 2$

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] } = \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & \\ & { d } \end{array} \right] } + \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \quad b } \\ { c } \end{array} \right] } = a { \mathrm { ~ t i m e s ~ } } d { \mathrm { ~ m i n u s ~ } } b { \mathrm { ~ t i m e s ~ } } c .\tag{3}
$$

Finally $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , A _ { 3 } , A _ { 4 }$ have determinants 2,3,4,5. You can guess that det $\mathbf { A _ { 5 } } = \mathbf { 6 }$ Same idea as before det $\mathbf { A _ { 5 } } = \mathbf { 2 }$ det A₄ - det $A _ { 3 } = 2 ( 5 ) - 4 = 6$ . We will explain.

## Cofactors and a Formula for $A ^ { - 1 }$

For $\smash { 3 \times 3 }$ determinants with 6 terms like aqz, I can explain the “cofactor formulas" for the determinant and the inverse matrix. The idea is to reduce from $\mathbf { 3 \times 3 }$ to $2 \times 2$ Two of the six terms in det A start with a and with b and with c from row 1.

Cofactor formula

3 × 3 matrix

$$
\left[ \operatorname* { d e t } A = a \left( q z - r y \right) + b \left( r x - p z \right) + c \left( p y - q x \right) . \right]\tag{4}
$$

We separated the factors $a , b ,$ c in row 1 from their “cofactors". Each cofactor is a 2 by 2 determinant. The factor a in the 1, 1 position takes its cofactor from row and column 2 and 3. Every row and column is used once ! Notice that b in row 1, column 2 has cofactor $\pmb { r x } - \pmb { p z }$ There we see the other rows $\mathbf { 2 } , \mathbf { 3 }$ and columns 1,3. But the actual 2 by 2 determinant would be $p z - r x$ . The cofactor $C _ { 1 2 }$ reversed those $\pm \sin \mathbf { \vec { s } } \mathbf { n } \mathbf { \vec { s } } : \mathbf { 1 } + \mathbf { 2 }$ is odd.

Here is the definition of cofactors $C _ { i j }$ and the $( - 1 ) ^ { i + j }$ rule for their plus and minus signs.

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \boxed { \mathrm { F o r t h e ~ } i , j \mathrm { ~ c o f a c t o r ~ } C _ { i j } , \mathrm { r e m o v e ~ r o w ~ } i \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ c o l u m n ~ } j \mathrm { ~ f r o m ~ t h e ~ m a t r i x ~ } A . } } \\ & { C _ { i j } \mathrm { ~ e q u a l s ~ } ( - 1 ) ^ { i + j } \mathrm { ~ t i m e s ~ t h e ~ d e t e r m i n a n t ~ o f ~ t h e ~ r e m a i n i n g ~ m a t r i x ~ } ( \mathrm { s i z e ~ } n - 1 ) . } \\ & { \boxed { \mathrm { T h e ~ c o f a c t o r ~ f o r m u l a ~ a l o n g ~ r o w ~ } i \mathrm { ~ i s } \quad \operatorname* { d e t } A = a _ { i 1 } C _ { i 1 } + \cdots + a _ { i n } C _ { i n } } } \end{array}\tag{5}
$$

Key point: The cofactor $c _ { i j }$ just collects all the terms in det A that are multiplied by $\pmb { a _ { i j } }$ Thus the cofactors of a 2 by 2 matrix involve 1 by 1 determinants d, c, b, a times $( - 1 ) ^ { i + j }$

The cofactors of $A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] }$ are in the cofactor matrix $C = \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { d } & { - c } \\ { - b } & { a } \end{array} \right]$

Now notice something wonderful. If A multiplies $c ^ { \mathbf { T } }$ (not C) we get det A times I :

$$
A C ^ { \bf T } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { { a d - b c } } & { { 0 } } \\ { { 0 } } & { { a d - b c } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { { \operatorname * { d e t } A } } & { { 0 } } \\ { { 0 } } & { { \operatorname * { d e t } A } } \end{array} \right] = \left( \operatorname * { d e t } A \right) I .\tag{6}
$$

Dividing by det A, cofactors give our first and best formula for the inverse matrix $A ^ { - 1 }$

$$
\boxed { \mathrm { I n v e r s e ~ m a t r i x ~ f o r m u l a ~ } \qquad A ^ { - 1 } = C ^ { \mathrm { T } } / \operatorname* { d e t } A }\tag{7}
$$

This formula shows why the determinant of an invertible matrix cannot be zero. We need to divide the matrix $C ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } }$ by the number det A. Every entry in the inverse matrix $A ^ { - 1 }$ is a ratio of two determinants (size $\pmb { n } - 1$ for the cofactor in $C ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } }$ divided by size n for det A).

The example below has determinant 1, so $A ^ { - 1 }$ is exactly $c ^ { \mathbf { T } } =$ adjugate matrix. Notice how $C _ { 3 2 }$ removes row 3 and column 2. That leaves a 2 by 2 matrix with determinant 1. Since $\mathbf { ( - 1 ) ^ { 2 + 3 } } = - \mathbf { 1 }$ , this becomes -1 in $C ^ { \mathbf { T } }$ . It goes into row 2, column 3.

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \mathrm { E x a m p l e ~ o f ~ } } A ^ { - 1 } } \\ & { { \mathrm { D e t e r m i n a n t ~ } } = 1 } \\ & { { \mathrm { C o f a c t o r s ~ i n ~ } } C ^ { \mathrm { T } } } \end{array} } \qquad A ^ { - 1 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { 1 } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] } ^ { - 1 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } & { - 1 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] } = { \frac { C ^ { \mathrm { T } } } { 1 } }\tag{8}
$$

The diagonal entries of $A C ^ { \pmb { \tilde { \mathbf { T } } } }$ are always det A. That is the cofactor formula (5). Problem 18 will show why the off-diagonal entries of $A C ^ { \mathsf { T } }$ are always zero. Those numbers turn out to be determinants of matrices with two equal rows. Automatically zero.

A typical cofactor $C _ { 3 1 }$ removes row 3 and column 1. In our 3 by 3 example, that leaves a 2 by 2 matrix of $\mathbf { \nabla } ^ { 1 } \mathbf { \dot { s } } ,$ with determinant = 0. This is the bold zero in $A ^ { - 1 } : 1 , 3$ position. If we change to $\mathbf { 2 } A ,$ the determinant is multiplied by $\left( 2 \right) \left( 2 \right) \left( 2 \right) = \ 8$ . All cofactors in C are multiplied by (2) (2) = 4. Then $( 2 A ) ^ { - 1 } { = } 4 C ^ { \mathsf { T } } / 8$ det A is $A ^ { - 1 }$ divided by 2. Right !

## Example: The -1, 2, -1 Tridiagonal Matrix

The cofactor formula reduces n by n determinants to their cofactors of size $\pmb { n } - 1$ The -1, 2, -1 matrix is a great example because row 1 has only two nonzeros 2 and -1. So we only need two cofactors of row 1—and they will lead us to $A _ { n - 1 }$ and $A _ { n - 2 }$ Watch how this happens for the determinant of the -1, 2, -1 matrix $A _ { n }$ •

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l l } { 2 } & { - 1 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 } & { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { - 1 } & { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { \cdot } & { \cdot } & { \cdot } \end{array} \right] } = 2 ( - 1 ) ^ { 1 + 1 } \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { 2 } & { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { \cdot } & { \cdot } & { \cdot } \end{array} \right] } - \mathbf { 1 } ( - 1 ) ^ { 1 + 2 } \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { - 1 } & { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { \cdot } & { \cdot } & { \cdot } \end{array} \right] }
$$

On the right hand side, the first matrix gives 2 det $\pmb { A _ { n - 1 } }$ . The last term has —1 from the 1, 2 entry of $A _ { n }$ . It also has $( - 1 ) ^ { 1 + 2 } = - 1$ from the sign $( - 1 ) ^ { i + j }$ that goes with every cofactor. And that last cofactor itself has -1 in the top left entry, with makes three $\mathbf { - 1 3 }$

That last cofactor of $A _ { n }$ is showing its own cofactor of size n —2. That matrix is $A _ { n - 2 } !$

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } A _ { n } = 2 \operatorname* { d e t } A _ { n - 1 } - \operatorname* { d e t } A _ { n - 2 } .\tag{9}
$$

Working directly we found det $A _ { n } = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5$ for $\pmb { n } = \pmb { 1 } , \pmb { 2 } , \pmb { 3 } , \pmb { 4 } .$ All those fit with equation (9), as in det $A _ { 4 } = 5 = 2 ( 4 ) - 3$ But now we have found det $A _ { n } = n + 1$ for every n. This fits the formula (9) because $n + 1 = 2 ( n ) - ( n - 1 )$

The cofactor formula is most useful when the matrix entries are mostly zero. Then we have few cofactors to find. And the entries of those cofactors are also mostly zero. For a dense matrix full of nonzeros, we look next for a better way to find its determinant. The better way brings back elimination, to produce easy determinants of L and U.

## 5.2 Computing and Using Determinants

1 Useful facts : det AT = det A and det AB = (det A) (det B) and | det Q| = 1.   
2 Elimination matrices have det E = 1 so det EA = det A is unchanged.   
3 Cramer's Rule finds ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb A } ^ { - 1 } { \pmb b }$ from ratios of determinants (a slow way).   
4 det A = ± product of the pivots in A = LU (a much faster way).   
5 The big formula for det A has n! terms from n! permutations (very slow if $\pmb { n } > 3 )$

The determinant of a square matrix tells us a lot. First of all, an invertible matrix has det $A \neq 0 .$ A singular matrix has det $\pmb { A } = \pmb { 0 }$ When we come to eigenvalues λ and eigenvectors x with $A { \pmb x } = \lambda { \pmb x }$ , we will write that eigenvalue equation as $( A - \lambda I ) { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 } .$ This means that $A - \lambda I$ is singular and det $( A - \lambda I ) = 0$ We have an equation for λ.

Overall, the formulas are useful for small matrices and also for special matrices. And the properties of determinants can make those formulas simpler. If the matrix is triangular or diagonal, we just multiply the diagonal entries to find the determinant :

Triangular matrix Diagonal matrix

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { \pmb { a } } & { b } & { c } \\ & { \pmb { q } } & { r } \\ & & { z } \end{array} \right] } = \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { \pmb { a } } & & \\ & { \pmb { q } } & \\ & & { z } \end{array} \right] } = \pmb { a q z }\tag{1}
$$

If we transpose A, the determinant formula gives the same result :

Transpose the matrix

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } ( A ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } } ) = \operatorname* { d e t } ( A )\tag{2}
$$

If we multiply AB, we just multiply determinants (this is a wonderful fact) :

Multiply two matrices

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } ( A B ) = \left( \operatorname* { d e t } A \right) \left( \operatorname* { d e t } B \right)\tag{3}
$$

A proof by algebra can get complicated. We will give a simple proof of (3) by geometry.

When we add matrices, we do not just add determinants! (See this from $I + I .$ The determinant is $2 ^ { n }$ not 2.) Here are two good consequences of equations (2) and (3) :

Orthogonal matrices Q have determinant 1 or -1

We know that $Q ^ { \mathrm { { T } } } Q = I .$ Then (det $Q ) ^ { 2 } = ( \operatorname * { d e t } Q ^ { \mathrm { \bf T } } ) ( \operatorname * { d e t } Q ) = 1$ . Therefore det Q is ±1.

Invertible matrices have det A = ± (product of the pivots)

(4)

If A = LU then det $A = ( \operatorname* { d e t } L ) \left( \operatorname* { d e t } U \right) = \operatorname* { d e t } U$ . Triangular U : Multiply the pivots

If $P A = L U$ because of row exchanges, then det $P = 1 \mathrm { o r } - 1$ . Permutation matrix!

Multiplying the pivots $U _ { 1 1 } \ U _ { 2 2 } \dots U _ { n n }$ on the diagonal reveals the determinant of A. Elimination is how determinants are computed by virtually all computer systems for linear algebra. The cost to find U in Chapter 2 was ${ \pmb n } ^ { 3 } / 3$ multiplications.

## Proving those Properties (1) to (4)

The proofs of (1) to (4) can begin with three simple properties of determinants.

1. The n by n identity matrix has det $\pmb { I } = \pmb { 1 }$

2. Exchanging two rows of A reverses det A to -det A.

3. If row 1 of A is a combination cv + dw, then add 2 determinants :

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { c } { c v + d w } \\ { \operatorname { r o w } 2 } \\ { \cdots } \\ { \operatorname { r o w } n } \end{array} \right] } = c \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { c } { v } \\ { \operatorname { r o w } 2 } \\ { \cdots } \\ { \operatorname { r o w } n } \end{array} \right] } + d \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { w } \\ { \operatorname { r o w } 2 } \\ { \cdots } \\ { \operatorname { r o w } n } \end{array} \right] }\tag{5}
$$

In other words “the determinant is linear with respect to row 1." Then Property 2 leads us further: det A is linear with respect to every row separately. We can exchange rows and exchange back. So nothing is special about row 1.

Property 2 also leads to this simple fact. If A has two equal rows, its determinant is zero. Exchanging the rows has no effect on A. Then det $A = - \operatorname* { d e t } A$ forces det $\pmb { A } = \pmb { 0 }$

Now use rule 3: Subtracting d times row i from row $\pmb { j }$ leaves det A unchanged.

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { c } { \mathbf { r o w } \ 1 } \\ { \mathbf { r o w } \ 2 - d \mathbf { r o w } \ 1 } \\ { \mathbf { r o w } \ n } \end{array} \right] } = \operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \mathbf { r o w } \ 1 } \\ { \mathbf { r o w } \ 2 } \\ { \mathbf { r o w } \ n } \end{array} \right] } - d { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { \mathbf { r o w } \ 1 } \\ { \mathbf { r o w } \ 1 } \\ { \mathbf { r o w } \ n } \end{array} \right] } = \operatorname* { d e t } A\tag{6}
$$

This was "linearity in row 2 with row 1 fixed". It means (again) that our elimination steps from the original matrix A to an upper triangular U do not change the determinant. Then elimination (without row exchanges) is the way to simplify A and its determinant.

No row exchange

$$
\boxed { \operatorname* { d e t } A = \operatorname* { d e t } U = U _ { 1 1 } U _ { 2 2 } \dots U _ { n n } = \mathrm { { \ p r o d u c t ~ o f ~ t h e ~ p i v o t s } } }\tag{7}
$$

Here is a proof that det $A B = ( \operatorname* { d e t } A ) ( \operatorname* { d e t } B )$ . Assume det $B \neq 0$ We will show that $D ( A ) = \operatorname* { d e t } A B / \operatorname* { d e t } B$ has properties 1, 2, 3 above. Then $\pmb { D } ( \pmb { A } )$ must be the same as det A. Here are those three properties confirmed for $\pmb { D } ( \pmb { A } )$

1. If A = I then $D ( I ) = \operatorname* { d e t } { B } /$ det B correctly gives the answer $D ( I ) = 1$

2. Exchanging rows of A will exchange rows of AB. Then $D ( A )$ changes sign!

3. Multiplying row 1 of A by c will multiply $D ( A )$ by c. If row 1 of A is $\pmb { v } + \pmb { w }$ , then row 1 of $\pmb { A } \pmb { B }$ is $\pmb { v } \pmb { B } + \pmb { w } \pmb { B }$ Equation (5) separates det(AB) into two determinants. So $D ( A )$ also follows equation (5). From 1, 2, 3, det(AB) /det B must be det A.

## Cramer's Rule to Solve $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$

A neat idea gives the first component $\pmb { x _ { 1 } }$ of the solution vector x to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ .Replace the first column of I by x. This triangular $M _ { 1 }$ has determinant $\pmb { x _ { 1 } }$ . When you multiply by A, the first column becomes Ax which is b. The other columns of $B _ { 1 }$ are copied from A.

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } { { \mathrm { K e y ~ i d e a } } } & { } \\ { A M _ { 1 } = B _ { 1 } } & { } \end{array} } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \quad A } & { } \\ { \quad A } & { } \end{array} \right] } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { x _ { 1 } } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { x _ { 2 } } & { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { x _ { 3 } } & { 0 } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l l } { b _ { 1 } } & { a _ { 1 2 } } & { a _ { 1 3 } } \\ { b _ { 2 } } & { a _ { 2 2 } } & { a _ { 2 3 } } \\ { b _ { 3 } } & { a _ { 3 2 } } & { a _ { 3 3 } } \end{array} \right] } = B _ { 1 } .\tag{8}
$$

We multiplied a column at a time. Take determinants of the three matrices to find $\pmb { x } _ { 1 }$

Product rule

$$
\bigg | \left( \operatorname * { d e t } A \right) \left( x _ { 1 } \right) = \operatorname * { d e t } B _ { 1 } \qquad \mathrm { o r } \qquad x _ { 1 } = \operatorname * { d e t } B _ { 1 } / \operatorname * { d e t } A . \bigg |\tag{9}
$$

This is the first component of x in Cramer's Rule. Changing a column of A gave $B _ { 1 }$ To find $\pmb { x _ { 2 } }$ and $B _ { 2 }$ , put the vectors x and b into the second columns of I and A :

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } { { \mathrm { S a m e ~ i d e a } } \quad } & { { \Bigg [ } a _ { 1 } \quad a _ { 2 } \quad a _ { 3 } { \Bigg ] } { \Bigg [ } { \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 } & { x _ { 1 } } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { x _ { 2 } } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { x _ { 3 } } & { 1 } \end{array} } { \Bigg ] } = { \Bigg [ } a _ { 1 } \quad b \quad a _ { 3 } { \Bigg ] } = B _ { 2 } . } \end{array} }\tag{10}
$$

Take determinants to find $( \operatorname* { d e t } A ) ( x _ { 2 } ) = \operatorname* { d e t } B _ { 2 }$ . This gives $x _ { 2 } = ( \operatorname* { d e t } B _ { 2 } ) / ( \operatorname* { d e t } A )$

Example 1 Solving ${ \bf 3 } x _ { 1 } + { \bf 4 } x _ { 2 } = { \bf 2 }$ and $\mathbf { 5 } x _ { 1 } + \mathbf { 6 } x _ { 2 } = 4$ needs three determinants :

Put 2 and 4 into each B

$$
\mathbf { d e t } \ A = { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { 3 } & { 4 } \\ { 5 } & { 6 } \end{array} \right| }
$$

det

$$
B _ { 1 } = { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { 2 } & { 4 } \\ { 4 } & { 6 } \end{array} \right| }
$$

det

$$
B _ { 2 } = { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { 3 } & { 2 } \\ { 5 } & { 4 } \end{array} \right| }
$$

The determinants of $B _ { 1 }$ and $B _ { 2 }$ are -4 and 2. Those are divided by det $A = - 2$

$$
{ \mathrm { F i n d ~ } } x = A ^ { - 1 } b \quad \quad x _ { 1 } = { \frac { - 4 } { - 2 } } = 2 \quad \ x _ { 2 } = { \frac { 2 } { - 2 } } = - 1 \quad { \mathrm { C h e c k } } \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { 3 } & { 4 } \\ { 5 } & { 6 } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { l } { 2 } \\ { - 1 } \end{array} } \right] = \left[ { \begin{array} { l } { 2 } \\ { 4 } \end{array} } \right]
$$

CRAMER's RULE If det A is not zero, $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ is solved by determinants :

$$
x _ { 1 } = { \frac { \operatorname* { d e t } B _ { 1 } } { \operatorname* { d e t } A } } \qquad x _ { 2 } = { \frac { \operatorname* { d e t } B _ { 2 } } { \operatorname* { d e t } A } } \qquad \ldots \qquad x _ { n } = { \frac { \operatorname* { d e t } B _ { n } } { \operatorname* { d e t } A } }\tag{11}
$$

The matrix $\mathbf { \delta } _ { B _ { j } }$ has the jth column of A replaced by the vector b.

To solve an n by n system, Cramer's Rule evaluates $\pm 1$ determinants (of A and the n different $B ^ { \prime } { \bf s } )$ . When each one is the sum of n! terms—applying the "big formula" with all permutations—this makes a total of $( n + 1 ) !$ terms. It would be crazy to solve equations that way. But we do finally have an explicit formula for the solution to $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$

Example 2 Cramer's Rule is not efficient for numbers but it is well suited to letters. For $\scriptstyle \pmb { n } = 2$ , find the two columns x and y of $A ^ { - 1 }$ by solving $A A ^ { - 1 } = A \left[ { \pmb x } \quad { \pmb y } \right] = I .$

$$
A x = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] } { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 1 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] } \qquad A y = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] } { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { y _ { 1 } } \\ { y _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 0 } \\ { 1 } \end{array} \right] }
$$

Those share the same matrix A. We need $| A |$ and four determinants for $x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 }$

$$
| A | = { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right| } \quad { \mathrm { a n d } } \quad { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { b } \\ { 0 } & { d } \end{array} \right| } \quad { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { 1 } \\ { c } & { 0 } \end{array} \right| } \quad { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { b } \\ { 1 } & { d } \end{array} \right| } \quad { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { 0 } \\ { c } & { 1 } \end{array} \right| }
$$

The last four determinants are $d , - c , - b ,$ and a. (They are the cofactors!) Here is $A ^ { - 1 }$

$$
x _ { 1 } = { \frac { d } { | A | } } , x _ { 2 } = { \frac { - c } { | A | } } , y _ { 1 } = { \frac { - b } { | A | } } , y _ { 2 } = { \frac { a } { | A | } } { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } A ^ { - 1 } = { \frac { 1 } { a d - b c } } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { d } & { - b } \\ { - c } & { a } \end{array} \right] } .
$$

$\pmb { A } ^ { - 1 }$ involves the cofactors of A. When the right side of $A { \pmb x } = { \pmb b }$ is a column of I, as in $A A ^ { - 1 } = I $ the determinant of each $\pmb { { \cal B } } _ { j }$ in Cramer's Rule is a cofactor of A.

You can see those cofactors for $\pmb { n = 3 }$ Solve $A { \pmb x } = ( 1 , 0 , 0 )$ to find column 1 of $A ^ { - 1 }$

Determinants of B's are Cofactors of A

$$
\left| \begin{array} { c c c } { \textbf { 1 } } & { a _ { 1 2 } } & { a _ { 1 3 } } \\ { \textbf { 0 } } & { a _ { 2 2 } } & { a _ { 2 3 } } \\ { \textbf { 0 } } & { a _ { 3 2 } } & { a _ { 3 3 } } \end{array} \right| \quad \left| \begin{array} { c c c } { a _ { 1 1 } } & { \textbf { 1 } } & { a _ { 1 3 } } \\ { a _ { 2 1 } } & { \textbf { 0 } } & { a _ { 2 3 } } \\ { a _ { 3 1 } } & { \textbf { 0 } } & { a _ { 3 3 } } \end{array} \right| \quad \left| \begin{array} { c c c } { a _ { 1 1 } } & { a _ { 1 2 } } & { \textbf { 1 } } \\ { a _ { 2 1 } } & { a _ { 2 2 } } & { \textbf { 0 } } \\ { a _ { 3 1 } } & { a _ { 3 2 } } & { \textbf { 0 } } \end{array} \right|
$$

That determinant of $B _ { 1 }$ is the cofactor $C _ { 1 1 } = a _ { 2 2 } a _ { 3 3 } - a _ { 2 3 } a _ { 3 2 }$ . Notice that the correct minus sign appears in det $B _ { 2 } = - ( a _ { 2 1 } a _ { 3 3 } - a _ { 2 3 } a _ { 3 1 } )$ . This cofactor $C _ { 1 2 }$ goes into column 1 of $A ^ { - 1 }$ . When we divide by det A, we have computed the same $A ^ { - 1 }$ as before :

$$
\boxed { \mathrm { F O R M U L A F O R \ } A ^ { - 1 } \qquad ( A ^ { - 1 } ) _ { i j } = \frac { C _ { j i } } { \operatorname* { d e t } A } \qquad A ^ { - 1 } = \frac { C ^ { \mathrm { T } } } { \operatorname* { d e t } A } }\tag{12}
$$

## The Big Formula for the Determinant : n! Terms

So far we have found two formulas for det A. One was the cofactor formula, which reduces det A to a combination of smaller determinants. (This worked well when A had only 3 nonzero diagonals and lots of zeros.) The second was the pivot formula, coming from elimination and $P A \ = \ L U$ This worked well because L and U are triangular in Chapter 2. And det $P = \pm 1$ . Our big formula is not so great, because it has all of the n! terms in det A.

Every n by n permutation matrix P (n! $P ^ { \bullet } )$ produces a term $D _ { P }$ in the big formula. Each matrix P has n 1's: a single 1 in each row and each column. We multiply the n numbers ${ \pmb a } _ { 1 \alpha } { \pmb a } _ { 2 \beta } \cdots { \pmb a } _ { n \omega }$ in those positions, to find their contribution $\pmb { D } _ { \pmb { P } }$ to the overall determinant of A. And we remember to include the factor det $P = \pm 1$ in $\pmb { D } _ { \pmb { P } }$ . This accounts for an even or odd permutation. Now add up all the terms like $\pmb { D _ { P } } = \pmb { a d }$ or aqz.

| Big Formula det A = Sum of all Dp = n! terms from n! permutations P|

(13)

For $\textbf { \em n } = \textbf { 2 }$ this formula is exactly ad – bc (2 permutations give $D _ { P } = a d \mathrm { \bf ~ a n d } - b c )$ For $\pmb { n = 3 }$ we have 3! = 6 permutations and 6 terms in equation (13).

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } A = + a q z + b r x + c p y - a r y - b p z - c q x .
$$

## 5.3 Areas and Volumes by Determinants

1 A parallelogram in 2D starts from $( 0 , 0 )$ with sides $\pmb { e } _ { 1 } = ( \pmb { a } , \pmb { b } )$ and $e _ { 2 } = ( c , d )$

2 Area of the parallelogram = | Determinant of the matrix $E = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { e _ { 1 } } & { e _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] \bigg \vert = \left. a d - b c \right.$

3 A tilted box in 3D starts with three edges $\mathbf { e } _ { 1 } , \mathbf { e } _ { 2 } , \mathbf { e } _ { 3 }$ out from $( \mathbf { 0 } , \mathbf { 0 } , \mathbf { 0 } )$

4 Volume of a tilted box = | Determinant of the $\mathbf { 3 \times 3 }$ edge matrix $\displaystyle { \boldsymbol { E } } { \mid } .$

Determinants lead to good formulas for areas and volumes. The regions have straight sides but they are not square. A typical region is a parallelogram—or half a parallelogram which is a triangle. The problem is: Find the area. For a triangle, the area is ${ \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \ b h$ half the base times the height. A parallelogram contains two triangles with equal area, so we omit the $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ . Then parallelogram area = base times height.

Those formulas are simple to remember. But they don't fit our problem, because we are not given the base and height. We only know the positions of the corners. For the triangle, suppose the corner points are (0, 0) and $( a , b )$ and $( c , d )$ . For the parallelogram (twice as large) the fourth corner will be $( a + c , b + d )$ . Knowing $a , b , c , d ,$ what is the area?

Triangle and

parallelogram

![](images/5dc1e452c4c628efe202e4860bd71855871fbc3fdc972be52c457c397c680f64.jpg)

The base could be the lowest side and its length is $\sqrt { a ^ { 2 } + b ^ { 2 } }$ .To find the height, we could create a line down from $( c , d )$ that is perpendicular to the baseline. The length h of that perpendicular line would involve more square roots. But the area itself does not involve square roots! Its beautiful formula ad — bc is simple for $a = d = 1 , b = c = 0$ (a square).

$$
{ \Biggl | } \mathrm { A r e a ~ o f ~ p a r a l l e l o g r a m } = { \left| \mathrm { ~ D e t e r m i n a n t ~ o f ~ m a t r i x } \right| } = \pm { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { c } \\ { b } & { d } \end{array} \right| } = \left| a d - b c \right| .\tag{1}
$$

Our goal is to find that formula by linear algebra: no square roots or negative volumes.   
We took the absolute value $\left. a d - b c \right.$ to avoid a negative area.

We also have a more difficult goal. We need to move into 3 dimensions and eventually into n dimensions. We start with four corners 0,0, 0 and a, b, c and ${ p , q , r }$ and $\pmb { x } , \pmb { y } , \pmb { z }$ of a box. (The box is tilted. Every side is a parallelogram. It will look lopsided.)

If we use the area formula (1) as a guide, we could guess the correct volume formula:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \boxed { \mathrm { V o l u m e ~ o f ~ b o x } = \left| \mathrm { ~ D e t e r m i n a n t ~ o f ~ m a t r i x } \right| = \pm \left| \begin{array} { c c c } { a } & { p } & { x } \\ { b } & { q } & { y } \\ { c } & { r } & { z } \end{array} \right| } } \end{array}\tag{2}
$$

Our first effort stays in a plane. For this case we use geometry. Figure 5.1 shows how adding pieces to a parallelogram can produce a rectangle. When we subtract the areas of those six pieces, we arrive at the correct parallelogram area ad — bc (no square roots). The picture is not very elegant, but in two dimensions it succeeds.

![](images/d59423166eb817169440dd9eeac613cfff8a2893deb31a70d0d1013500f9098f.jpg)

$$
( a + c , b + d ) = ( { \mathrm { b a s e , h e i g h t ) o f r e c t a n g l e } }
$$

$$
{ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \mathrm { \ A r e a \ o f \ p a r a l l e l o g r a m } } } \\ & { { \mathrm { \ R e c t a n g l e \ m i n u s \ 6 \ p i e c e s } } } \\ & { ( a + c ) \left( b + d \right) - 2 b c - a b - c d } \\ & { \qquad = a d - b c } \end{array} }
$$

Figure 5.1: Adding six simple pieces to a parallelogram produces a rectangle.

Would a similar construction be possible in three dimensions? Following Figure 5.1, I believe we could add simple pieces to make a tilted box into a rectangular box— but it doesn't look easy. And there is a much better way : Use linear algebra.

## Areas and Volumes by Linear Algebra

In working on this problem, I came to an understanding. If we do more algebra, then we need less geometry. Very often, linear algebra comes down to factoring a matrix. We will look there for ideas.

A box in n dimensions has n edges $e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } , \ldots , e _ { n }$ going out from the origin. The parallelogram in two dimensions had two vectors $\pmb { e } _ { 1 } = ( \pmb { a } , \pmb { b } )$ and ${ e _ { 2 } } \ = \ ( c , d )$ . Those vectors e give two corners or n corners of the "box". In the 2-dimensional picture, the fourth corner was $e _ { 1 } + e _ { 2 }$ . In the n-dimensional picture, the other corners of the box would be sums of the $\pmb { e ^ { \prime } { \mathsf { s } } } .$ The box is totally determined by the n edges in the matrix $\pmb { { \cal E } }$

Edge matrix

$$
E _ { 2 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { c } \\ { b } & { d } \end{array} \right] } \quad { \mathrm { a n d } } \ E _ { n } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \displaystyle | } & { \displaystyle | } \\ { e _ { 1 } \cdots e _ { n } } \\ { \displaystyle | } & { \displaystyle | } \end{array} \right] } \quad { \mathrm { B o x ~ e d g e s } }
$$

Our goal is to prove that the volume of the box is | det $\pmb { { \cal E } } |$ . We considered three possible factorizations of $\pmb { { \cal E } } ,$ to reach this goal. They are taken from Chapters 2 and 4 and 7.

The third factorization is called the Singular Value Decomposition of E: the SVD.

Lower times upper triangular

$$
{ \pmb { { \cal E } } } = { \pmb { { \cal L } } } { \pmb { U } }
$$

Orthogonal times upper triangular R E = QR

Orthogonal-Diagonal-Orthogonal

$$
\pmb { { \cal E } } = \pmb { { \cal U } } \pmb { \Sigma } \pmb { V } ^ { \pmb { \tau } }
$$

Those factors of E are square matrices because $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ is square (n by n). Remember that the determinant of L is 1 (all ones on its diagonal). The determinant of any orthogonal matrix $Q$ is 1 $\pmb { \mathrm { o r } } - \pmb { 1 }$ . Then det L = | det $\pmb { Q } | = |$ det U| = | det $\mathbf { \nabla } V \vert = \mathbf { 1 }$ . We will certainly depend on the multiplication rule det $A B = \left( \operatorname* { d e t } A \right)$ (det B). Three options for | det $E |$ •

$$
\mathrm { B o x ~ v o l u m e } = | \operatorname* { d e t } E | = | \operatorname* { d e t } U | = | \operatorname* { d e t } R | = | \operatorname* { d e t } \Sigma | .\tag{3}
$$

The problem is to connect the volume of the box to one of those determinants—to connect geometry to linear algebra. Start with the geometry of an orthogonal matrix $Q .$

Key idea for any region in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { \pmb { n } }$ : Multiplying all points by an orthogonal matrix $Q$ does not change the volume. Let me understand this first and then use $\pmb { { \cal E } } = \pmb { { \cal Q } } \pmb { { \cal R } }$

Multiply by any matrix : Straight lines stay straight, areas can change

Multiply by an orthogonal $Q : { \pmb x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } { \pmb x }$ and $\pmb { x } ^ { \mathsf { T } } \pmb { \updownarrow }$ y are the same as $( Q \pmb { x } ) ^ { \operatorname { T } } ( Q \pmb { x } ) \operatorname { a n d } { \left( Q \pmb { x } \right) ^ { \operatorname { T } } ( Q \pmb { y } ) }$

Lengths and angles and box shapes and volumes are not changed by rotations Q. $\pmb { Q }$

This remains true for curved regions. We divide them into many small cubes plus thin curved pieces. The total volume of those curved pieces can approach zero. The volumes of the cubes are not changed by $Q .$ The shapes for R and for $E = Q R$ have the same volume.

R is a triangular matrix. Its box has a volume we can compute. For a parallelogram in the xy plane, the base and height are the diagonal entries u and w of R in ${ \pmb E } = { \pmb Q } { \pmb R }$

$$
R = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { u } & { v } \\ { 0 } & { w } \end{array} \right] } \quad \underbrace { \overbrace { \int _ { \mathrm { ~ { \Gamma } ~ } \psi } ^ { \{ v , w \} } } ^ { \{ v , w \} } } _ { \underbrace { \mathrm { ~ { \Gamma } ~ } \psi } \mathrm { ~ { \Gamma } ~ } \psi } \quad \mathbf { b a s e } = u { \mathrm { , ~ h e i g h t } } = w \qquad 
$$

The key point is : The main diagonal of R shows the height in each new dimension. When we multiply those numbers on the diagonal of R, we get the volume of the box and also the determinant of the triangular matrix R. The volume formula | det $E |$ is now proved in all dimensions because |det $\pmb { Q } | = 1$ and |det $\mathbf { \vert } E \vert = \vert \mathbf { d e t } R \vert$

Final comment : The Singular Value Decomposition $\pmb { { \cal E } } = \pmb { { \cal U } } \pmb { \Sigma } \pmb { { \cal V } } ^ { \pmb { \Upsilon } }$ has two orthogonal matrices U and V. The number | det $\pmb { { \cal E } } |$ is equal to | det Σ|. And this matrix Σ is diagonal. Σ gives a perfectly normal rectangular box in $\pmb { \mathbb { R } } ^ { \pmb { n } }$ . This SVD approach by $U { \boldsymbol { \Sigma } } V ^ { \mathbf { T } }$ looks simpler than $\scriptstyle Q R ,$ where the triangular matrix R produced the tilted box above. But...

But that tilted figure shows a clear geometric meaning for the diagonal entries u and w : base and height. The geometry of the SVD will be seen in Chapter 7. It is beautifully clear for ellipses in n dimensions. But the singular values are not so clear for boxes. Σ gives the lengths of the axes of an ellipse but not the sides of a rectangular box. For a box with straight sides, $E = Q R$ leads directly to volume of box $\mathbf { \tau } = | \operatorname* { d e t } R |$

Every shape has the growth factor det E when all points are multiplied by E.

# Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

6.1 Introduction to Eigenvalues : $A x = \lambda x$

6.2 Diagonalizing a Matrix

6.5 Solving Linear Differential Equations

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors have new information about a square matrix—deeper than its rank or its column space. We look for eigenvectors x that don't change direction when they are multiplied by A. Then $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \lambda \pmb { x }$ with eigenvalue λ. (You could call λ the stretching factor.) Multiplying again gives $A ^ { 2 } x = \lambda ^ { 2 } x$ . We can go onwards to $A ^ { 1 0 0 } x = \lambda ^ { 1 0 0 } x$ . And we can combine two or more eigenvectors :

$$
A ( { \pmb x } _ { 1 } + { \pmb x } _ { 2 } ) = \lambda _ { 1 } { \pmb x } _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { 2 } { \pmb x } _ { 2 } \qquad A ^ { 2 } ( c _ { 1 } { \pmb x } _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } { \pmb x } _ { 2 } ) = c _ { 1 } \lambda _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } { \pmb x } _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } \lambda _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } { \pmb x } _ { 2 }
$$

When we separate the input into eigenvectors, each eigenvector just goes its own way.

The eigenvalues are the growth factors in $A ^ { n } x = \lambda ^ { n } x$ . If all $| \lambda _ { i } | < 1$ then $A ^ { n }$ will eventually approach zero. If any $| \lambda _ { i } | > 1$ then $A ^ { n }$ eventually grows. If $\lambda = 1$ then ${ \pmb A } ^ { \pmb n } { \pmb x }$ never changes (a steady state). For the economy of a country or a company or a family, the size of λ is a critical number.

Properties of a matrix are reflected in the properties of the λ's and the x's. A symmetric matrix S has perpendicular eigenvectors—and all its eigenvalues are real numbers. The kings of linear algebra are symmetric matrices with positive eigenvalues. These "positive definite matrices" signal a minimum point for a function like the energy $\begin{array} { r } { f ( \pmb { x } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \pmb { x } ^ { \top } S \pmb { x } } \end{array}$ That is the n-dimensional form of the calculus test $d ^ { 2 } f / d x ^ { 2 } > 0$ for a minimum of $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$

This chapter ends by solving linear differential equations $d \pmb { u } / d t = A \pmb { u }$ .The pieces of the solution are ${ \pmb u } ( t ) = e ^ { \lambda t } { \pmb x }$ instead of $u _ { n } = \lambda ^ { n } x .$ —exponentials instead of powers. The whole solution is ${ \pmb u } ( t ) = e ^ { { \pmb A } t } { \pmb u } ( 0 )$ . For linear differential equations with a constant matrix A, please use its eigenvectors.

Section 6.4 gives the rules for complex matrices—including the famous Fourier matrix

## 6.1 Introduction to Eigenvalues : $A x = \lambda x$

1 $\mathbf { I f } \left[ A x = \lambda x \right]$ then $\pmb { x } \neq \pmb { 0 }$ is an eigenvector of A and the number λ is the eigenvalue.   
2 Then $\boxed { A ^ { n } x = \lambda ^ { n } x }$ for every n and $( A + c I ) { \pmb x } = ( \lambda + c ) { \pmb x }$ and $A ^ { - 1 } x = x / \lambda { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } \lambda \neq 0 .$   
3 $( A - \lambda I ) \pmb { x } = \mathbf { 0 } \Rightarrow$ the determinant of A — λI is zero: this equation produces n $\pmb { \lambda ^ { \prime } 5 } .$   
4 Check λ's by (λ₁)(λ₂) · · ·. (λn) = det A and λ₁+ · · · +λn = diagonal sum $a _ { 1 1 } + \cdots + a _ { n n } .$   
5 Projections have λ = 1 and 0. Rotations have $\lambda \ = \ e ^ { i \theta }$ and $e ^ { - i \theta }$ :complex numbers!

This chapter enters a new part of linear algebra. The first part was about $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ linear equations for a steady state. Now the second part is about change. Time enters the picture—continuous time in a differential equation $d u / d t \ = \ A u$ or time steps $k = 1 , 2 , 3 , . . . \sin u _ { k + 1 } = A u _ { k }$ . Those equations are NOT solved by elimination.

We want “eigenvectors"x that don't change direction when you multiply by A. The solution vector ${ \pmb u } ( t )$ or $\pmb { u } _ { k }$ stays in the direction of that fixed vector x. Then we only look for the number (changing with time) that multiplies x : a one-dimensional problem.

A good model comes from the powers $A , A ^ { 2 } , A ^ { 3 } , \ldots$ of a matrix. Suppose you need the hundredth power $A ^ { 1 0 0 }$ . Its columns are very close to the eigenvector $\pmb { x } = ( . \pmb { 6 } , . \pmb { 4 } )$

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { . 8 } & { . 9 } \\ { . 2 } & { . 7 } \end{array} \right] } \quad A _ { 2 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { . 7 0 } & { . 4 5 } \\ { . 3 0 } & { . 5 5 } \end{array} \right] } \quad A _ { 3 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { . 6 5 0 } & { . 5 2 5 } \\ { . 3 5 0 } & { . 4 7 5 } \end{array} \right] } \qquad A ^ { 1 0 0 } \approx { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { . 6 0 0 0 } & { . 6 0 0 0 } \\ { . 4 0 0 0 } & { . 4 0 0 0 } \end{array} \right] }
$$

$A ^ { 1 0 0 }$ was found by using the eigenvalues 1 and $\mathbf { 1 / 2 }$ of this A, not by multiplying 100 matrices. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are a new way to see into the heart of a matrix.

To explain eigenvalues, we first explain eigenvectors. Almost all vectors will change direction, when they are multiplied by A. Certain exceptional vectors x are in the same direction as Ax. Those are the "eigenvectors". Multiply an eigenvector by A, and the vector Ax is a number λ times the original x.

The basic equation is $A { \pmb x } = \lambda { \pmb x }$ . The number λ is an eigenvalue of A.

The eigenvalue λ tells whether the special vector x is stretched or shrunk or reversed when it is multiplied by A. We may find $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda = 2 \ : \mathbf { o r } \ : \frac { 1 } { 2 } \ : \mathbf { o r } - 1 } \end{array}$ . The eigenvalue λ could be zero! Then $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 } \pmb { x }$ means that this eigenvector x is in the nullspace of A.

If A is the identity matrix, every vector has $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { x } .$ All vectors are eigenvectors of I. All eigenvalues “lambda" are $\lambda = 1$ . This is unusual to say the least. Most 2 by 2 matrices have two eigenvector directions and two eigenvalues. We will show that det $( A - \lambda I ) = 0$

This section explains how to compute the $\pmb { x } \mathbf { \ ' s }$ and $\lambda ^ { \bullet }$ It can come early in the course. We only need the determinant ad — bc of a 2 by 2 matrix. The eigenvector $\pmb { x } _ { 1 }$ is a “steady state" that doesn't change (because it has $\pmb { \lambda _ { 1 } } = \pmb { 1 } )$ The eigenvector $\pmb { x _ { 2 } }$ is a “decaying mode" that virtually disappears (because $\lambda _ { 2 } = . 5 )$ The higher the power of $A ,$ the more closely its columns approach the steady state.

This particular A is called a Markov matrix. Its largest eigenvalue is $\lambda = 1$ . Its eigenvector ${ \pmb x } _ { 1 } = ( . 6 , . 4 )$ is the steady state—which all columns of $A ^ { k }$ will approach. See Appendix 8. A giant Markov matrix is the key to Google's superfast web search.

For projection matrices P, the column space projects to itself $( P x = x )$ . The nullspace of P projects to zero $( P \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 } \pmb { x } )$ . The eigenvalues of $P$ are $\lambda = 1$ and $\lambda = 0$

Example 2 The projection matrix $P = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { . 5 } & { . 5 } \\ { . 5 } & { . 5 } \end{array} \right] }$ has eigenvalues $\lambda = 1$ and $\lambda = 0$

Then $P { \pmb x } _ { 1 } = { \pmb x } _ { 1 }$ (steady state) and $P { \pmb x } _ { 2 } = { \pmb 0 }$ (nullspace). This example is a Markov matrix and a singular matrix (with $\lambda = 0 )$ Most important, $P$ is a symmetric matrix. That makes its eigenvectors orthogonal.

1. Markov matrix : Each column of P adds to 1. Then $\lambda = 1$ is an eigenvalue.

2. $\pmb { P }$ is a singular matrix. $\lambda = 0$ is an eigenvalue.

The only eigenvalues of a projection matrix are 0 and 1. The eigenvectors for $\lambda = 0$ (which means $\pmb { P x } = \pmb { 0 x } )$ fill up the nullspace. The eigenvectors for $\lambda = 1$ (which means $P \pmb { x } = \pmb { x } )$ fill up the column space. The nullspace is projected to zero. The column space projects onto itself. The Equation for the Eigenvalues : det $( A - \lambda I ) = 0$

For projection matrices we found λ's and $\pmb { x } \mathbf { \ ' s }$ by geometry: $\textbf {  { P x } } = \textbf {  { x } }$ and $P { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 } .$ For other matrices we use determinants and linear algebra. This is the key calculation almost every application starts by solving det $\left( A - \lambda I \right) = 0$ and $A { \pmb x } = \lambda { \pmb x }$

First move λx to the left side. Write the equation $A { \pmb x } = \lambda { \pmb x }$ as $( A - \lambda I ) { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 } .$ The matrix $A - \lambda I$ times the eigenvector x is the zero vector. The eigenvectors make up the nullspace of $A - \lambda I$ . When we know an eigenvalue λ, we find an eigenvector by solving $( A - \lambda I ) \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$

Eigenvalues first. If $( A - \lambda I ) \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ has a nonzero solution, $A - \lambda I$ is not invertible. The determinant of A — λI must be zero. This is how to recognize an eigenvalue λ :

(5)

This “characteristic polynomial' det $( A - \lambda I )$ involves only λ, not x. Since λ appears all along the main diagonal of $A { - } { \lambda } I$ , the determinant in (5) includes $( - \lambda ) ^ { n }$ . Then equation (5) has n solutions $\lambda _ { 1 }$ to $\lambda _ { n }$ and A has n eigenvalues.

6.1. Introduction to Eigenvalues : Ax = λx

An n by n matrix has n eigenvalues (repeated λ's are possible !) Each λ leads to x :

For each eigenvalue λ solve $( A - \lambda I ) { \pmb x } = \mathbf { 0 } ~ \mathbf { o r } ~ A { \pmb x } = \lambda { \pmb x }$ to find an eigenvector x.

Example 4 $A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 } \end{array} \right] }$ is already singular (zero determinant). Find its λ's and $\pmb { x ^ { \prime } 5 } .$

When A is singular, $\lambda = 0$ is one of the eigenvalues. The equation $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 } \pmb { x }$ has solutions. They are the eigenvectors for $\lambda = 0$ But det $( A - \lambda I ) = 0$ is the way to find all $\lambda ^ { \bullet }$ and $\pmb { x } \mathbf { \ ' s }$ . Always subtract λI from A:

Subtract λ along the diagonal to find

$$
A - \lambda I = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { 1 - \lambda } & { 2 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 - \lambda } \end{array} \right] .\tag{6}
$$

Take the determinant $" a d \mathrm { ~ - ~ } b c "$ of this 2 by 2 matrix. From $1 - \lambda$ times $4 \mathrm { ~ - ~ } \lambda ,$ the “ad” part is $\lambda ^ { 2 } - 5 \lambda + 4$ . The $" b c "$ part, not containing λ, is 2 times 2.

$$
\operatorname* { d e t } { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 - \lambda } & { 2 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 - \lambda } \end{array} \right] } = ( 1 - \lambda ) ( 4 - \lambda ) - ( 2 ) ( 2 ) = \lambda ^ { 2 } - 5 \lambda .\tag{7}
$$

Set this determinant $\lambda ^ { 2 } - 5 \lambda$ to zero. One solution is $\lambda = 0$ (as expected, since A is singular). Factoring into λ times $\lambda - 5$ , the other root is $\lambda = 5$

$\operatorname* { d e t } ( A - \lambda I ) = \lambda ^ { 2 } - 5 \lambda = 0$ yields the eigenvalues $\pmb { \lambda _ { 1 } } = \pmb { 0 }$ and $\lambda _ { 2 } = 5 .$

Now find the eigenvectors. Solve $( A - \lambda I ) { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ separately for $\lambda _ { 1 } = 0$ and $\lambda _ { 2 } = 5$

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { ( A - 0 I ) \mathbf { x } = { } } & { { } \left[ { \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { 2 } \\ { 2 } & { 4 } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { c } { y } \\ { z } \end{array} } \right] = \left[ { \begin{array} { c } { 0 } \\ { 0 } \end{array} } \right] } \end{array}
$$

yields an eigenvector

$$
\boxed { y } = \boxed { 2 }
$$

$$
( A - 5 I ) { \pmb x } = \left[ \frac { - 4 } { 2 } - 1 \right] \left[ \pmb { y } \right] = \left[ 0 \right]
$$

yields an eigenvector

$$
{ \Bigg | } { \Bigg [ } { \pmb y } { \Bigg ] } = { \Bigg [ } { \pmb 1 } { \Bigg ] } \quad { \Bigg | } \mathbf { f o r } \lambda _ { 2 } = 5
$$

The matrices $A - 0 I$ and $A - 5 I$ are singular (because 0 and 5 are eigenvalues). The eigenvectors $( 2 , - 1 )$ and (1, 2) are in the nullspaces: $( A - \lambda I ) { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ is $A { \pmb x } = \lambda { \pmb x }$

We need to emphasize: There is nothing exceptional about $\lambda = 0$ Like every other number, zero might be an eigenvalue and it might not. If A is singular, the eigenvectors for $\lambda = 0$ fill the nullspace: $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \mathbf { 0 } \pmb { x } = \mathbf { 0 }$ . If A is invertible, zero is not an eigenvalue.

In the example, the shifted matrix $A - 5 I$ is singular and 5 is the other eigenvalue.

Summary To solve the eigenvalue problem for an n by n matrix, follow these steps :

1. Compute the determinant of $A - \lambda I$ With λ subtracted along the diagonal, this determinant starts with $\lambda ^ { n } _ { 0 } \tau - \lambda ^ { n }$ . It is a polynomial in λ of degree n.

2. Find the roots of this polynomial, by solving det $( A - \lambda I ) = 0$ The n roots are the n eigenvalues of A. They make $A - \lambda I$ singular.

3. For each eigenvalue $\lambda ,$ solve $( A - \lambda I ) { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ to find an eigenvector x.

A note on the eigenvectors of 2 by 2 matrices. When $A - \lambda I$ is singular, both rows are multiples of a vector (a, b). The eigenvector is any multiple of $( b , - a )$ . The example had

λ = 0 : rows of A − 0I in the direction (1, 2); eigenvector in the direction (2, −1)

λ = 5 : rows of A − 5I in the direction (−4, 2); eigenvector in the direction (2, 4).

Previously we wrote that last eigenvector as (1, 2). Both (1, 2) and (2, 4) are correct.   
There is a whole line of eigenvectors—any nonzero multiple of x is as good as x.   
MATLAB's eig(A) divides by the length, to make each eigenvector x into a unit vector.

We must add a warning. Some 2 by 2 matrices have only one line of eigenvectors. This can only happen when two eigenvalues are equal. (On the other hand $A = I$ has equal eigenvalues and plenty of eigenvectors.) Without a full set of eigenvectors, we don't have a basis. We can't write every v as a combination of eigenvectors. In the language of the next section, we can't diagonalize a matrix without n independent eigenvectors.

## Determinant and Trace

Bad news first: If you add a row of A to another row, or exchange rows, the eigenvalues usually change. Elimination does not preserve the λ's. The triangular U has its eigenvalues sitting along the diagonal—they are the pivots. But they are not the eigenvalues of A! Eigenvalues are changed when row 1 is added to row 2:

$$
U = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 3 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] } \quad \mathrm { h a s ~ } \lambda = 0 \ \mathrm { a n d ~ } \lambda = 1 ; \quad A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 3 } \\ { 2 } & { 6 } \end{array} \right] } \quad \mathrm { h a s ~ } \lambda = 0 \ \mathrm { a n d ~ } \lambda = 7 .
$$

Good news second: The product $\lambda _ { 1 }$ times $\lambda _ { 2 }$ and the sum $\lambda _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { 2 }$ can be found quickly from the matrix. For this A, the product is 0 times 7. That agrees with the determinant of A (which is 0). The sum of eigenvalues is ${ \bf 0 } + { \bf 7 } .$ That agrees with the sum down the main diagonal (the trace is $\mathbf { 1 + 6 } )$ . These quick checks always work

The product $( \lambda _ { 1 } ) \cdots ( \lambda _ { n } )$ of the n eigenvalues equals the determinant of A $\lambda _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { 2 } + \cdots + \lambda _ { n }$ equals the sum of the n diagonal entries = (trace of A)

Those checks are very useful. They are proved in Problems 16–17 and again in the next section. They don't remove the pain of computing $\pmb { \lambda ^ { \bullet } }$ . But when the computation is wrong, they generally tell us so. To compute the correct $\lambda ^ { \bullet }$ go back to det $( A - \lambda I ) = 0$

The trace and determinant do tell everything when the matrix is 2 by 2. We never want to get those wrong! Here trace = 3 and det = 2, so they all have λ = 1 and 2 :

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { 1 } & { 9 } \\ { 0 } & { 2 } \end{array} \right] \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { 3 } & { 1 } \\ { - 2 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } \left[ \begin{array} { r r } { 7 } & { - 3 } \\ { 1 0 } & { - 4 } \end{array} \right] .\tag{8}
$$

That first A is one of the best matrices for finding eigenvalues: because it is triangular.

Why do the eigenvalues 1 and 2 of that triangular matrix lie along its diagonal ?

## Imaginary Eigenvalues

One more bit of news (not too terrible). The eigenvalues might not be real numbers.

Example 5 $\pmb { T h e 9 0 } ^ { \circ }$ rotation $Q = \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { - 1 } \\ { 1 } & { \phantom { - } } \end{array} } \right]$ has no real eigenvectors. Its eigenvalues   
are $\pmb { \lambda _ { 1 } } = \pmb { i }$ and $\lambda _ { 2 } = - i$ Then λ₁ + λ2 = trace = 0 and $\lambda _ { 1 } \lambda _ { 2 } = d e t e r m i n a n t { = } 1 .$

After a rotation, no real vector $\pmb { Q x }$ stays in the same direction as x $( { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ is useless).   
There cannot be an eigenvector, unless we go to imaginary numbers. Which we do.

To see how $i = \sqrt { - 1 }$ can help, look at $Q ^ { 2 }$ which is -I. If Q is rotation through $9 0 ^ { \circ }$ then $Q ^ { 2 }$ is rotation through $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ . Its eigenvalues are −1 and -1. (Certainly -Ix = -1x.) Squaring $Q$ will square each $\lambda ,$ so we must have $\lambda ^ { 2 } = - 1$ . The eigenvalues of the $9 0 ^ { \circ }$ rotation matrix $Q a r e + i a n d - i .$ , because $i ^ { 2 } = - 1$

Those $\lambda \mathbf { \dot { s } }$ come as usual from det $( Q - \lambda I ) = 0$ .This equation gives $\lambda ^ { 2 } + 1 = 0$ Its roots are i and -i. We meet the imaginary numbers i and -i also in the eigenvectors :

Complex

eigenvectors

$$
\left[ { \begin{array} { r r } { 0 } & { - 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 0 } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { r } { 1 } \\ { i } \end{array} } \right] = - i \left[ { \begin{array} { r } { 1 } \\ { i } \end{array} } \right] \qquad { \mathrm { a n d } } \qquad \left[ { \begin{array} { r r } { 0 } & { - 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 0 } \end{array} } \right] \left[ { \begin{array} { r } { i } \\ { 1 } \end{array} } \right] = i \left[ { \begin{array} { r } { i } \\ { 1 } \end{array} } \right] .
$$

Somehow these complex vectors ${ \pmb x } _ { 1 } = ( 1 , i )$ and ${ \pmb x } _ { 2 } = ( i , 1 )$ keep their direction as they are rotated in complex space. Don't ask me how. This example makes the important point that real matrices can easily have complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The particular eigenvalues i and —i also illustrate two properties of the special matrix $Q$

1. $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix so the absolute value of each λ is $| \lambda | = 1$

2. $Q$ is a skew-symmetric matrix so each λ is pure imaginary.

A symmetric matrix $( \pmb { S } ^ { \pmb { T } } = \pmb { S } )$ can be compared to a real number. A skew-symmetric matrix $( A ^ { \mathbf { T } } = - A )$ can be compared to an imaginary number. An orthogonal matrix $( Q ^ { \mathbf { T } } Q = I )$ corresponds to a complex number with $| \lambda | = 1$ . For the eigenvalues of S and A and $Q .$ , those are more than analogies—they are facts to be proved.

The eigenvectors for all these special matrices are perpendicular. Somehow (i, 1) and $( 1 , i )$ are perpendicular (Section 6.4 will explain the dot product of complex vectors).

## Eigenvalues of AB and $\pmb { A } \mathrm { + } \pmb { B }$

The first guess about the eigenvalues of AB is not true. An eigenvalue λ of A times an eigenvalue $\beta$ of B usually does not give an eigenvalue of AB:

False proof

$$
A B x = A \beta x = \beta A x = \beta \lambda x .\tag{9}
$$

It seems that $\beta$ times λ is an eigenvalue. When x is an eigenvector for A and B, this proof is correct. The mistake is to expect that A and B automatically share the same eigenvector x. Usually they don't. Eigenvectors of A are generally not eigenvectors of B.

A and B could have all zero eigenvalues while 1 is an eigenvalue of AB and $A + B$

$$
A = \left[ 0 \quad 1 \right] \quad { \mathrm { a n d } } \quad B = \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { 1 } & { 0 } \end{array} } \right] ; \quad { \mathrm { t h e n } } \quad A B = \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} } \right] \quad { \mathrm { a n d } } \quad A + B = \left[ { \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 0 } \end{array} } \right] .
$$

For the same reason, the eigenvalues of $A + B$ are generally not $\lambda + \beta$ Here $A + B$ has eigenvalues 1 and -1 while λ and $\beta$ are zero. (At least the trace of $A + B$ is zero.)

The false proof suggests what is true. Suppose x really is an eigenvector for both A and B. Then we do have $A B \pmb { x } = \lambda \beta \pmb { x }$ and $B A \pmb { x } = \lambda \beta \pmb { x }$ . When all n eigenvectors are shared by A and B, we can multiply eigenvalues and we find $A B = B A$ . That test is important in quantum mechanics—time out to mention this application of linear algebra :

A and B share the same n independent eigenvectors if and only if $A B = B A .$

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle In quantum mechanics, the position matrix P and the momentum matrix $\pmb { Q }$ do not commute. In fact $Q P - P Q = I$ (these are infinite matrices). To have $P \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ at the same time as $Q \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ would require $\pmb { x } = I \pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ If we knew the position exactly, we could not also know the momentum exactly. Problem 36 derives Heisenberg's uncertainty principle $\| P x \| \| Q x \| \geq { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \| x \| ^ { 2 }$

## REVIEW OF THE KEY IDEAS

1. Ax = λx says that eigenvectors x keep the same direction when multiplied by A.

2. Ax = λx also says that $\operatorname* { d e t } ( A - \lambda I ) = 0$ This equation determines n eigenvalues.

3. The sum of the λ's equals the sum down the main diagonal of A (the trace). The product of the λ's equals the determinant of A.

4. Projections P, exchanges E, 90° rotations Q have eigenvalues $1 , 0 , - 1 , i , - i .$ Singular matrices have $\lambda = 0$ . Triangular matrices have λ's on their diagonal.

5. Special properties of a matrix lead to special eigenvalues and eigenvectors. That is a major theme of Chapter 6.

6.1. Introduction to Eigenvalues : $A x = \lambda x$

Solution The eigenvalues of A come from det $( A - \lambda I ) = 0$

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { \quad 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { - 1 } & { \quad 2 } \end{array} \right] } \qquad \operatorname* { d e t } ( A - \lambda I ) = { \left| \begin{array} { l l } { 2 - \lambda } & { - 1 } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 - \lambda } \end{array} \right| } = \lambda ^ { 2 } - 4 \lambda + 3 = 0 .
$$

This factors into $( \lambda - 1 ) ( \lambda - 3 ) = 0$ so the eigenvalues of A are $\lambda _ { 1 } = 1$ and $\lambda _ { 2 } = 3$ . For the trace, the sum $\mathbf { 2 } + \mathbf { 2 }$ agrees with $\mathbf { 1 } + \mathbf { 3 } .$ The determinant 3 agrees with the product $\lambda _ { 1 } \lambda _ { 2 }$

The eigenvectors come separately by solving $( A - \lambda I ) { \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ which is $A { \pmb x } = \lambda { \pmb x }$

$$
\lambda = 1 \colon ( A - I ) { \pmb x } = \left[ - 1 - 1 \right] \left[ { \pmb x } \right] = \left[ 0 \right] \mathrm { g i v e s t h e ~ e i g e n v e c t o r ~ } { \pmb x } _ { 1 } = \left[ 1 \right]
$$

$$
\lambda = 3 \colon ( A - 3 I ) { \pmb x } = \left[ - 1 - 1 \right] \left[ { \pmb x } \right] = \left[ 0 \right] \mathrm { { g i v e s \ t h e \ e i g e n v e c t o r } } x _ { 2 } = \left[ - 1 \right]
$$

$A ^ { 2 }$ and $A ^ { - 1 }$ and $A + 4 I$ keep the same eigenvectors as A itself. Their eigenvalues are $\lambda ^ { 2 }$ and $\lambda ^ { - 1 }$ and $\lambda + 4$

$$
A ^ { 2 } { \mathrm { ~ h a s ~ e i g e n v a l u e s ~ } } 1 ^ { 2 } = 1 { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } 3 ^ { 2 } = 9 A ^ { - 1 } { \mathrm { ~ h a s ~ } } { \frac { 1 } { 1 } } { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } { \frac { 1 } { 3 } } A + 4 I { \mathrm { ~ h a s ~ } } ^ { 1 + 4 } = 7
$$

Notes for later sections: A has orthogonal eigenvectors (Section 6.3 on symmetric matrices). A can be diagonalized since $\lambda _ { 1 } \neq \lambda _ { 2 }$ (Section 6.2). A is similar to every 2 by 2 matrix with eigenvalues 1 and 3 (Section 6.2). A is a positive definite matrix (Section 6.3) since $A = A ^ { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { T } } }$ and the $\lambda ^ { \bullet }$ are positive.

6.1 B How can you estimate the eigenvalues of any A? Gershgorin gave this answer.

Every eigenvalue of A must be “near" at least one of the entries ${ a } _ { i i }$ on the main diagonal. For λ to be “near $\pmb { a _ { i i } } ^ { \prime \prime }$ means that $\left| a _ { i i } - \lambda \right|$ is no more than the sum $\pmb { R _ { i } }$ of all other $| a _ { i j } |$ in that row i of the matrix. Then Ri is the radius of a circle centered at $R _ { i }$ $\pmb { a _ { \mathrm { i i } } }$

Every λ is in the circle around one or more diagonal entries $a _ { i i } \colon | a _ { i i } - \lambda | \leq R _ { i }$

Here is the reasoning. When λ is an eigenvalue, $A - \lambda I$ is not invertible. Then $A - \lambda I$ cannot be diagonally dominant (see Section 2.5). So at least one diagonal entry $\mathbf { \delta } \mathbf { a } _ { i i } - \lambda$ is not larger than the sum $R _ { i }$ of all other entries $\left| a _ { i j } \right|$ (we take absolute values!) in row i.

Example Every eigenvalue λ of this A falls into one or both of the Gershgorin circles: The centers are a and d. The radii of the circles are $R _ { 1 } = \left| \boldsymbol { b } \right|$ and $R _ { 2 } = | c |$

$$
A = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] } \qquad { \mathrm { F i r s t ~ c i r c l e : } } \quad | \lambda - a | \leq | b |
$$

Those are circles in the complex plane, since λ could certainly be a complex number.

6.1 C Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of this symmetric 3 by 3 matrix $s$

Symmetric matrix

Singular matrix

$$
S = \left[ { \begin{array} { r r r } { 1 } & { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 } & { - 1 } \\ { 0 } & { - 1 } & { 1 } \end{array} } \right]
$$

Trace 1 + 2 + 1 = 4

Solution Since all rows of S add to zero, the vector $\pmb { x } = ( 1 , 1 , 1 )$ gives $\pmb { S x } = \pmb { 0 }$ This is an eigenvector for $\lambda = 0$ To find $\lambda _ { 2 }$ and $\lambda _ { 3 }$ , compute the 3 by 3 determinant :

$$
\mathsf { d e t } ( S - \lambda I ) = \left| \begin{array} { l l l } { 1 - \lambda } & { - 1 } & { 0 } \\ { - 1 } & { 2 - \lambda } & { - 1 } \\ { ~ 0 } & { - 1 } & { 1 - \lambda } \end{array} \right| = ( 1 - \lambda ) ( 2 - \lambda ) ( 1 - \lambda ) - 2 ( 1 - \lambda )
$$

Those three factors give $\lambda = 0 , 1 , 3$ as the solutions to det $( S - \lambda I ) = 0$ . Each eigenvalue corresponds to an eigenvector (or a line of eigenvectors) :

$$
\mathbf { x } _ { 1 } = { \left[ 1 \atop 1 \right] } S x _ { 1 } = \mathbf { 0 } x _ { 1 } x _ { 2 } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 1 } \\ { 0 } \\ { - 1 } \end{array} \right] } S x _ { 2 } = \mathbf { 1 } x _ { 2 } x _ { 3 } = { \left[ - 2 \atop 1 \right] } S x _ { 3 } = 3 x _ { 3 } .
$$

I notice again that eigenvectors are perpendicular when S is symmetric. We were lucky to find $\pmb { \lambda = 0 , 1 , 3 }$ For a larger matrix I would use $\mathbf { e i g } ( A )$ , and never touch determinants.

The full command $[ { \pmb X } , { \pmb E } ] = { \bf e i g } ( { \pmb A } )$ will produce unit eigenvectors in the columns of X.
