This chapter combines calculus with linear algebra. The overall problem is to minimize a function ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ that depends on many variables $\pmb { x } = \left( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \right)$ . Suppose we know the first derivatives of F—those are partial derivatives and they go into the gradient vector $\nabla F = ( \partial F / \partial x _ { 1 } , \dots , \partial F / \partial x _ { n } )$ . Then at a “smooth" minimum point $\pmb { x } ^ { \ast }$ of ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ calculus tells us that $\nabla F ( { \pmb x } ^ { * } ) = { \pmb 0 }$ . That is a fundamental problem : To solve n equations $\nabla F ( { \pmb x } ) = { \pmb 0 }$ with n unknowns $\pmb { x _ { 1 } }$ to $\pmb { x _ { n } }$

An important model problem has a quadratic function $\begin{array} { r } { Q ( { \pmb x } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } { \pmb x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } S { \pmb x } - { \pmb b } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { \mathrm x } } \end{array}$ e. In this case the gradient vector is $\nabla Q ( x ) = S x - b . \ S _ { 0 } \ \nabla Q = 0$ is a set of n linear equations $\pmb { S x } = \pmb { b }$ .When S is a symmetric positive definite (constant) matrix, the solution $\pmb { x } ^ { * }$ will be the minimum point for $\pmb { Q } ( \pmb { x } )$

When F is not quadratic, its gradient $\nabla F$ is not linear and its second derivative matrix ${ \pmb S } ( { \pmb x } )$ is not constant. But if ${ \pmb S } ( { \pmb x } )$ is everywhere positive definite, then $\pmb { F }$ is a convex function. Its graph is still (roughly) a bowl. Section 9.1 follows $- \nabla F$ down towards $\pmb { x } ^ { \ast }$ And Section 9.2 shows how to compute that gradient $\nabla F$ by “backpropagation".

There is another serious possibility to deal with in 9.3 and 9.4. There can be restrictions (constraints) on the allowed solutions x. A model problem could minimize a quadratic $\pmb { Q } ( \pmb { x } )$ or a linear cost $\pmb { c } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { x }$ with the constraints $\pmb { A } \pmb { x } = \pmb { b }$ and ${ \pmb x } \geq { \pmb 0 }$ (meaning that every ${ \pmb x } _ { i } \geq { \bf 0 } )$ . Now the graph of $\pmb { Q } ( \pmb { x } )$ (the bowl) is chopped off by m vertical planes $\pmb { x _ { i } } = \pmb { 0 }$ The key problem is to know if $\pmb { x _ { i } } > 0$ or $\pmb { x _ { i } } = \pmb { 0 }$ at the minimum.

The way to deal with a constraint like ${ \pmb x } _ { 1 } \geq { \pmb 0 }$ is to introduce a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda _ { 1 }$ Before that, Sections 9.1-2 explain gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent. Those are the workhorses of deep learning in Chapter 10, with many variables in x.

## 9.1 Minimizing a Multivariable Function

Suppose $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { x } _ { n } )$ is a function of n variables. We need basic information about the first and second derivatives of F. Those are “partial derivatives" when $n > 1$

The important facts are in equations (1) and (2). I don't believe you need a whole course (too much about integrals) to use these facts in minimizing the function ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$

$$
| \begin{array} { l } { \mathrm { O n e ~ f u n c t i o n ~ } F } \\ { \mathrm { O n e ~ v a r i a b l e ~ } x } \end{array}  F ( x + \Delta x ) \approx F ( x ) + \Delta x \displaystyle \frac { d F } { d x } ( x ) + \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \Delta x ) ^ { 2 } \displaystyle \frac { d ^ { 2 } F } { d x ^ { 2 } } ( x ) |\tag{1}
$$

This is the beginning of a Taylor series—and we don't often go beyond that second order term. The first terms ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } ) + ( \Delta { \pmb x } ) ( d { \pmb F } / d { \pmb x } )$ give a first order approximation to $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } + \Delta \pmb { x } )$ using information at x. Then $1 / 2 ( \dot { \Delta x } ) ^ { 2 } \dot { F } ^ { \prime \prime }$ makes it a second order approximation.

The $\Delta \pmb { x }$ term gives a point on the tangent line—tangent to the graph of ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ . The $( \Delta x ) ^ { 2 }$ term moves from the tangent line to the “tangent parabola". The function $\pmb { F }$ will be convex—its slope increases and its graph bends upward, as in $y = x ^ { 2 } - \mathsf { w h e n }$ the second derivative is positive : $d ^ { 2 } F / d x ^ { 2 } > 0$ Equation (2) lifts (1) into n dimensions.

$$
{ \left| \begin{array} { l } { \scriptstyle { \mathrm { O n e ~ f u n c t i o n ~ } } F } \\ { \scriptstyle { \mathrm { V a r i a b l e s ~ } } x _ { 1 } \ { \mathrm { t o } } x _ { n } } \end{array} \right. } F ( x + \Delta x ) \approx F ( x ) + ( \Delta x ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } \ \nabla F + { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \ ( \Delta x ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } \ S \left( \Delta x \right)\tag{2}
$$

This is the important formula! The vector ∇F is the gradient of F—the column vector of n partial derivatives $\partial { \pmb F } / \partial { \pmb x } _ { 1 }$ to $\partial F / \partial x _ { n }$ . S is the symmetric matrix (Hessian matrix) of second derivatives $S _ { i j } = { \partial ^ { 2 } } F / { \partial x _ { i } \partial x _ { j } } = { \partial ^ { 2 } } F / { \partial x _ { j } \partial x _ { i } }$

The graph of $y = F ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ is now a surface in $( n + 1 )$ -dimensional space. The tangent line becomes a tangent plane at x. When the second derivative matrix S is positive definite, $\pmb { F }$ is a strictly convex function: it stays above its tangents. A convex function F has a minimum at $\pmb { x } ^ { \ast }$ if $\nabla F ( { \pmb x } ^ { * } ) = { \pmb 0 } ;$ n equations for $\pmb { x } ^ { * }$

This third formula from calculus goes directly to our vector equation $\nabla F ( { \pmb x } ) = { \pmb 0 }$ Starting from a point x, we want to take a step $\pmb { \triangle x }$ that brings us close to the solution.

$$
\boxed { \nabla F ( \boldsymbol { x } + \Delta \boldsymbol { x } ) \approx \nabla F ( \boldsymbol { x } ) + S ( \boldsymbol { x } ) \Delta \boldsymbol { x } = 0 \mathrm { ~ l e a d s ~ t o ~ } \Delta \boldsymbol { x } = - S ^ { - 1 } ( \boldsymbol { x } ) \nabla F ( \boldsymbol { x } ) } \boxed { 0 } \left[ \left( \left( \boldsymbol { x } + \Delta \boldsymbol { x } \right) + \left( \boldsymbol { x } \right) \Delta \boldsymbol { x } \right) + \left( \left( \boldsymbol { x } + \Delta \boldsymbol { x } \right) \Delta \boldsymbol { x } \right) \right] .\tag{3}
$$

That formula for $\pmb { \triangle x }$ tells us one step in Newton's Method. We are at a point $\pmb { x } _ { k }$ and we move to $x _ { k + 1 } = x _ { k } + \Delta x$ . The points ${ \pmb x } _ { 0 } , { \pmb x } _ { 1 } , { \pmb x } _ { 2 } , . . .$ . often converge quickly to the minimum point $\pmb { x } ^ { * }$ where $\nabla F ( { \pmb x } ^ { * } ) = { \pmb 0 }$ But the cost of fast convergence can be very high, to compute at each step all the second derivatives $\partial ^ { 2 } F / \partial x _ { i } \partial x _ { j }$ in the matrix $\pmb { S } ( \pmb { x } )$

Example 1 Our model function $\begin{array} { r } { F ( { \boldsymbol x } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } { \boldsymbol x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } S { \boldsymbol x } - { \boldsymbol x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } b } \end{array}$ has $\nabla F ~ = ~ S x - b .$ Newton's method using equation (3) solves $\nabla F { \bar { ( } } x ^ { * } ) = S x ^ { * } - b = 0$ in one step!

$$
x _ { 1 } - x _ { 0 } = \Delta x = - S ^ { - 1 } \nabla F ( x _ { 0 } ) = - S ^ { - 1 } ( S x _ { 0 } - b ) = - x _ { 0 } + S ^ { - 1 } b
$$

Cancel $- \pmb { x _ { 0 } }$ to see the point $\pmb { x } _ { 1 }$ where $\nabla F = \mathbf { 0 } : { \mathrm { i t ~ i s ~ } } x _ { 1 } = S ^ { - 1 } b = x ^ { * }$

Example 2 Apply Newton's method to solve $\nabla F = x ^ { 2 } - 4 = 0$ . The derivative is $S ( x ) = 2 x$ . Step k is $\Delta x = - ( 1 / S ( x _ { k } ) ) \nabla F ( x _ { k } )$

$$
x _ { k + 1 } - x _ { k } = \left( - 1 / 2 x _ { k } \right) \left( x _ { k } ^ { 2 } - 4 \right) \quad { \mathrm { o r } } \quad x _ { k + 1 } = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left( x _ { k } + { \frac { 4 } { x _ { k } } } \right) .\tag{4}
$$

The square root is $\begin{array} { r } { { \pmb x } ^ { * } = \sqrt { 4 } = 2 = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left( { \bf 2 } + \frac { 4 } { 2 } \right) } \end{array}$ . The key point is fast convergence to $\pmb { x } ^ { \bullet } .$ Start from $\pmb { x _ { 0 } = 4 }$

$$
x _ { 1 } = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left( x _ { 0 } + { \frac { 4 } { x _ { 0 } } } \right) = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left( 4 + { \frac { 4 } { 4 } } \right) = 2 . 5
$$

$$
x _ { 2 } = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left( x _ { 1 } + { \frac { 4 } { x _ { 1 } } } \right) = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left( 2 . 5 + { \frac { 4 } { 2 . 5 } } \right) = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left( 2 . 5 + 1 . 6 \right) = 2 . 0 5
$$

If you take 2 more steps, you see how quickly the error (the distance from ${ \sqrt { 4 } } = 2 )$ goes to zero. The count of zeros after the decimal point in $\pmb { x _ { k } } - 2$ doubles at every step.

$$
x _ { 0 } = 4 \qquad x _ { 1 } = 2 . 5 \qquad x _ { 2 } = 2 . 0 5 \qquad x _ { 3 } = 2 . 0 0 0 6 \qquad x _ { 4 } = 2 . 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 9
$$

The wrong decimal is twice as far out at each step. The error ${ \pmb x } _ { { \pmb k } } - { \pmb 2 }$ is squared :

$$
\boxed { x _ { k + 1 } - 2 = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( x _ { k } + \frac { 4 } { x _ { k } } ) - 2 = \frac { 1 } { 2 x _ { k } } ( x _ { k } - 2 ) ^ { 2 } } \lceil \| x _ { k + 1 } - x ^ { * } \| \approx \frac { 1 } { 4 } | | x _ { k } - x ^ { * } | | ^ { 2 } ,
$$

Squaring the error explains the speed of Newton's method—provided $\pmb { x } _ { \pmb { k } }$ is close to $\pmb { x } ^ { * }$

Summary Newton's method is fast near the true solution $\pmb { x } ^ { * }$ , because it uses the second derivatives of ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ . But those can be too expensive to compute—especially in high dimensions. Often neural networks are simply too large to use all the second derivatives of ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ . Gradient descent is the algorithm of choice for deep learning.

$$
\mathrm { G r a d i e n t D e s c e n t } = \mathrm { S t e e p e s t D e s c e n t }
$$

This section is about a fundamental problem: Minimize a function $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { x } _ { n } )$ Calculus teaches us that all the first derivatives $\partial \pmb { F } / \partial \pmb { x } _ { i }$ are zero at the minimum (when $\pmb { F }$ is smooth). If we have $\textbf { \textit { n } } = \textbf { 2 0 }$ unknowns (a small number in deep learning), then minimizing one function F produces 20 equations $\partial F / \partial x _ { i } = 0$ “Gradient descent" uses the derivatives $\partial { \pmb F } / \partial { \pmb x } _ { i }$ to find a direction that reduces ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ . The steepest direction, in which ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ decreases fastest at $\pmb { x } _ { \pmb { k } }$ , is given by the negative gradient $- \nabla F ( \pmb { x } _ { k } )$

Steepest Direction

$$
\mathrm { G r a d i e n t \ d e s c e n t } \qquad x _ { k + 1 } = x _ { k } - s _ { k } \nabla F ( x _ { k } )\tag{5}
$$

(5) is a vector equation for each step $k = 1 , 2 , 3 , . .$ . and ${ \pmb s } _ { \pmb { k } }$ is the stepsize or the learning rate. We hope to move toward the point $\pmb { x } ^ { \star }$ where the graph of ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ hits bottom.

We are willing to assume for now that 20 first derivatives exist and can be computed. We are not willing to assume that those 20 functions also have 20 convenient derivatives $\partial / \partial x _ { j } ( \partial F / \partial x _ { i } )$ . Those are the 210 second derivatives of F—which go into a 20 by 20 symmetric matrix S. (Symmetry reduces $n ^ { 2 } = 4 0 0$ to ${ \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ( n ^ { 2 } + n ) = 2 1 0$ derivatives.) The second derivatives would be very useful extra information, but in many problems we have to go without.

You should know that 20 first derivatives and 210 second derivatives don't multiply the computing cost by 20 and 210. The neat idea of automatic differentiation—rediscovered and extended as backpropagation in machine learning—makes the cost much smaller.

Return for a moment to equation (5). The step $- s _ { k } \nabla f ( \pmb { x } _ { k } )$ includes a minus sign (to descend) and a factor ${ \pmb s } _ { \pmb k }$ (to control the the stepsize) and the downhill vector $\nabla F$ (containing the first derivatives of $\pmb { F }$ computed at the current point ${ \pmb x } _ { k } )$ . A lot of thought and computational experience have gone into the choice of stepsize and search direction.

## The Derivative of ${ \pmb f } ( { \pmb x } ) : { \pmb n } = { \pmb 1 }$

The derivative of $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$ involves a limit—this is the key difference between calculus and algebra. We are comparing the values of $\pmb { f }$ at two nearby points x and $x + \Delta x .$ as $\Delta \pmb { x }$ approaches zero. More accurately, we are watching the slope $\Delta f / \Delta x$ between two points on the graph of $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$

$$
\mathrm { D e r i v a t i v e ~ o f ~ } f \mathrm { ~ a t ~ } x \quad \quad \frac { d f } { d x } = \operatorname* { l i m i t } \mathrm { ~ o f ~ } \frac { \Delta f } { \Delta x } = \operatorname* { l i m i t } \mathrm { ~ o f ~ } \left[ \frac { f ( x + \Delta x ) - f ( x ) } { \Delta x } \right] .\tag{6}
$$

This is a forward difference when $\Delta \pmb { x } > \mathbf { 0 }$ .It is a backward difference when $\Delta x < 0$ When we have the same limit from both sides, that number is the slope of the graph at x.

The ramp function ReL $\mathbf { U } ( x ) = f ( x ) = \mathbf { m } \mathbf { a } \mathbf { x } ( 0 , x )$ is heavily involved in deep learning. ReLU has unequal slopes 1 to the right and 0 to the left of $\textbf { \em x } = \textbf { 0 }$ . So the derivative of ReLU does not exist at that corner point in the graph.

For the smooth function $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } ) = \pmb { x } ^ { 2 } .$ the ratio $\Delta f / \Delta x$ will safely approach the derivative ${ d f } / { d x }$ from both sides. But the approach could be slow (just first order). Look again at the point ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$ , where the true derivative $d f / d x = 2 x$ is now zero :

$$
\mathrm { T h e ~ r a t i o } { \frac { \Delta f } { \Delta x } } { \mathrm { ~ a t ~ } } x = 0 { \mathrm { i s ~ } } { \frac { f ( \Delta x ) - f ( 0 ) } { \Delta x } } = { \frac { ( \Delta x ) ^ { 2 } - 0 } { \Delta x } } = \Delta x \mathrm { T h e n ~ l i m i t } = { \frac { d f } { d x } } = 0 .
$$

As explained in Section 2.5, we get a better ratio (closer to the limiting slope ${ d f } / { d x } )$ by averaging the forward difference (where $\Delta \mathfrak { x } > 0 )$ with the backward difference (where $\Delta x < 0 )$ . Their average is a more accurate centered difference.

$$
\begin{array}{c} { \begin{array} { l } { { \mathrm { C e n t e r e d ~ } } \displaystyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left[ { \frac { f ( x + \Delta x ) - f ( x ) } { \Delta x } } + { \frac { f ( x - \Delta x ) - f ( x ) } { - \Delta x } } \right] = { \frac { f ( x + \Delta x ) - f ( x - \Delta x ) } { 2 \Delta x } } } \\ { \displaystyle \qquad { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } } \end{array} } { \mathrm { ~ } } { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }  \end{array}\tag{7}
$$

For the example $f ( x ) = x ^ { 2 }$ this centering will produce the exact derivative $d f / d x = 2 x$ In the picture we are averaging plus and minus slopes to get the correct slope 0 at ${ \pmb x } = { \pmb 0 }$

For all smooth functions, the centered differences reduce the error to size $( \Delta x ) ^ { 2 }$ . This is a big improvement over the error of size $\pmb { \Delta x }$ for uncentered differences $f ( x + \Delta x ) - f ( x )$

![](images/332ea0c9a0eb18fdc244394f8ba8a56abfa3c7e44076e9174e0e41f9d3260ab3.jpg)  
Figure 9.1: ReLU function = Ramp from deep learning. Centered slope of $\scriptstyle f = x ^ { 2 }$ is exact.

Most finite difference approximations are centered for extra accuracy. But we are still dividing by a small number $\mathbf { 2 } \Delta \pmb { x } .$ And for a multivariable function $F ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ we will need ratios $\Delta F / \Delta x _ { i }$ in n different directions—possibly for large n. Those ratios approximate the n partial derivatives that go into the gradient vector grad ${ \pmb F } = \pmb \nabla F$

The gradient of $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { x } _ { n } )$ is the column vector $\nabla F = \left( { \frac { \partial F } { \partial x _ { 1 } } } , \ldots , { \frac { \partial F } { \partial x _ { n } } } \right)$

Its components are the n partial derivatives of F. ∇F points in the steepest direction. Examples 3-5 will show the value of vector notation $( \nabla F$ is always a column vector)

Example 3 For a constant column vector a, $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } ) = \pmb { a } ^ { \dag } \pmb { x }$ has gradient $\nabla F = \mathbf a$ The partial derivatives of $\pmb { F } = a _ { 1 } x _ { 1 } + \cdots + a _ { n } x _ { n }$ are the numbers $\partial F / \partial x _ { k } = a _ { k }$

Example 4 For a symmetric matrix S, the gradient of ${ \pmb F } = \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } { \pmb x } ^ { \mathsf { T } } S { \pmb x }$ is $\nabla F = S x$ To see this for ${ \pmb n = 2 }$ , write out the function ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } _ { 1 } , { \pmb x } _ { 2 } )$ . The matrix $\pmb { S }$ is 2 by 2 :

$$
F = \frac { \left[ x _ { 1 } \quad x _ { 2 } \right] } { 2 } \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { a } & { b } \\ { b } & { c } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { c } { x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] = \begin{array} { c c } { \frac { 1 } { 2 } a x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } c x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } &  \left[ \begin{array} { c } { \partial f / \partial x _ { 1 } } \\ { \partial f / \partial x _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { a x _ { 1 } + b x _ { 2 } } \\ { b x _ { 1 } + c x _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] = S \left[ \begin{array} { c } { x _ { 1 } } \\ { x _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] . \end{array}
$$

Example 5 For a positive definite symmetric matrix $\pmb { S } ,$ the minimum of a quadratic $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \pmb { x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \pmb { S x } - \dot { \pmb { a } } ^ { \mathrm { T } } } \end{array}$ x is the negative number $\begin{array} { r } { { \cal F } _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } { \bf a } ^ { \mathrm { T } } S ^ { - 1 } { \bf a } } \end{array}$

This is an important example! The gradient is $\nabla F = S x - a$ .The minimum occurs at ${ \pmb x } ^ { * } = { \pmb S } ^ { - 1 } { \pmb a }$ where first derivatives of $\pmb { F }$ are zero:

$$
\begin{array} { r }  \boxed { \nabla F = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { \partial F / \partial x _ { 1 } } \\ { \vdots } \\ { \partial F / \partial x _ { n } } \end{array} \right] = S x - a = 0 \mathrm { a t } x ^ { * } = S ^ { - 1 } a = \arg \operatorname* { m i n } F . } \end{array}\tag{8}
$$

As always, that notation arg min $\pmb { F }$ stands for the point $\pmb { x } ^ { \ast }$ where the minimum of ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ is reached. Often we are more interested in this minimizing point $\pmb { x } ^ { \bullet }$ than in the actual minimum value ${ \cal F } _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = { \cal F } ( x ^ { * } )$ at that point.

$$
F _ { \mathrm { m i n } } \mathrm { i s } \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( S ^ { - 1 } a ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } S ( S ^ { - 1 } a ) - a ^ { \mathrm { T } } ( S ^ { - 1 } a ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } a ^ { \mathrm { T } } S ^ { - 1 } a - a ^ { \mathrm { T } } S ^ { - 1 } a = - \frac { 1 } { 2 } a ^ { \mathrm { T } } S ^ { - 1 } a .
$$

The graph of F is a bowl passing through zero at $\pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ and dipping to ${ \pmb { F } } _ { \mathbf { m i n } }$ at $\pmb { x } ^ { \ast }$

Example 6 The determinant $F ( { \pmb x } ) = \operatorname* { d e t } { \pmb X }$ is a function of all $n ^ { 2 }$ variables $\pmb { x _ { i j } }$ In the formula for det X, each $\pmb { x _ { i j } }$ along a row is multiplied by its “cofactor" $C _ { i j }$ . This cofactor in Chapter 5 is a determinant of size $\pmb { n } - 1$ , using all the entries in $\pmb { X }$ except row i and column j—and $C _ { i j }$ also includes the plus or minus sign $( - 1 ) ^ { i + j }$

Partial derivatives $\nabla F = \frac { \partial ( \operatorname* { d e t } { X } ) } { \partial x _ { i j } } = C _ { i j }$ in the matrix C of cofactors of X.

Example 7 The logarithm of the determinant is a most remarkable function :

$L ( X ) = \log \left( \operatorname* { d e t } X \right)$ has partial derivatives ${ \frac { \partial { \pmb { L } } } { \partial x _ { i j } } } = { \frac { C _ { i j } } { \operatorname* { d e t } X } } = j ,$ i entry of $\pmb { X } ^ { - 1 }$

The chain rule for L = log $F \operatorname { i s } \ ( \partial L / \partial F ) ( \partial F / \partial x _ { i j } ) = ( 1 / F ) ( \partial F / \partial x _ { i j } ) = ( 1 / \operatorname* { d e t } X ) C _ { i i }$ Then this ratio of cofactor $c _ { i j }$ to det X gives the j, i entry of the inverse matrix $\pmb { X } ^ { - 1 }$

It is neat that $\pmb { X } ^ { - 1 }$ contains the $\scriptstyle n ^ { 2 }$ first derivatives of L = log det X. The second derivatives of L are remarkable too. We have $n ^ { 2 }$ variables $\pmb { x } _ { i j }$ and $n ^ { 2 }$ first derivatives in $\pmb { \nabla } \pmb { L } = ( \pmb { X } ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { \pmb { \Gamma } }$ . This means $n ^ { 4 }$ second derivatives ! What is amazing is that the matrix of second derivatives is negative definite when $\pmb { X } = \pmb { S }$ is symmetric positive definite. So we reverse the sign of L: positive definite second derivatives ⇒ convex function. $\pmb { L }$

– log (det S) is a convex function of the entries of the positive definite matrix S.

## The Geometry of the Gradient Vector ∇F

Start with a function $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { y } )$ of n = 2 variables. Its gradient is $\nabla F = ( \partial F / \partial x , \partial F / \partial y )$ This vector changes length as we move the point x, y where the derivatives are computed :

$$
\nabla F = \left( { \frac { \partial F } { \partial x } } , { \frac { \partial F } { \partial y } } \right) \quad { \mathrm { L e n g t h } } = | | \nabla F | | = { \sqrt { \left( { \frac { \partial F } { \partial x } } \right) ^ { 2 } + \left( { \frac { \partial F } { \partial y } } \right) ^ { 2 } } } = { \mathrm { s t e e p e s t ~ s l o p e ~ o f ~ } } F
$$

That length $| | \nabla F | |$ tells us the steepness of the graph of $z = F ( x , y )$ The graph is normally a curved surface—like a valley in xyz space. At each point there is a slope $\partial \pmb { F } / \partial \pmb { x }$ in the x-direction and a slope $\partial \pmb { F } / \partial \pmb { y }$ in the y-direction. The steepest slope is in the direction of $\nabla F = \operatorname { g r a d } F .$ The magnitude of that steepest slope is $| | \nabla F | |$

Example 8 The graph of a linear function $F ( x , y ) = a x + b y$ is the plane $z = a x + b y$ The gradient is the vector $\nabla F = { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { a } \\ { b } \end{array} \right] }$ of partial derivatives. The length of that vector is $\left| \left| \nabla F \right| \right| = \sqrt { a ^ { 2 } + b ^ { 2 } } = \mathrm { s l o p e }$ of the roof. The slope is steepest in the direction of $\nabla F .$

That steepest direction is perpendicular to the level direction. The level direction z = constant has $a x + b y = { \mathrm { c o n s t a n t } } .$ It is the safe direction to walk, perpendicular to $\mathbf { v } \pmb { F }$ The component of $\nabla F$ in that flat direction is zero. Figure 9.2 shows the two perpendicular directions (level and steepest) on the plane $z = F ( x , y ) = x + 2 y$

![](images/4924f1c9b5bf3e4d113d083111f4c37c39bb1eeb22509eadad289233df812e94.jpg)  
Figure 9.2: The negative gradient –∇F gives the direction of steepest descent.

Our basic Example 9 will be $F ( x , y ) = a x ^ { 2 } + b y ^ { 2 }$ . Its gradient is $\pmb { \nabla } \pmb { F } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { 2 a x } \\ { 2 b y } \end{array} \right]$

$\nabla F$ tells us the steepest direction, changing from point to point. We are on a curved surface (a bowl opening upward). The bottom of the bowl is at $\scriptstyle x = y = 0$ where the gradient vector is zero. The slope in the steepest direction is $| | \nabla F | |$ . At the minimum, $\overleftarrow { \nabla } F = ( 2 a x , 2 b y ) = ( 0 , 0 )$ and $s l o p e = z e r o$ . The bowl is circular if ${ \pmb a } = { \pmb b } .$

The level direction has $z = a x ^ { 2 } + b y ^ { 2 } = \mathrm { c o n s t a n t h e i g h t }$ That plane $z =$ constant cuts through the bowl in a level curve. In this example the level curve $a x ^ { 2 } + b y ^ { 2 } = c$ is an ellipse. But there is a serious difficulty for steepest descent :

The steepest direction changes as you go down! The gradient doesn't point to the bottom!

![](images/832fdb89b804af3b0ed99cefa6c7cbd889b2320d00b5560d919112c2ea68bf59.jpg)

steepest direction ∇F up and down the bowl $a x ^ { 2 } + b y ^ { 2 } = z$ flat direction $( \nabla F ) ^ { \perp }$ along the ellipse $a x ^ { 2 } + b y ^ { 2 } = { \mathrm { c o n s t a n t } }$

The steepest direction is perpendicular to the flat direction but x the steepest direction is not aimed at the minimum point

Figure 9.3: Steepest descent moves down the bowl in the gradient direction $\left[ { \frac { - 2 a x } { - 2 b y } } \right]$

Let me repeat. At the point $\pmb { x _ { 0 } }$ , yo the gradient direction for $\pmb { F } = \pmb { a x ^ { 2 } } + b y ^ { 2 }$ is along $\nabla F = \left( 2 a x _ { 0 } , 2 b y _ { 0 } \right)$ . The steepest line is $( x , y ) = ( x _ { 0 } , y _ { 0 } ) - s ( 2 a x _ { 0 } , 2 b y _ { 0 } )$ for all s. But if $a \neq b ,$ the lowest point $( { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } ) = ( { \pmb 0 } , { \pmb 0 } )$ does not lie on that line for any s.

We will not find that minimum point (0, 0) in one step of “gradient descent". The steepest direction does not lead to the bottom of the bowl—except when $\pmb { b } = \pmb { a }$ and the bowl is circular.

Water changes direction as it goes down a mountain. Sooner or later, we must change direction too. In practice we keep going in the gradient direction and stop when our cost function $\pmb { F }$ is not decreasing quickly. At that point Step 1 ends and we recompute the gradient ∇F. This gives a new descent direction for Step 2.

## An Important Example with Zig-Zag

The example $\begin{array} { r } { F ( x , y ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( x ^ { 2 } + b y ^ { 2 } ) } \end{array}$ is extremely useful for $0 < b \leq 1$ . Its gradient ∇ F has two components ${ \bar { \partial } } F / \partial x = x$ and $\partial \pmb { F } / \partial y = \pmb { b y }$ . The minimum value of $\pmb { F }$ is zero. That minimum is reached at the point $( x ^ { * } , y ^ { * } ) = ( 0 , 0 )$ . Best of all, steepest descent with exact line search (the best s) produces a simple formula for each $( x _ { k } , y _ { k } )$ in the·slow progress down the bowl toward (0, 0). Starting at $( x _ { 0 } , y _ { 0 } ) = ( b , 1 )$ we find these points :

$$
\left[ x _ { k } = b \left( { \frac { b - 1 } { b + 1 } } \right) ^ { k } y _ { k } = \left( { \frac { 1 - b } { 1 + b } } \right) ^ { k } F ( x _ { k } , y _ { k } ) = \left( { \frac { 1 - b } { 1 + b } } \right) ^ { 2 k } F ( x _ { 0 } , y _ { 0 } ) \right]\tag{9}
$$

If $b = 1$ , you see immediate success in one step. The point $\left( x _ { 1 } , y _ { 1 } \right)$ is (0, 0). The bowl is perfectly circular with $F = { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ( x ^ { 2 } + y ^ { 2 } )$ . The negative gradient direction goes exactly through (0, 0). Then the first step of gradient descent finds that correct minimizing point.

The real purpose of this example is seen when b is small. The crucial ratio in equation (9) is $r = ( 1 - b ) / ( 1 + b )$ . For $\ b = \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 1 0 } }$ this ratio is $r = 9 / 1 1$ . For $\begin{array} { r } { b = \frac { 1 } { 1 0 0 } } \end{array}$ the ratio is 99/101. The ratio is approaching 1 and the progress toward (0,0) has virtually stopped when b is very small.

Figure 9.4 shows the frustrating zig-zag pattern of the steps toward (0, 0). Every step is short and progress is very slow. This is a case where the stepsize $\pmb { s _ { k } }$ in ${ \pmb x } _ { k + 1 } = { \pmb x } _ { k } -$ $\mathbf { \mathop { s } } _ { k } \nabla F ( \mathbf { \mathop { x } } _ { k } )$ was exactly chosen to minimize $\pmb { F }$ (an exact line search). But the direction of $- \mathbf { v } \pmb { F }$ , even if steepest at $( x _ { k } , y _ { k } )$ , is pointing far from the final answer $( { \pmb x } ^ { * } , { \pmb y } ^ { * } ) = ( 0 , 0 )$

The bowl has become a narrow valley when b is small. We are uselessly crossing the valley instead of moving down the valley to the bottom at (0, 0).

## Momentum and the Path of a Heavy Ball

The slow zig-zag path of steepest descent is a real problem. We have to improve it. Our model example $\overrightarrow { F } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( x ^ { 2 } + b y ^ { 2 } )$ has only two variables x, y and its second derivative matrix is diagonal—constant entries ${ \cal F } _ { z z } = 1$ and ${ \pmb { F } } _ { { \pmb { u } } { \pmb { y } } } = { \pmb { b } } .$ But it shows the zig-zag problem very clearly when $b = \lambda _ { \mathrm { m i n } } / \lambda _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ is small.

Key idea: Zig-zag would not happen for a heavy ball rolling downhill. Its momentum carries it through the narrow valley—bumping the sides but moving mostly forward. So we add momentum with coefficient $\beta$ to the gradient (Polyak's important idea). This gives one of the most convenient and potentially useful ideas in deep learning.

![](images/e6bb4d8c3db0b10705204a6e43e3cbfb2bb08c2b2f603a4411d5dbfcabe6af03.jpg)

The first descent step starts out perpendicular to the level set. As it crosses through lower level sets, the function ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ is decreasing. Eventually its path is tangent to a level set L. Descent has stopped. Going further will increase F. The first step ends. The next step is perpendicular to L. So the zig-zag path took a 90 ° turn.

Note to the reader Deep learning in Chapter 10 involves a sum of many functions ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb v } _ { i } )$ —one for every vector ${ \pmb v } _ { \pmb i }$ in the training set. The the gradient is a sum of many gradients—too many to compute at each step. The solution in Section 9.2 is to randomly (“stochastically") choose only one or a few functions at every descent step.

Figure 9.4: Slow convergence on a zig-zag path to the minimum of $\pmb { F } = \pmb { x } ^ { 2 } + \pmb { b y } ^ { 2 }$

Key idea: The direction ${ z } _ { k }$ of the new step remembers the previous direction ${ z } _ { k - 1 }$

Descent with momentum

$$
\boxed { x _ { k + 1 } = x _ { k } - s z _ { k } \mathrm { ~ w i t h ~ } z _ { k } = \nabla F ( x _ { k } ) + \beta z _ { k - 1 } }\tag{10}
$$

Now we have two coefficients to choose—the stepsize s and also $\beta .$ Most important, the step to $\pmb { x } _ { k + 1 }$ in equation (10) involves $z _ { k - 1 }$ . Momentum has turned a one-step method (gradient descent) into a two-step method. To get back to one step, we have to rewrite equation (10) as two equations (one vector equation) for $( { \pmb x } , { \pmb z } )$ at time $k + 1$

Descent with

momentum

$$
\boxed { \begin{array} { l l } { { \pmb x } _ { k + 1 } } & { = { \pmb x } _ { k } - \pmb { s } { \pmb z } _ { k } } \\ { { \pmb z } _ { k + 1 } - \pmb \nabla F ( { \pmb x } _ { k + 1 } ) } & { = \qquad \beta { \pmb z } _ { k } } \end{array} }\tag{11}
$$

With those two equations, we have recovered a one-step method. This is exactly like reducing a single second order differential equation to a system of two first order equations.

## The Quadratic Model

When $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \pmb { x } ^ { \mathsf { T } } S \pmb { x } } \end{array}$ is quadratic, its gradient $\pmb { \nabla } \pmb { F } = S \pmb { x }$ is linear. This is the model problem to understand: S is symmetric positive definite and $\nabla F ( { \pmb x } _ { k + 1 } )$ becomes $S x _ { k + 1 }$ in equation (11). Our 2 by 2 supermodel is included, when the matrix S is diagonal with entries 1 and b. For every matrix $s ,$ you will see that its largest and smallest eigenvalues determine the best choices for $\beta$ and the stepsize s—so our 2 by 2 case actually contains the essence of the whole problem.

To follow the steps of accelerated descent, track each eigenvector q of S. Suppose $S q = \lambda q$ and $\pmb { x } _ { k } = \pmb { c } _ { k } \pmb { q }$ and $z _ { k } = d _ { k } q$ and $\nabla F _ { k } = S x _ { k } = \lambda c _ { k } \pmb { q } .$ Then our equation (11) connects the numbers $\pmb { c _ { k } }$ and $d _ { k }$ at step k to the next $c _ { k + 1 }$ and $d _ { k + 1 }$ at step $\pm 1$

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathrm { F o l l o w i n g ~ t h e } \qquad c _ { k + 1 } \qquad = c _ { k } - s d _ { k } \quad \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { - \lambda } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { c _ { k + 1 } } \\ { d _ { k + 1 } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { - s } \\ { 0 } & { \beta } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { c c } { c _ { k } } \\ { d _ { k } } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}\tag{12}
$$

Finally we invert the first matrix (−λ becomes +λ) to see each descent step clearly :

Descent step multiplies by R

$$
\begin{array} { r }  \boxed { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { c _ { k + 1 } } \\ { d _ { k + 1 } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { \lambda } & { 1 } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { - s } \\ { 0 } & { \beta } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { c _ { k } } \\ { d _ { k } } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { - s } \\ { \lambda } & { \beta - \lambda s } \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array} { l } { c _ { k } } \\ { d _ { k } } \end{array} \right] = R \left[ \begin{array} { l } { c _ { k } } \\ { d _ { k } } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}\tag{13}
$$

After k steps the starting vector is multiplied by $R ^ { k }$ . For fast convergence to zero (which is the minimum of $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { F } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \pmb { x } ^ { \mathrm { T } } S \pmb { x } ) } \end{array}$ we want both eigenvalues $_ { e _ { 1 } }$ and $e _ { 2 }$ of $R$ to be as small as possible. Clearly those eigenvalues of R depend on the eigenvalue λ of S. That eigenvalue λ could be anywhere between $\lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } ( S )$ and $\lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } ( S )$ . Our problem is :

Choose s and $\beta$ to minimize max $\Big [ \big | e _ { 1 } ( \lambda ) \big | , \big | e _ { 2 } ( \lambda ) \big | \Big ]$ for $\lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } ( S ) \leq \lambda \leq \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } }$ (S).

It seems a miracle that this problem has a beautiful solution. The optimal s and $\beta$ are

$$
| s = ( \frac { 2 } { \sqrt { \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } } + \sqrt { \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } } } ) ^ { 2 } \qquad \mathrm { a n d } \qquad \beta = ( \frac { \sqrt { \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } } - \sqrt { \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } } } { \sqrt { \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } } + \sqrt { \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } } } ) ^ { 2 } .\tag{14}
$$

Think of the 2 by 2 supermodel, when $s$ has eigenvalues $\lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } = 1$ and $\lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } = b$

$$
s = \left( { \frac { 2 } { 1 + { \sqrt { b } } } } \right) ^ { 2 } \quad \quad { \mathrm { a n d } } \quad \quad \beta = \left( { \frac { 1 - { \sqrt { b } } } { 1 + { \sqrt { b } } } } \right) ^ { 2 }\tag{15}
$$

These choices of stepsize and momentum give a convergence rate that looks like the rate in equation (9) for ordinary steepest descent (no momentum). But there is a crucial difference : The number b in (9) is replaced by $\sqrt { b }$ in (15).

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } { \boxed { \begin{array} { c c c } { \mathrm { ~ O r d i n a r y } } & { \left( \frac { 1 - b } { 1 + b } \right) ^ { 2 } } & & { \mathrm { A c c e l e r a t e d } } \\ { \mathrm { d e s c e n t ~ f a c t o r } } & { \left( \frac { 1 - b } { 1 + b } \right) ^ { 2 } } & & { \mathrm { d e s c e n t ~ f a c t o r } } \end{array} } } & { \left( \frac { 1 - \sqrt { b } } { 1 + \sqrt { b } } \right) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}\tag{16}
$$

So similar but so different. The real test comes when $\pmb { b }$ is very small. Then the ordinary descent factor is essentially $1 - 4 b$ very close to 1. The accelerated descent factor is essentially $1 - 4 { \sqrt { b } } ,$ much further below 1.

To emphasize the improvement that momentum brings, suppose $b = 1 / 1 0 0$ Then ${ \sqrt { b } } = 1 / 1 0$ (ten times larger than $\pmb { b } )$ . The convergence factors in equation (16) are

Steepest descent

$$
\left( \frac { . 9 9 } { 1 . 0 1 } \right) ^ { 2 } \approx . 9 6
$$

Accelerated descent

$$
\left( { \frac { . 9 } { 1 . 1 } } \right) ^ { 2 } \approx . 6 7
$$

Ten steps of ordinary descent multiply the starting error by 0.67. This is matched by a single momentum step. Ten steps with the momentum term multiply the error by 0.018.

Notice that the condition number $\lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } / \lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } ~ = ~ 1 / b$ of $\pmb { S }$ controls everything.

Note 1 Nesterov also created an improvement on gradient descent—different from momentum.

Note 2 “Adaptive" methods use all earlier choices of the step direction to modify the current direction $\nabla L _ { k }$ for the step to $\pmb { x } _ { k + 1 }$ . The formula for the current direction becomes $D _ { k } = \delta D _ { k - 1 } + ( 1 - \delta ) \nabla L _ { k }$ . Class projects confirmed the speedup that comes from using the earlier directions which went into $D _ { k - 1 }$

The batch size B in stochastic gradient descent can increase at later steps.

## 9.2 Backpropagation and Stochastic Gradient Descent

This short section explains the key computational step in deep learning. The goal of that step is to optimize the set of weights x in the learning function $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } )$ . We are given the “training data"—a large set of input vectors $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { N }$ . For each input vector ${ \pmb v } _ { i }$ we know the correct output vector $\pmb { w _ { i } }$ . Our goal is to choose the weights x so that the error vectors $\pmb { e } _ { i } = \pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } _ { i } ) - \pmb { w } _ { i }$ are as small as possible. We are fitting the learning function $\pmb { F }$ to the N points of training data, by choosing weights x that minimize the total loss $\pmb { L } ( \pmb { x } )$

Minimize

$$
L ( \pmb { x } ) = \frac { 1 } { N } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } \ell ( \pmb { e } _ { i } ) = \frac { 1 } { N } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } \ell ( \pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } _ { i } ) - \pmb { w } _ { i } ) .\tag{1}
$$

The best weights x will depend on the form we choose for the learning function ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb v } )$ The weights also depend on the loss function l that we choose to measure the errors $\pmb { e _ { i } }$ If we choose the “square loss" $\pmb { \ell } ( \pmb { e } ) = | | \pmb { e } | | ^ { 2 }$ , our problem is to find a least squares fit of the training data $( { \pmb v } _ { 1 } , { \pmb w } _ { 1 } ) , \dots , ( { \pmb v } _ { N } , { \pmb w } _ { N } )$

Here is a big picture of the problem. We are creating a function $\pmb { F }$ that approximates or even “interpolates" the training data: $F ( v _ { i } ) \approx w _ { i } \mathrm { f o r } i = 1 , . . . , N$ .Then when we have new test data V, we will estimate the unknown output W by our function ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb V } )$ Suppose we are trying to read a handwritten number W. We have N pictures $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { N }$ of known numbers $\pmb { w } _ { 1 } , \dots , \pmb { w } _ { N }$ . Based on that training data, how do we weight the pixels in the new picture V to learn the number W in that picture ?

Interpolation is an old problem. Deep learning is a new approach—much more successful than past approaches. One of the worst approaches is to fit the data by a very high degree polynomial F. The result is extremely unstable. A small change in the input V produces a large change in the output $\mathbf { \delta W } = \mathbf { \delta F } ( \mathbf { \delta V } )$ We have chosen the wrong form (a polynomial) for the learning function F. Chapter 10 will describe a much better choice for the form of ${ \pmb F } .$ This section is about "fitting the function $\pmb { F }$ to the training data". We are choosing the weights x to achieve $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } _ { i } ) \approx \pmb { w } _ { i }$ for each data point.

Three big steps are involved in constructing and using the learning function $\pmb { F }$

1 Choose the form of $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } )$ . It includes a nonlinear function, often $\mathbf { \ddot { R e L U } } ^ { \mathbf { \ " } }$

2 Compute the weights x in F that best fit the training data $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } _ { i } ) \approx \pmb { w } _ { i }$

3 Using those weights, evaluate ${ \pmb W } = { \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb V } )$ for new test data $\mathbf { v }$

Step 1 is the goal of Chapter 10 in this book. We will create a “neural $\mathbf { n e t } ^ { \prime \prime }$ to describe the form of ${ \pmb F } .$ The key point is that $\pmb { F }$ is produced by a chain of simpler functions ${ \pmb F } _ { 1 }$ to $\pmb { F } _ { \pmb { L } }$ •

$$
F ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } ) = F _ { L } ( F _ { L - 1 } ( . . . ( F _ { 2 } ( F _ { 1 } ( \pmb { v } ) ) ) ) )\tag{2}
$$

Each function $\pmb { F } _ { \pmb { k } }$ in that chain has its own set of weights $\pmb { x } _ { k }$ . You will see in Chapter 10 that the individual functions $\pmb { F } _ { \pmb { k } }$ have a simple piecewise linear form. It is the chain of functions ${ \pmb F } _ { 1 }$ to ${ { \pmb { F } } _ { L } }$ that produces a powerful learning function ${ \pmb F } .$

Section 10.1 will count the (large) number of linear pieces of $\pmb { F }$ created by ReLU.

This section describes the backpropagation algorithm that efficiently finds the derivatives of $\pmb { F }$ with respect to the weight matrices $\pmb { x } _ { 1 }$ to $\pmb { x } _ { L }$ in the functions ${ \pmb F } _ { 1 }$ to ${ { \pmb { F } } _ { L } }$ . By knowing those derivatives $\partial F _ { k } / \partial x _ { k }$ , we can use gradient descent (or stochastic gradient descent) to optimize the weights. So once the form of $\pmb { F }$ is chosen, deep learning is all about computing the weights x that minimize a sum of losses $\pmb { \ell } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } _ { i } )$

Loss function

$$
\ell ( x , v _ { i } ) = F ( x , v _ { i } ) - w _ { i } = \mathrm { a p p r o x i m a t e } - { \mathrm { t r u e } }
$$

A personal note. I am greatly in debt to two friends who explained the computation of the gradients $\mathbf { v } \mathbf { \mathbf { \mathbf { F } } }$ and ∇l (the derivatives of the loss with respect to the weights). One is Alexander Craig, who was a student in my Math 18.065 class at MIT. His project for the class was backpropagation, and his report waş wonderful. Alex shared in the writing of this section 9.2. My other source of support was Andreas Griewank, one of the principal creators of “automatic differentiation". This algorithm finds the derivatives of $\pmb { F }$ and l with respect to each of the weights with amazing speed. Applied recursively to the chain of L functions $\pmb { F } = \pmb { F } _ { L } ( \pmb { F } _ { L - 1 } ( \dots \pmb { F } _ { 1 } ) )$ this is backpropagation.

The reader will know that based on this computational engine, deep learning has been an overwhelming success.

## The Multivariable Chain Rule

We begin with the chain rule for a composite function $\pmb { h } ( \pmb { x } ) = \pmb { f } ( \pmb { g } ( \pmb { x } ) )$ of several input variables $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { m }$ . The outputs from ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb x } )$ have n components $g _ { 1 } , \ldots , g _ { n }$ . Then the outputs from ${ \pmb h } ( { \pmb x } ) = { \pmb f } ( { \pmb g } ( { \pmb x } ) )$ have $\pmb { p }$ components $h _ { 1 } , \ldots , h _ { p }$ The Jacobian matrices $\pmb { \partial } f / \pmb { \partial } \pmb { g }$ and $\pmb { \partial } \pmb { g } / \pmb { \partial } \pmb { x }$ contain the partial derivatives of $f$ and g separately :

$$
{ \frac { \partial f } { \partial g } } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c c } { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial f _ { 1 } } { \partial g _ { 1 } } } } } & { { \cdots } } & { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial f _ { 1 } } { \partial g _ { n } } } } } \\ { { \vdots } } & { { \vdots } } \\ { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial f _ { p } } { \partial g _ { 1 } } } } } & { { \cdots } } & { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial f _ { p } } { \partial g _ { n } } } } } \end{array} \right] \qquad { \frac { \partial g } { \partial x } } = \left[ \begin{array} { c c c } { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial g _ { 1 } } { \partial x _ { 1 } } } } } & { { \cdots } } & { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial g _ { 1 } } { \partial x _ { m } } } } } \\ { { \vdots } } & { { \vdots } } \\ { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial g _ { n } } { \partial x _ { 1 } } } } } & { { \cdots } } & { { \displaystyle { \frac { \partial g _ { n } } { \partial x _ { m } } } } } \end{array} \right]\tag{3}
$$

Each $h _ { i }$ depends on the $\pmb { g } ^ { \prime } \pmb { \mathrm { s } }$ and each ${ \pmb g } _ { \pmb j }$ depends on the $\pmb { x } \mathbf { \ ' s }$ .Therefore $h _ { i }$ depends on $\pmb { x } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { x } _ { m }$ . The chain rule aims to find all the derivatives $\partial h _ { i } / \partial x _ { k }$ . The scalar rule is a dot product (row i of $\pmb { \theta f } / \pmb { \theta g } )$ · (column k of ${ \pmb \theta } { \pmb g } / { \pmb \theta } { \pmb x } )$ . The multivariable chain rule for ${ \partial h } / { \partial x }$ is exactly the matrix product $\left( \partial f / \partial g \right) \left( \partial g / \partial x \right)$

$$
{ \frac { \partial h _ { i } } { \partial x _ { k } } } = { \frac { \partial h _ { i } } { \partial g _ { 1 } } } { \frac { \partial g _ { 1 } } { \partial x _ { k } } } + \cdots + { \frac { \partial h _ { i } } { \partial g _ { n } } } { \frac { \partial g _ { n } } { \partial x _ { k } } } = { \bigg ( } \mathbf { r o w } i \mathbf { o f } { \frac { \partial f } { \partial g } } { \bigg ) } \cdot { \bigg ( } \mathbf { c o l u m n } j \mathbf { o f } { \frac { \partial g } { \partial x } } { \bigg ) }\tag{4}
$$

The learning function $\pmb { F }$ is a chain of functions ${ \pmb F } _ { 1 }$ to ${ { \pmb { F } } _ { \pmb { L } } }$ . Then the matrix chain rule for the x-derivatives of $F _ { L } ( F _ { L - 1 } ( . . . F _ { 1 } ( v ) ) )$ becomes a product of $\pmb { L }$ matrices :

$$
\frac { \partial F } { \partial x } = \frac { \partial F _ { L } } { \partial F _ { L - 1 } } \frac { \partial F _ { L - 1 } } { \partial F _ { L - 2 } } \cdots \frac { \partial F _ { 1 } } { \partial x } 
$$

Matrix Chain Rule

## Stochastic Gradient Descent

Before we compute derivatives by backpropagation, there is an important decision to make. The loss function $\pmb { L } ( \pmb { x } )$ that we minimize is a sum of individual errors $\pmb { \ell } ( \pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } _ { i } ) - \pmb { w } _ { i } )$ for every sample ${ \pmb v } _ { \pmb i }$ in the training set. The derivative of ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb v } _ { i } )$ for one sample is hard enough! Computing derivatives for every sample with respect to every weight at every step of steepest descent is an enormous task. We have to reduce this computation.

Stochastic gradient descent randomly selects one sample input or a small batch of $B$ samples, to improve the weights from $\pmb { x } _ { k }$ to $\pmb { x } _ { k + 1 }$ . This works surprisingly well. Often the first descent steps show big improvements in the weights x. Close to the optimal weights, the iterations can become erratic and we may not see fast convergence—but high precision is not needed or expected. Often we can stop the descent iterations early. SGD reduces the cost of each gradient step (from weights $\pmb { x } _ { k }$ to $\pmb { x } _ { k + 1 } )$ to an acceptable level.

## SGD for Ordinary Least Squares

Least squares provides an excellent (and optional) test of this “stochastic"idea. We are minimizing $| | A \pmb { x } - \pmb { b } | | ^ { 2 }$ . At each step we randomly choose one sample row ${ \pmb a } _ { i }$ of A. We adjust the current approximation $\pmb { x } _ { \pmb { k } }$ so the column $\pmb { x } _ { k + 1 }$ solves equation i of Ax = b:

$$
\pmb { x } _ { k + 1 } = \pmb { x } _ { k } + \frac { { b } _ { i } - { a } _ { i } \pmb { x } _ { k } } { | | \pmb { a } _ { i } | | ^ { 2 } } { \pmb { a } _ { i } ^ { \operatorname { T } } } \quad \mathrm { s o l v e s } \quad \pmb { a } _ { i } \pmb { x } _ { k + 1 } = { b } _ { i } .\tag{6}
$$

Kaczmarz introduced this method, thinking to cycle over and over from the first row of A to the last row. Strohmer and Vershynin changed to randomly chosen rows $\pmb { a _ { i } }$ (stochastic descent). They proved a form of exponential convergence to the solution of the least squares equation $A ^ { \mathrm { T } } A { \widehat { \mathbf { x } } } = A ^ { \mathrm { T } } b .$ A key point in the convergence shows up in Figure 9.5 : Fast start toward the best $\pmb { x } ^ { * }$ and oscillating finish. So stop early.

![](images/10a3f2a0e8911d505b9b287619657d4e66448e003e7fe53af652ef5f7328e4ca.jpg)

![](images/cc787dc18171217d13a603d6f0ebc82636310ca9ade6d528212fb2c9d16c9a93.jpg)  
Figure 9.5: The left figure shows a trajectory of stochastic gradient descent with two unknowns. The early iterations succeed but later iterations oscillate (as shown in the inset). On the right, the quadratic cost function decreases quickly at first and then fluctuates instead of converging. The four paths in that graph start from the same $\pmb { x _ { 0 } }$ with random choices of i as in equation (6).

## The Key Ideas of Backpropagation

For the present, we keep the idea simple and the notation simple. Our learning function F depends on the weights x (the matrices $\pmb { A } _ { 1 }$ to $A _ { L }$ and the vectors ${ \pmb b } _ { 1 }$ to $\pmb { b } _ { L }$ at layers 1 to L). The special simplifying feature is that each weight enters only one of the functions ${ \pmb F } _ { 1 }$ to ${ { \pmb { F } } _ { L } }$ in the chain. We will write $\pmb { x } _ { j }$ for the matrix $A _ { j }$ and vector $b _ { j }$ that enter layer j : $F _ { j } \ = \ \operatorname { R e L U } ( A _ { j } F _ { j - 1 } + b _ { j } )$ . ReLU is a famously simple function—see Figure 10.1. The chain rule for the derivative of the loss l with respect to the weights $\pmb { x } _ { j }$ in $\pmb { F } _ { j }$ is

$$
\frac { \partial \ell } { \partial x _ { j } } = \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F _ { L } } \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { L } } { \partial F _ { L - 1 } } \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { L - 1 } } { \partial F _ { L - 2 } } \cdot \cdot \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { j + 1 } } { \partial F _ { j } } \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { j } } { \partial x _ { j } }\tag{7}
$$

The key point is that this involves only the weights $\pmb { x _ { j } }$ to xL—not earlier weights. So the efficient computation starts with $\partial \ell / \partial F _ { L } \cdot \partial F _ { L } / \partial F _ { L - 1 }$ (involving $A _ { L }$ and $b _ { L } )$ Then the next step introduces only the weights $A _ { L - 1 }$ and $\pmb { b } _ { L - 1 }$ in $\pmb { x } _ { L - 1 }$ . We have every reason to choose the backward mode in this differentiation:

Computing $\pmb { \partial } \pmb { F } / \pmb { \partial } \pmb { x } _ { j }$ involves only the last weights from $\pmb { x _ { j } }$ to $\pmb { x } \pmb { L }$

Remember that the weights $\pmb { x } _ { j }$ include the matrix $A _ { j }$ and the vector $b _ { j }$ . The derivative of $F _ { j }$ with respect to $A _ { j }$ will need three components (this makes it a tensor). We will compute that derivative a few pages onward. Here we take the final step from the gradient of $\boldsymbol { F }$ to the gradient of the loss l. This step displays the second big reward for computing successive derivatives backward from the output.

Second key point: The loss $\pmb \ell ( \pmb x , \pmb v )$ is a scalar function of the output vector $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } )$ In the simplest case of a “square loss", that function is the squared length of the error :

$$
{ \mathrm { L o s s } } \colon \quad \ell ( x ) = ( w - F ( x , v ) ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } ( w - F ( x , v ) ) \quad { \mathrm { a n d } } \quad { \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F } } = 2 ( w - F ( x , v ) )\tag{8}
$$

Here w is the true (desired) output from the original training sample v, and $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } )$ is the computed output at layer L using the weights. The key point for this and other choices of l is that $\dot { \partial } \pmb { \ell } / \partial \pmb { F }$ is a vector. Then the backward chain of matrices $M _ { k } = \partial F _ { k } / \partial F _ { k - 1 }$ multiplies that vector. At every step this multiplication becomes a vector times a matrix!

(vector)(matrix)

not (matrix)(matrix)

$$
\frac { \partial \ell } { \partial x _ { j } } = \left( \left( \left( \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F } _ { } { M _ { L } } \right) { M _ { L - 1 } } \right) \ldots { M _ { j + 1 } } \right)\tag{9}
$$

Suppose for example that each matrix M is n by n. Then each vector-matrix step in the chain needs $\pmb { n } ^ { 2 }$ multiplications. If we choose the opposite order, with matrix-matrix steps, those would have $\pmb { n } ^ { \Im }$ multiplications. The backward order (L first) is very much faster.

## Summary

Reverse-mode differentiation is more efficient than forward-mode for two key reasons :

1. Most operations are vector-matrix multiplications (or vector-tensor)

2. Work will be reused for the remaining derivative computations.

Reverse mode differentiation achieves these efficiencies by rearranging the parentheses in the chain rule from left to right—from the loss function at the output back to layer $j \colon$

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \boxed { \mathrm { B a c k - P r o p } } \qquad \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial b _ { j } } = \left( \left( \left( \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F _ { L } } \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { L } } { \partial F _ { L - 1 } } \right) \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { L - 1 } } { \partial F _ { L - 2 } } \right) \cdot \cdot \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { j + 1 } } { \partial F _ { j } } \right) \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { j } } { \partial b _ { j } } } \end{array}\tag{10}
$$

Since $\partial \pmb { \ell } / \partial F _ { L }$ is a vector, our intermediate results are mostly vectors. So we are performing vector-matrix multiplications. When we compute $\partial \pmb { \ell } / \partial A _ { j }$ we cannot avoid a single vector-tensor contraction at the end—because A is a matrix. Section 10.2 computes that matrix $\partial { F _ { j } } / \partial { A _ { j } }$

Summary In addition to this speed-up for every operation, reverse-mode also requires fewer total operations because it allows us to reuse work in a remarkably elegant way. The key insight here is that the chain rule expressions for all derivatives at layers $j \leq k$ share the same prefix $\partial \pmb { \ell } / \partial F _ { \pmb { k } }$ . Since reverse-mode groups the terms from the left, it can reuse $\partial \ell / \partial F _ { k }$ in all computations for layers $j \leq k$ Backpropagation uses this optimization at every layer, resulting in the following algorithm :

```latex
To initialize, perform a forward pass through the chain using input v, and store
all intermediate results $F _ { j }$ . Also, compute $\partial \pmb { \ell } / \partial F _ { L }$ . Then,
for $j = L \to 1$ do
Compute and store
$\frac { \partial \ell } { \partial b _ { j } } = \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F _ { j } } \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { j } } { \partial b _ { j } } \quad \mathrm { a n d } \quad \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial A _ { j } } = \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F _ { j } } \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { j } } { \partial A _ { j } }$
$\mathbf { i } \mathbf { f } \ j \neq 1$ then
Compute $\partial \pmb \ell / \partial F _ { j - 1 }$ to be used at the next iteration :
$\frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F _ { j - 1 } } = \frac { \partial \ell } { \partial F _ { j } } \cdot \frac { \partial F _ { j } } { \partial F _ { j - 1 } }$
end if
end for
```

Thus backpropagation computes all the required derivatives in a single backward pass through the network. It requires only 2L vector-matrix multiplies and L vector-tensor contractions. To compute the same values, forward-mode differentiation would require $O ( L ^ { 2 } )$ matrix-tensor contractions and matrix-matrix multiplies. Backpropagation is more efficient by multiple orders of magnitude.

## Backpropagation in Keras and TensorFlow

Keras is one of the most popular machine learning libraries available today. It provides an simple interface to neural networks in Python, and it executes backpropagation internally using the TensorFlow library.

TensorFlow's implementation of backpropagation (see arXiv 1610.01178) is a significantly more complex and powerful generalization of the algorithm we described above. TensorFlow is designed to differentiate arbitrarily complex chains of functions. To do this, it constructs a computational graph representing the function to be differentiated. Then it inserts into that graph the operations representing the derivatives, usually working backwards from output to input. At that point, TensorFlow can perform the derivative computation for arbitrary input to the network. In the case where the network has the structure we describe above, TensorFlow's computational graph with derivatives would produce the same operations as our pseudocode.

The essay https://www.simplilearn.com/keras-vs-tensorflow-vs-pytorch-article may be useful in coding backbpropagation.

## Backpropagation on the Website

Coding for deep learning is discussed on the website https://math.mit.edu/linearalgebra. It has its own section on that site—we hope it allows you to create a learning function $\pmb { F } ( \pmb { x } , \pmb { v } )$ and test it on examples. Python and Julia and MATLAB are the website languages.

Derivatives of $A v + b$

We now compute the derivatives of each layer $F _ { j }$ with respect to the weights $A _ { j }$ and $\pmb { b } _ { j }$ introduced at that layer. The layer equation begins with the vector $\pmb { w } _ { j } = \pmb { A } _ { j } \pmb { v } _ { j - 1 } + \pmb { b } _ { j }$ and then computes ${ \pmb v } _ { j } = { \bf R e L U } ( { \pmb w } _ { j } )$ . We will take the easiest step first, and we drop the index j for now. Our function is ${ \pmb w } ( { \pmb A } , { \pmb b } ) = { \pmb A } { \pmb v } + { \pmb b }$

First of all, what is the derivative of the ith output ${ \pmb w } _ { i } = ( A { \pmb v } + { \pmb b } )$ with respect to the jth input $\mathbf { 6 } _ { j } : \mathbf { ? }$ An unusual question with an easy answer:

$$
{ \mathrm { I f } } i = j { \mathrm { , ~ } } { \mathrm { t h e n } } { \mathrm { ~ } } { \frac { \partial w _ { i } } { \partial b _ { i } } } = 1 \qquad { \mathrm { I f } } i \neq j { \mathrm { ~ t h e n ~ } } { \frac { \partial w _ { i } } { \partial b _ { j } } } = 0 { \mathrm { . } }\tag{11}
$$

This ${ \bf 1 } - { \bf 0 }$ alternative appears so often in mathematics that it has its own notation $\delta _ { i j }$

$$
\delta _ { i j } = { \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { { \mathrm { i f ~ } } i = j } \\ { 0 } & { { \mathrm { i f ~ } } i \neq j } \end{array} \right\} } = { \mathrm { t h e ~ e n t r i e s ~ i n ~ t h e ~ i d e n t i t y ~ m a t r i x ~ } } I
$$

Next, what is the derivative of the ith output ${ \pmb w } _ { \pmb i }$ with respect to the $( j , k )$ input $A _ { \ j \ k }$ ? Suddenly we have three indices $i , j , k$ .This indicates that our derivative is a tensor (more exactly, a 3-way tensor). Tensors are like matrices but with more indices—instead of a rectangle of numbers in a matrix, we now have a 3-dimensional "box of numbers".

Note We remark here that tensors are important, theoretically and also computationally. (They enter multilinear algebra.) But they are not trivial extensions of the idea of matrices. Even the rank of a tensor is not easy to define, and the SVD factorization (for example) fails. At least rank one seems straightforward: The tensor entries $T _ { i j k }$ have the product form $\pmb { a _ { i } b _ { j } c _ { k } }$ for three vectors a, b, c—like $\pmb { A _ { i } } b _ { j }$ for a rank one matrix.

Here is the tensor derivative formula when $\pmb { w } = \pmb { A v } + \pmb { b }$

$$
T _ { i j k } = \frac { \partial w _ { i } } { \partial A _ { j k } } = v _ { k } \delta _ { i j } \mathrm { a s } \mathrm { i n } T _ { 1 1 1 } = v _ { 1 } \mathrm { a n d } T _ { 1 2 2 } = 0 .\tag{12}
$$

This says: Row $j$ of A affects component i of $\pmb { w } = \pmb { A v } + \pmb { b }$ only if $j = i$ And when we do have $j = i$ the number $A _ { j k }$ in that row is multiplying ${ \boldsymbol { v } } _ { \boldsymbol { k } }$ . So the derivative of the output ${ \pmb w } _ { \pmb i }$ with respect to the matrix entry $A _ { j k }$ is just ${ \pmb v } _ { { \pmb k } }$ when $i = j$

Example There are six b's and a's in ${ \left[ \begin{array} { l } { w _ { 1 } } \\ { w _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] } ~ = ~ { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { b _ { 1 } } \\ { b _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] } ~ + ~ { \left[ \begin{array} { l } { a _ { 1 1 } v _ { 1 } + a _ { 1 2 } v _ { 2 } } \\ { a _ { 2 1 } v _ { 1 } ~ + a _ { 2 2 } v _ { 2 } } \end{array} \right] } .$

Derivatives of ${ \pmb w } _ { 1 } \frac { \partial w _ { 1 } } { \partial b _ { 1 } } = { \bf 1 } , \frac { \partial w _ { 1 } } { \partial b _ { 2 } } = { \bf 0 } , \frac { \partial w _ { 1 } } { \partial a _ { 1 1 } } = { \pmb v } _ { 1 } , \frac { \partial w _ { 1 } } { \partial a _ { 1 2 } } = { \pmb v } _ { 2 } , \frac { \partial w _ { 1 } } { \partial a _ { 2 1 } } = \frac { \partial w _ { 1 } } { \partial a _ { 2 2 } } = { \pmb 0 } .$

## Derivatives for Hidden Layers

Now suppose there is one hidden layer, so ${ \pmb { L } } = { \pmb { 2 } }$ The output is $\pmb { w } = \pmb { v } _ { L } = \pmb { v } _ { 2 }$ , the hidden layer contains ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 }$ , and the input is ${ \pmb v } _ { \bf 0 } = { \pmb v }$

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { v } _ { 1 } = \mathrm { R e L U } \left( \pmb { b } _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } \pmb { v } _ { 0 } \right) \quad \mathrm { a n d } \quad \pmb { w } = b _ { 2 } + A _ { 2 } \pmb { v } _ { 1 } = b _ { 2 } + A _ { 2 } \mathrm { R e L U } \left( b _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } \pmb { v } _ { 0 } \right) . } \end{array}
$$

Equations (11)–(12) give the derivatives of w with respect to the last weights $\pmb { b _ { 2 } }$ and $A _ { 2 }$ The function ReLU is absent at the output and v is ${ \pmb v } _ { 1 }$ . But the derivatives of w with respect to ${ \pmb b } _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 1 }$ do involve the nonlinear function ReLU acting on ${ \pmb { b } } _ { 1 } + { \pmb { A } } _ { 1 } { \pmb { v } } _ { 0 }$

So the derivatives in $\partial { \pmb w } / \partial A _ { 1 }$ need the chain rule $\partial f / \partial x = ( \partial f / \partial g ) ( \partial g / \partial x )$

$$
\mathrm { C h a i n \ r u l e } \quad \frac { \partial w } { \partial A _ { 1 } } = \frac { \partial \big [ A _ { 2 } \mathrm { R e L U } ( b _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } v _ { 0 } ) \big ] } { \partial A _ { 1 } } = A _ { 2 } \mathrm { R e L U } ^ { \prime } ( b _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } v _ { 0 } ) \frac { \partial ( b _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } v _ { 0 } ) } { \partial A _ { 1 } } .\tag{13}
$$

That chain rule has three factors. Starting from ${ \pmb v _ { 0 } }$ at layer $L - 2 = 0$ , the weights $\pmb { b } _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 1 }$ bring us toward the layer $L - 1 = 1$ . The derivatives of that step are exactly like (11) and (12). But the output of that partial step is not ${ \pmb v } _ { { \pmb L } - 1 }$ . To find that hidden layer we first have to apply ReLU. So the chain rule includes its derivative $\mathbf { R e L U } ^ { \prime }$ . Then the final step (to w) multiplies by the last weight matrix $A _ { 2 }$

The Problem Set extends these formulas to L layers. They could be useful. But with pooling and batch normalization, automatic differentiation seems to defeat hard coding.

Very important Notice how formulas like (13) go backwards from w to v. Automatic backpropagation will do this too. "Reverse mode" starts with the output.

## Details of the Derivatives $\scriptstyle \partial w / \partial A _ { 1 }$

We feel some responsibility to look more closely at equation (13). Its nonlinear part $\mathbf { R e L U } ^ { \prime }$ comes from the derivative of the nonlinear activation function. The usual choice is the ramp function ReLU $( x ) ~ = ~ ( x ) _ { + } ~ = ~ \mathrm { l i m i t i n g }$ case of an S-shaped sigmoid function

$$
\frac { d ( \mathrm { R e L U } ) } { d x } = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { \ x < 0 } \\ { 1 } & { \ x > 0 } \end{array} \right. \qquad \mathrm { R e L U } ^ { \prime } ( b _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } v _ { 0 } ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 0 } & { \quad \mathrm { w h e n } \ ( b _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } v _ { 0 } ) _ { i } < 0 } \\ { 1 } & { \quad \mathrm { w h e n } \ ( b _ { 1 } + A _ { 1 } v _ { 0 } ) _ { i } > 0 } \end{array} \right.
$$

![](images/a9ad98d41f047a32cbeb5749d28dd6f88e83bcec47bbaa4b21749450797d89f2.jpg)

![](images/2bd6c2fed462c2d635389c03bcd0ae7aeea7238c3a31f539df6a3c09f7033408.jpg)  
Figure 9.6: The graphs of ReLU and Leaky ReLU (two options for nonlinear activation).

Returning to formula (13), write A and b for the matrix $A _ { L - 1 }$ and the vector $\pmb { b } _ { L - 1 }$ that produce the last hidden layer. Then ReLU and $A _ { L }$ and ${ \pmb { b } } _ { { \pmb { L } } }$ produce the final output ${ \pmb w } = { \pmb v } _ { L }$ Our interest is in $\partial w / \partial A$ , the dependence of w on the next to last matrix of weights.

$$
\boxed { w = A _ { L } ( \mathrm { R e L U } ( A v + b ) ) + b _ { L } \quad \mathrm { a n d } \quad \frac { \partial w } { \partial A } = A _ { L } \mathrm { R e L U } ^ { \prime } ( A v + b ) \frac { \partial ( A v + b ) } { \partial A } }\tag{14}
$$

We think of ReLU as a diagonal matrix of ReLU functions acting component by component on $A v + b$ Then $J = \mathrm { R e L U } ^ { \prime } ( A \pmb { v } + \pmb { b } )$ is a diagonal matrix with 1's for positive components and $\mathbf { 0 } ^ { \bullet } \mathbf { s }$ for negative components. (Don't ask about the derivative of ReLU at 0) :

$$
{ \pmb w } = A _ { L } \operatorname { R e L U } \left( { \pmb A } { \pmb v } + { \pmb b } \right) \quad \mathrm { a n d } \quad \frac { \partial { \pmb w } } { \partial { \pmb A } } = A _ { L } J \frac { \partial ( { \pmb A } { \pmb v } + { \pmb b } ) } { \partial { \pmb A } }\tag{15}
$$

We know every component $( v _ { k }$ or zero) of the third factor from the derivatives in (11)(12).

When the sigmoid function $\scriptstyle \mathbf { R e L U } _ { \mathbf { a } }$ replaces the ReLU function, the diagonal matrix $J = \mathrm { R e L U } _ { a } ^ { \prime } ( A \pmb { v } + \pmb { b } )$ no longer contains 1's and $\mathbf { 0 ^ { \circ } s }$ Now we evaluate the derivative $d R _ { a } / d x$ at each component of $A v + b$

In practice, backpropagation finds the derivatives with respect to all $A { \boldsymbol { \mathsf { s } } }$ and ${ \pmb { b } } \mathbf { \dot { s } } .$ It creates those derivatives automatically and very effectively.
